## Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1840s–1860s)

### Jurisdiction Overview

- **Formed:** 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties
- **County seat:** Pottsville
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominant from the 1820s; Reading Railroad (chartered 1833); also agriculture, iron furnaces, and trade
- **Ethnic composition:** Welsh, Irish (especially post-1845 Famine), English, German miners and laborers; earlier Pennsylvania Dutch farming families
- **Key events:** Rapid coal industrialization 1840s–1850s; heavy Irish immigration; Civil War (1861–1865)

---

### Available Record Types

#### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **No statewide civil registration** existed for births or deaths during the 1840s–1860s — Pennsylvania's statewide system did not begin until 1906.
- **Marriage records** exist at the county level:
  - [Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) (FamilySearch collection 1571957)
  - [Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) (FamilySearch collection 1502909)
- **Substitutes for births/deaths:** Church registers and 1850/1860 census mortality schedules

#### Church Records
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** Schuylkill County **Lutheran Church Records, 1840–1875** (imageGroupNumber 004288771) — 198 images; in English and German; **0% indexed, must be browsed page by page**
- **Denominations present:** Welsh Calvinist Methodist, Roman Catholic, German Lutheran, German Reformed, Methodist Episcopal, Presbyterian, Episcopal
- **Physical holdings:** Historical Society of Schuylkill County (Pottsville); Diocese of Allentown archives (Catholic records); individual synod/presbytery archives

#### Census Records
- **1850 and 1860 federal censuses:** FamilySearch volume 007621224 — 412 images, **96% name-indexed and full-text searchable** — the most accessible record class for this period
- Also on Ancestry: [1850 U.S. Federal Census — Schuylkill County](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/) (collection 1276)
- **Mortality schedules** (1850 and 1860) list persons who died in the year before each census — key substitute for missing death records
- **1840 census** exists but names only head of household for most entries

#### Probate and Court Records
- **FamilySearch volume:** Schuylkill County **Probate Records, 1845–1880** (imageGroupNumber 004812990) — 286 images; **4% indexed; full-text searchable** but mostly browse-only
- **Statewide:** [Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) (collection 1999196) — 3.2 million images, **0% indexed**, browse-only
- **Record types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions, orphans' court
- **Naturalization records:** Pre-1906 declarations of intention and petitions were filed in the Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas — critical for immigrant miners

#### Land Records
- Pennsylvania is a **metes-and-bounds (state-land) state** — no federal BLM patents
- **Warrants and patents:** Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg)
- **Deed transfers:** Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds (Pottsville) — **not yet digitized online**

#### Military Records
- **Mexican-American War (1846–1848)** and **Civil War (1861–1865)**
- Types: Union service records, pension files, draft registrations (NARA RG 94), state muster rolls and bounty records (Pennsylvania State Archives)
- Civil War pensions and some service records indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch; full pension files require a NARA order

#### Cemetery Records
- **Major cemeteries:** Charles Baber Cemetery (Pottsville), St. Patrick's Roman Catholic Cemetery, and numerous mining-town church cemeteries
- **Online:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves have indexed many Schuylkill County cemeteries
- **Physical records:** Sexton records at individual churches/cemeteries

#### Newspaper Records
- **The Miners' Journal** (Pottsville, est. 1825) — primary source for obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices, and mining news
- **Obituaries often name place of origin** for immigrant miners (e.g., "a native of County Mayo" or "from Merthyr Tydfil") — invaluable for tracing immigrant origins
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Library, Historical Society of Schuylkill County, Pottsville Free Public Library (microfilm); partial digitization at [Chronicling America](https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/)

#### Immigration Records
- **Primary ports:** Philadelphia (main), New York (Castle Garden), Baltimore
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists (Philadelphia manifests often include specific parish/townland of origin in the "last legal residence" column); naturalization petitions at the county courthouse
- **Where held:** NARA / Ancestry / FamilySearch for passenger lists; Schuylkill County Courthouse for naturalizations

#### Tax Records
- Annual county property tax assessment books (real and personal property)
- **Critical substitutes** for intercensal years (1841–1849, 1851–1859, 1861–1869) and for the limited 1840 census
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Courthouse and/or Pennsylvania State Archives — **not digitized online**

#### Coal Mining Company Records *(Unique to this region)*
- Payroll ledgers, employment records, accident reports for anthracite operators
- **Where held:** Historical Society of Schuylkill County; Eleutherian Mills-Hagley Foundation — not in any online genealogy database

---

### Repository Guide

#### Online
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 1850–1860 Census (vol. 007621224, 96% indexed); Probate 1845–1880 (vol. 004812990, 4%/full-text); Lutheran Church Records 1840–1875 (vol. 004288771, browse-only); PA Probate 1683–1994 (collection 1999196); PA Civil Marriages (1571957); PA Compiled Marriages (1502909) | Free |
| Ancestry | 1850 Federal Census — Schuylkill Co. ([collection 1276](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/)); PA Tax & Exoneration Lists 1768–1801 ([collection 7667](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7667/)) | Subscription |
| Chronicling America (Library of Congress) | Miners' Journal digitized issues | Free |

#### Physical
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville | Deed books, probate originals, marriage licenses, naturalization records, court minute books |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | State land warrants/patents, military bounty records, state-level records |
| Historical Society of Schuylkill County, Pottsville | Local histories, newspapers, genealogical files, mining company records, cemetery transcriptions |
| Diocese of Allentown Archives | Roman Catholic sacramental registers |
| NARA, Philadelphia region | Federal census originals, naturalization records, military pension files |

---

### Records NOT Yet Online
- Deed and mortgage books (Recorder of Deeds)
- County tax assessment books
- Court minute books and naturalization records (county courthouse)
- Roman Catholic sacramental registers
- Welsh Calvinist Methodist, German Reformed, and most non-Lutheran church registers
- Coal mining company employment/payroll records
- Most Miners' Journal issues (microfilm locally; partial digitization at Chronicling America)

---

### Key Research Tips

1. **No civil birth/death registration in this period.** Use church registers and census mortality schedules as substitutes.
2. **Start with the 1850 and 1860 censuses** — 96% indexed and full-text searchable on FamilySearch. Establishes family composition, ages, birthplaces, and neighbors.
3. **Lutheran church records require page-by-page browsing** and portions are in German — plan for a German-language reader.
4. **Naturalization records are critical for immigrant families.** Welsh, Irish, and German miners filed declarations and petitions in the Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas — may be the only document linking a person to their home country. Pre-1906 naturalization could be filed in any court of record.
5. **The Miners' Journal obituaries often name Irish or Welsh parishes of origin** — check the obit column for the year of death when civil and church records fail.
6. **Tax assessment books fill the intercensal gaps** — annual lists track arrival, movement, and departure year by year.
7. **Coal mining creates unique record classes** not found in civil repositories — the Historical Society of Schuylkill County is the best starting point.
8. **Philadelphia passenger manifests** (1840s–1860s) list all passengers including infants; the "last legal residence" column often names the specific townland or parish of origin.

# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1840s–1860s)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** 1811, carved from Berks and Northampton counties
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Commonwealth of Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the population tool for this place and period; no verified figure can be stated
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining was the dominant industry from the 1820s onward. The Reading Railroad (chartered 1833) served the region and generated occupational records. Agriculture, iron furnaces, and trade supplemented coal
- **Ethnic composition:** Large influxes of Welsh, Irish (especially post-1845 Famine), English, and German miners and laborers settled the anthracite region in this period. Earlier German and Pennsylvania Dutch farming families predated the mining boom
- **Religious denominations:** Welsh Calvinist Methodist (Calvinistic Methodists), Welsh Congregational, Roman Catholic (for Irish immigrants), German Lutheran, German Reformed, Episcopal, Methodist Episcopal, and Presbyterian congregations were all established in this period
- **Key historical events:** Rapid industrialization of the coal region in the 1840s–1850s; heavy Irish immigration post-1845; the Civil War (1861–1865) produced draft, service, and pension records

## Boundary changes

Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties and its boundaries were stable throughout the 1840s–1860s target period. No boundary change during the target window splits records across jurisdictions; a single-county search is sufficient.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date and level:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records all redirected to a generic page and did not return the state-specific article; no registration date or level can be cited from that page. It is broadly known from the general genealogy article returned that many U.S. states did not require statewide registration until the early 1900s. Given that Pennsylvania statewide civil registration is generally known to have started in 1906 (the date returned in the Pennsylvania Death Certificates collection: "1906–1968"), **no statewide civil vital registration was in place during the 1840s–1860s target period**. The Pennsylvania Civil Marriages collection returned by `collections_search` (id: 1571957, "Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950") and the Compiled Marriages collection (id: 1502909, "Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900") indicate that some marriage records exist for this period, but those are compiled or county-level records, not statewide civil registration.
- **What exists:** County-level marriage records may exist; births and deaths were not subject to statewide civil registration during this window. Church records (see below) are the primary substitute for births and deaths
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Courthouse (Pottsville) for any county marriage licenses. The collections above are also accessible on FamilySearch:
  - "Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950" — [FamilySearch collection 1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957)
  - "Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900" — [FamilySearch collection 1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909)
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth or death registration during the 1840s–1860s; rely on church records and census mortality schedules
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptisms, burials, and marriage registers (see Church records below); 1850 and 1860 mortality schedules within the federal census

### Church records

- **What exists:** A FamilySearch digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 004288771) covers Schuylkill County **Lutheran Church Records, 1840–1875**, with 198 images. This volume is in English and German, has **0% name-indexed and is not full-text searchable** — it must be browsed image by image, and the researcher must be able to read German for the German-language portions
- The FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" (id: SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, dates 1708–1985) also appears in the tool results — this collection is flagged as a synthetic test fixture in the tool output and should be treated with caution; verify its actual existence and content directly at [FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) before relying on it
- **Denominations present:** Welsh Calvinist Methodist, Roman Catholic, German Lutheran, German Reformed, Methodist Episcopal, Presbyterian, Episcopal — all active in the county during the target period
- **Where held:** FamilySearch has at minimum the Lutheran volume noted above. Other denominational records may be held at local parishes, diocesan archives (the Diocese of Allentown for Catholic records), and the Historical Society of Schuylkill County (Pottsville)
- **Language:** Lutheran records in this volume are in English and German. Welsh Calvinist Methodist registers were sometimes kept in Welsh

**Digitization level:** Browse-only images (Lutheran volume, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable). Bring together with a German reader for German-language entries.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** The 1850 and 1860 federal censuses are available for Schuylkill County. A FamilySearch digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 007621224) covers Schuylkill County's **U.S. Federal Census, 1850–1860**, with 412 images, **96% name-indexed and full-text searchable** — this is among the most accessible record classes for this place and period
- The 1840 federal census also exists for Schuylkill County but is less informative (it does not name individuals beyond the head of household for most entries); no separate volume entry appeared for 1840 in tool results
- Additionally, Ancestry.com hosts the **1850 United States Federal Census — Schuylkill County** as a curated external collection: [Ancestry collection 1276](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/)
- **Mortality schedules:** The 1850 and 1860 mortality schedules (listing people who died in the year preceding each census) are part of the decennial census records and are a key substitute for missing death registration
- **State census:** No Pennsylvania state census existed during this period
- **Access:** The FamilySearch 1850–1860 volume is indexed at 96% and full-text searchable — search by name directly on FamilySearch

**Digitization level:** Indexed + images (FamilySearch volume 007621224, 96% indexed, full-text searchable)

### Probate and court records

- **What exists:** A FamilySearch digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 004812990) covers Schuylkill County **Probate Records, 1845–1880**, with 286 images. It is **4% name-indexed and full-text searchable** — the vast majority must be browsed image by image, though full-text search may help locate some entries
- The broader FamilySearch statewide collection "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (id: 1999196) includes 3,200,560 images but **0 indexed records** — browse-only at the statewide level as well, at [FamilySearch collection 1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196)
- **Types:** Wills (testate estates), administrations (intestate), guardianships, inventories, and estate distributions. Wills and administrations are the primary series; also look for orphans' court records, which handled guardianship of minor children
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Courthouse (Register of Wills, Pottsville); FamilySearch has the digitized volume noted above
- **Naturalization records:** Pre-1906 declarations of intention and petitions for naturalization were filed in any Pennsylvania court of record — this includes the Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas. These are a critical source for immigrant miners of the 1840s–1860s and are typically held in the county courthouse records

**Digitization level:** Mostly browse-only images (4% indexed; full-text search available but not comprehensive)

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Pennsylvania is a metes-and-bounds (state-land) state; there are no federal BLM land patents for Schuylkill County
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania granted land through the Land Office of Pennsylvania; the original warrants and patents are held by the Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg). County deed transfers after original grant are held at the Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds (Pottsville)
- **Types:** Deed books (grantor/grantee), mortgages, land warrants and patents from the state. Tax records (see Tax records below) also document land ownership
- **Date range:** Deed records run from county formation (1811) forward
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds (Pottsville) for deeds; Pennsylvania State Archives for warrants and patents. No digitized FamilySearch volume for Schuylkill County deed records appeared in tool results — this is a gap

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848); Civil War (1861–1865) — both generated records for Schuylkill County men
- **Civil War record types:** Union service records (NARA, Record Group 94), pension files (NARA), draft registration records (Provost Marshal records, NARA), and state bounty records (Pennsylvania State Archives)
- **Where held:** NARA (federal service and pension records); Pennsylvania State Archives (state muster rolls, bounty records); the Historical Society of Schuylkill County may hold local rosters and regimental histories
- **Online access:** Civil War pension files and some service records are indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch; full pension files require a NARA order

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Charles Baber Cemetery (Pottsville), St. Patrick's Roman Catholic Cemetery, and numerous small mining-town church cemeteries throughout the county
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves have indexed many Schuylkill County cemeteries; search at findagrave.com. No FamilySearch curated link to a Schuylkill County FindAGrave collection appeared in tool results for this period, but the general databases are searchable online
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are held at individual churches and cemeteries

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The Miners' Journal (Pottsville) began publication in 1825 and ran continuously through this period — it is the primary source for obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices (sheriff's sales, estate notices), and mining news. Other papers served specific immigrant communities
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Library (Harrisburg), Historical Society of Schuylkill County, and Pottsville Free Public Library hold microfilm runs. Some issues are digitized through Chronicling America (Library of Congress) and the Pennsylvania Newspaper Archive
- **Content value:** Obituaries in the Miners' Journal often name place of origin for immigrant miners — invaluable for tracing back to Ireland, Wales, or Germany

### Immigration/emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was the primary port of entry for immigrants to Schuylkill County in the 1840s–1860s, with some arriving via New York (Castle Garden, not yet Ellis Island) or Baltimore
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists (NARA, available on Ancestry and FamilySearch for Philadelphia and New York arrivals); declarations of intention and naturalization petitions filed in Schuylkill County courts; and, for post-1862 arrivals, Civil War-era alien registrations
- **Where held:** Passenger lists: NARA / online databases. Naturalization papers: Schuylkill County Courthouse
- **Content note:** Philadelphia arrival manifests from the 1840s–1860s list every person aboard including infants. When researching an immigrant family, examine the full manifest page — siblings and parents traveling together are all recorded, sometimes with the specific townland or parish of origin written in the "last legal residence" column

### Tax records

- **Types:** County property tax (real and personal property) assessment books, held at the Schuylkill County Courthouse and potentially at the Pennsylvania State Archives
- **Date range:** Assessment records run from county formation; annual lists exist through the target period
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are critical substitutes for the 1840 census (which does not name individuals below head of household) and for the intercensal years (1841–1849, 1851–1859, 1861–1869). A man's appearance or disappearance on the tax rolls tracks his residence year by year

- **Coal mining company records:** Because the anthracite industry dominated the county, company employment records, payroll ledgers, and accident reports exist for some operators. The Reading Company records and records of other coal firms may be held at the Historical Society of Schuylkill County or the Eleutherian Mills-Hagley Foundation. These are not in any FamilySearch database returned by tools but are unique to this region
- **School records:** Township school boards kept enrollment records; survival is uneven. The Pennsylvania State Archives holds some county superintendents' reports

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pulaski County, Kentucky (1840-1880)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** December 10, 1798, from Lincoln County and Green County
- **County seat:** Somerset
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Kentucky (state)
- **Population during period:** Not returned by place_population tool — data gap.
- **Economy:** Subsistence agriculture (tobacco, grain); timber; limited manufacturing in Somerset.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Scots-Irish and English; small free Black population; no large immigrant industrial workforce.
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist (largest), Methodist, Presbyterian. Roman Catholic presence minimal.
- **Key historical events:** Sharp Civil War division; Battle of Mill Springs (Jan 1862) partly in Pulaski County. Courthouse disasters 1838 and 1871.

## Boundary changes
- Formed 1798 from Lincoln and Green counties. Pre-1798 records held by Lincoln County and Green County.
- Boundaries stable throughout 1840-1880 target period.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **County-level births/deaths:** 1853-1862, 1874-1878 (minimal compliance). Statewide registration began 1911. Entire target window is pre-statewide.
- **Marriages:** From county formation (1799); available online at FamilySearch through 1871.
- **Primary repositories:** Pulaski County Courthouse; KDLA (microfilm); FamilySearch (marriage bonds 1799-1871).
- **Gaps:** No civil births/deaths for 1840-1852, 1863-1873, 1879-1892. Records lost in 1838 and 1871 courthouse disasters.
- **Substitutes:** Church records, mortality schedules, cemetery inscriptions, family bibles.

### Church records
- **Denominations:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian (largest before 1900 in Kentucky).
- **Online:** FamilySearch — Kentucky Church Records 1818-1995 (index + images, incomplete); Kentucky Births and Christenings 1839-1960 (index only); Kentucky Marriages 1785-1979 (index only); Kentucky Deaths and Burials 1843-1970 (index only).
- **Physical:** Pulaski County Historical Society (most comprehensive county collection); FamilySearch Library microfilm; Kentucky Historical Society; individual active congregations.
- **Denominational archives:** Southern Baptist Historical Library (Nashville); Methodist conference archives; Presbyterian Historical Society (Philadelphia).

### Census records
- **Federal:** 1840, 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880 — full target window covered.
- **Mortality schedules:** 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880 — critical death substitutes.
- **Slave schedules:** 1850, 1860 — enslaved persons listed by age/sex under slaveholder's name.
- **Agricultural/manufacturing schedules:** 1850, 1860, 1870 — valuable for farmers and tradespeople.
- **State census:** Kentucky held no separate state census in this period.
- **Access:** Indexed + images on Ancestry and FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships, estate distributions.
- **Start dates:** Probate from 1801; court records from 1799.
- **Online:** Will books 1801-1929 digitized on FamilySearch.
- **Physical:** Pulaski County Courthouse; KDLA microfilm.

### Land records
- **System:** State-land state (not federal public-land). All grants from Virginia government (pre-1792) or Kentucky Land Office (post-1792).
- **Online:** FamilySearch — Kentucky Land Office warrants/surveys/grants/patents 1700-1955. Ancestry — Kentucky land grants.
- **County deeds:** Deed books from 1799 at Pulaski County Courthouse and KDLA microfilm.
- **Repositories:** Kentucky Land Office, Frankfort; Kentucky Historical Society; Pulaski County Courthouse.

### Military records
- **Conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846-1848); Civil War (1861-1865); post-war pension period.
- **Civil War:** Both Union (NARA RG 94) and Confederate (NARA RG 109; Kentucky State Archives for state pension files).
- **Online:** Fold3 (subscription) for digitized NARA records; Ancestry.

### Cemetery records
- **Online:** Find A Grave; Pulaski County Historical Society cemetery surveys.
- **Physical:** Church sexton records; rural family cemeteries (often no formal records).

### Newspaper records
- **Online:** Newspapers.com — check for Somerset-area coverage.
- **Value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices (estate settlements, land sales).

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** Predominantly native-born population; large-scale foreign immigration not a feature.
- **Naturalizations (pre-1906):** Filed in any court of record — county circuit court or district court.
- **Internal migration:** Virginia land grants and parent-county records document arrivals from Virginia and Carolinas.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Annual county property tax lists (personal property and real estate) from 1799.
- **Substitute value:** Fills gap years between censuses and compensates for missing civil vital records.
- **Access:** Some digitized on Ancestry; full run at KDLA microfilm and Pulaski County Courthouse.

### Other record types
- **Freedmen's Bureau (post-1865):** NARA RG 105, indexed on FamilySearch — labor contracts, marriage registers, ration records for African American families.
- **County histories:** Check WorldCat and Kentucky Historical Society.
- **School records:** KDLA; limited coverage expected.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Marriage bonds 1799-1871; will books 1801-1929; church records 1818-1995; births/christenings, marriages, deaths indexes; land office records 1700-1955; Freedmen's Bureau; federal census | Free |
| Ancestry (ancestry.com) | Federal census; tax lists; land grants; vital indexes | Subscription |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military service records and pension files | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery memorials | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Military records, Freedmen's Bureau, federal court records | Free/fee for copies |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Pulaski County Courthouse, 100 N. Main St. #208, Somerset, KY 42502 | Marriage bonds 1799+; deeds 1799+; court orders 1799+; probate 1801+ | In-person / county clerk |
| Pulaski County Historical Society, Somerset, KY | Church records (most comprehensive); cemetery surveys; surname vertical files | In-person |
| KDLA, Frankfort, KY | Microfilmed county records; pre-1911 birth/death records | In-person; kdla.ky.gov |
| Kentucky Land Office, Frankfort, KY | Grants, warrants, surveys, patents | In-person; some at FamilySearch |
| Kentucky Historical Society, Frankfort, KY | Manuscripts; land records; county histories | In-person |
| NARA, Atlanta Region / Washington DC | Federal military, pension, Freedmen's Bureau, federal court | In-person or mail; many on Ancestry/Fold3 |

## Records NOT online
- County deed books (person-to-person transactions): likely physical/microfilm at KDLA and courthouse.
- County court minute books: physical at courthouse and KDLA microfilm.
- Full run of county tax lists: some on Ancestry; complete run at KDLA.
- Probate records beyond will books (administrations, inventories, guardianships): physical at courthouse and KDLA microfilm.
- Individual church congregation records not captured in statewide collections: Pulaski County Historical Society and active congregations.

## Known record losses
A courthouse disaster in 1838 and another in 1871 destroyed some records. Marriage bonds are confirmed available through 1871, suggesting the 1871 disaster affected records at or near that date. The exact records lost in each event are not fully itemized in available sources. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy

## Research tips
- Civil birth and death registration barely existed during 1840-1880. Church records, mortality schedules, and cemetery inscriptions are the primary vital substitutes.
- Marriage bonds are the strongest vital record series — available from 1799, online through 1871.
- Will books 1801-1929 are digitized on FamilySearch.
- Pre-1798 records go to Lincoln County and Green County.
- Both Union and Confederate military records apply for Civil War research.
- Kentucky is a state-land state — all grants from Virginia government or Kentucky Land Office, not the BLM GLO.
- Search neighboring counties (Laurel, Rockcastle, Lincoln, Casey, Russell, Wayne, McCreary) for border families.
- Freedmen's Bureau records (NARA RG 105, indexed on FamilySearch) are essential for post-1865 African American research.

| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Marriage bonds 1799-1871; will books 1801-1929; church records 1818-1995; births/christenings, marriages, deaths indexes; land office records 1700-1955; Freedmen's Bureau; federal census | Free |
| Ancestry (ancestry.com) | Federal census; tax lists; land grants; vital indexes | Subscription |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military service records and pension files | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery memorials | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Military records, Freedmen's Bureau, federal court records | Free/fee for copies |

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Pulaski County Courthouse, 100 N. Main St. #208, Somerset, KY 42502 | Marriage bonds 1799+; deeds 1799+; court orders 1799+; probate 1801+ | In-person / county clerk |
| Pulaski County Historical Society, Somerset, KY | Church records (most comprehensive); cemetery surveys; surname vertical files | In-person |
| KDLA, Frankfort, KY | Microfilmed county records; pre-1911 birth/death records | In-person; kdla.ky.gov |
| Kentucky Land Office, Frankfort, KY | Grants, warrants, surveys, patents | In-person; some at FamilySearch |
| Kentucky Historical Society, Frankfort, KY | Manuscripts; land records; county histories | In-person |
| NARA, Atlanta Region / Washington DC | Federal military, pension, Freedmen's Bureau, federal court | In-person or mail; many on Ancestry/Fold3 |

- County deed books (person-to-person transactions): likely physical/microfilm at KDLA and courthouse.
- County court minute books: physical at courthouse and KDLA microfilm.
- Full run of county tax lists: some on Ancestry; complete run at KDLA.
- Probate records beyond will books (administrations, inventories, guardianships): physical at courthouse and KDLA microfilm.

A courthouse disaster in 1838 and another in 1871 destroyed some records. Marriage bonds are confirmed available through 1871, suggesting the 1871 disaster affected records at or near that date. The exact records lost in each event are not fully itemized in available sources. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy

- Will books 1801-1929 are digitized on FamilySearch.

- Both Union and Confederate military records apply for Civil War research.
- Kentucky is a state-land state — all grants from Virginia government or Kentucky Land Office, not the BLM GLO.
- Search neighboring counties (Laurel, Rockcastle, Lincoln, Casey, Russell, Wayne, McCreary) for border families.
- Freedmen's Bureau records (NARA RG 105, indexed on FamilySearch) are essential for post-1865 African American research.

- **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (Aix-en-Provence, France)** – French colonial records predating the Spanish period.
- **FamilySearch** – Marriage, probate, land, and church record collections from 1803 onward; some browse-only digitized volumes of territorial court and Washington County records (1803–1820).

**Important caveats:**
- No civil registration of births or deaths existed during this period.
- **Church records** are the only source for births, marriages, and deaths — Catholic registers in Mobile (going back to the French colonial era) and scattered Methodist and Baptist circuit records in the interior.

**Recommended next step:** Narrow down which part of Alabama your ancestor lived in (Mobile coastal area vs. interior) and which specific early county, so research can be targeted to the right courthouse, land office, and church affiliation.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (Territorial Era, ca. 1780–1820)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Alabama did not become a state until December 14, 1819. Around 1800, the region was part of the **Mississippi Territory** (established April 7, 1798). In 1817 the eastern portion became the separate **Alabama Territory**, which lasted until statehood.
- **County seat / administrative center:** The territorial capital was Washington, MS. The major center in present-day Alabama was **Mobile**, held by Spain until 1813.
- **Parent jurisdictions:** Mississippi Territory (1798–1817) → Alabama Territory (1817–1819) → State of Alabama (1819–). For Mobile: France (1702–1763) → Britain (1763–1780) → Spain (1780–1813) → United States.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, frontier trade, deerskin trade, early cotton planting. Mobile served as port and commercial hub.
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek, Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw nations; Anglo-American settlers from Carolinas/Virginia/Georgia; French Creole families in Mobile; Spanish colonial settlers; enslaved African Americans.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (Mobile area); Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian circuits in the interior.
- **Key historical events:** Mississippi Territory established (1798); U.S. seizure of Mobile from Spain (1813); Creek War (1813–1814); Alabama Territory formed (1817); statehood (1819).

## Boundary changes
- Before 1798: No organized American territory. Interior records fall under Georgia's western land claims; Mobile under Spanish administration.
- 1798–1817: Present-day Alabama was the eastern half of the **Mississippi Territory**.
- 1817–1819: **Alabama Territory** separated from Mississippi Territory.
- After 1819: State of Alabama.
- Key consequence: Records created before 1817 are Mississippi Territory records. Search Mississippi Territory collections alongside Alabama ones — they form one continuous research trail.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration of births or deaths existed in the territorial era. Marriage records begin at the county level from 1809.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch collection 'Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950' (id: 1598408) — 612,345 records, indexed + images.
- **Where held:** ADAH; county probate courts.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the only source for vital events before any civil system.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mobile, French-era through Spanish-era); Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian (interior).
- **Where held:** Diocese of Mobile archives; Mobile Municipal Archives (microfilm of French records); Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence (French originals); Archivo General de Indias, Seville, with copies at Library of Congress (Spanish originals). FamilySearch collection 'Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950' (id: 1986396) — 156,789 records, indexed + images.
- **Language:** French (pre-1763), Spanish (1780–1813), English.

### Census records
- **Territorial censuses:** 1801, 1805, 1808, 1810 — held at ADAH; not systematically digitized online.
- **Federal census:** 1810 (Mississippi Territory) and 1820 (State of Alabama) are the relevant federal enumerations.
- **Compiled index:** 'Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890' (id: 2016756) — 287,634 records, indexed, no images. Also: 'Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890' (id: 1927171) — 198,340 records, indexed, no images.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, territorial court proceedings.
- **Browse-only volumes:** FamilySearch vol. 004512889 — Alabama territorial court and land records, 1808–1819, 214 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable. Vol. 004512890 — Washington County deed and probate, 1803–1820, 96 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable.
- **Indexed collection:** 'Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985' (id: 1537764) — 438,210 records, indexed + images.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular survey. Alabama is a federal-land state.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** U.S. General Land Office; Huntsville Land Office opened 1811.
- **Where held:** BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) for patents; NARA for case files; ADAH for claims files. 'Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907' (id: 1919694) — 312,450 records, indexed + images — covers territorial-era Alabama land records before 1817.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War (1813–1814); War of 1812; territorial militia; Spanish colonial militia (Mobile).
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C. and Atlanta); Fold3 (fold3.com); ADAH for state militia records.

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) — sparse pre-1820 coverage.
- **Physical records:** Diocese of Mobile archives for Catholic cemeteries; interior Protestant burials largely unrecorded.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Mobile Centinel (founded 1811) is among the earliest; interior had very limited publishing before statehood.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com; ADAH microfilm; Library of Congress Chronicling America.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile; New Orleans.
- **Where held:** NARA (post-1820 passenger lists); Archivo General de Indias (Spanish colonial Mobile arrivals); Library of Congress.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial and county property and poll tax lists.
- **Where held:** ADAH; some microfilm at FamilySearch.
- **Substitute value:** Critical substitute for missing census years; places a person in a specific county annually.

### Other record types
- Spanish colonial records for Mobile District (1780–1813): Archivo General de Indias (Seville); copies at Library of Congress.
- French colonial records for Mobile (1702–1763): Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives.
- Territorial court minute books: document road assignments, poor relief, appointments — naming ordinary people in no other series.
- County and local histories: ADAH and university libraries.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 8 indexed collections (see above) + 3 browse-only volumes | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records | Subscription |
| NARA | National Archives holdings | Free (in-person) / some online |
| BLM GLO | Federal land patents | Free |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| ADAH, Montgomery, AL | Territorial censuses; tax lists; state/county records | In-person; archives.alabama.gov |
| NARA Southeast, Atlanta, GA | Federal territorial court and land records | In-person or NARA request |
| NARA, Washington, D.C. | Military service, pension, bounty land, GLO records | In-person, mail, or online |
| Mobile Municipal Archives | French colonial microfilm; early county records | In-person |
| Diocese of Mobile Archives | Catholic parish registers including pre-1813 records | In-person or written request |
| Library of Congress | Spanish colonial record copies; early maps/newspapers | In-person; loc.gov |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville | Original Spanish colonial records for Mobile District | In-person or written request |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence | French colonial records for Mobile | In-person or written request |
| County probate courts | Earliest deed books, probate files, court minutes | In-person or mail |

## Records NOT online
- Territorial censuses 1801, 1805, 1808 (ADAH)
- Spanish colonial census and church registers for Mobile District (Seville / LoC / Mobile Municipal Archives)
- French colonial records for Mobile (Aix-en-Provence / Mobile Municipal Archives)
- County court minute books for Washington County and earliest counties (browse-only at best)
- Early county tax lists (ADAH)
- Interior Protestant church registers (scattered or lost)

## Known record losses
No specific record destruction event for Alabama territorial-era records was confirmed by tool results in this survey. Sparse digitization results reflect coverage gaps, not confirmed destruction.

## Research tips
- Work Mississippi Territory and Alabama collections in parallel — records before 1817 are filed under the Territory.
- Mobile requires a separate colonial research track in French, Spanish, and English archives.
- Alabama is a federal-land state — search BLM GLO for patents, then request NARA case files for witness names.
- Use territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808) at ADAH as your earliest substitutes for the federal census.
- Tax lists fill annual gaps between censuses.
- Creek War pension and bounty land files at NARA name wives and children — use them as vital record substitutes.
- Church records are the only vital record source for this period.

The most useful American records — territorial censuses from 1801, 1805, and 1808; early county court and deed books; and the earliest land grant files — are held at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History** in Montgomery and at **NARA's Southeast facility in Atlanta**. No civil registration of births or deaths existed at all during this period; **church records** — Catholic registers in Mobile going back to the French colonial era, and scattered Methodist and Baptist circuit records in the interior — are the only source for births, marriages, and deaths. Federal land patent records are searchable free online at the BLM General Land Office website, but the underlying case files (which name witnesses and neighbors) must be requested from NARA. Several FamilySearch collections covering marriage, probate, land, and church records from 1803 onward are freely searchable online, and two digitized volumes of territorial court and Washington County records from 1803–1820 are available as browse-only images.

The next step is to narrow down which part of Alabama your ancestor was in — Mobile area or interior — and which specific county, so that a targeted research plan can identify the right county courthouse, land office, and church affiliation for that location.

added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (Territorial Era, ca. 1780–1820)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Alabama did not become a state until December 14, 1819. Around 1800, the region was part of the **Mississippi Territory** (established April 7, 1798). In 1817 the eastern portion became the separate **Alabama Territory**, which lasted until statehood.
- **County seat / administrative center:** The territorial capital was Washington, MS. The major center in present-day Alabama was **Mobile**, held by Spain until 1813.
- **Parent jurisdictions:** Mississippi Territory (1798–1817) → Alabama Territory (1817–1819) → State of Alabama (1819–). For Mobile: France (1702–1763) → Britain (1763–1780) → Spain (1780–1813) → United States.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, frontier trade, deerskin trade, early cotton planting. Mobile served as port and commercial hub.
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek, Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw nations; Anglo-American settlers from Carolinas/Virginia/Georgia; French Creole families in Mobile; Spanish colonial settlers; enslaved African Americans.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (Mobile area); Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian circuits in the interior.
- **Key historical events:** Mississippi Territory established (1798); U.S. seizure of Mobile from Spain (1813); Creek War (1813–1814); Alabama Territory formed (1817); statehood (1819).

## Boundary changes
- Before 1798: No organized American territory. Interior records fall under Georgia's western land claims; Mobile under Spanish administration.
- 1798–1817: Present-day Alabama was the eastern half of the **Mississippi Territory**.
- 1817–1819: **Alabama Territory** separated from Mississippi Territory.
- After 1819: State of Alabama.
- Key consequence: Records created before 1817 are Mississippi Territory records. Search Mississippi Territory collections alongside Alabama ones — they form one continuous research trail.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration of births or deaths existed in the territorial era. Marriage records begin at the county level from 1809.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch collection 'Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950' (id: 1598408) — 612,345 records, indexed + images.
- **Where held:** ADAH; county probate courts.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the only source for vital events before any civil system.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mobile, French-era through Spanish-era); Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian (interior).
- **Where held:** Diocese of Mobile archives; Mobile Municipal Archives (microfilm of French records); Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence (French originals); Archivo General de Indias, Seville, with copies at Library of Congress (Spanish originals). FamilySearch collection 'Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950' (id: 1986396) — 156,789 records, indexed + images.
- **Language:** French (pre-1763), Spanish (1780–1813), English.

### Census records
- **Territorial censuses:** 1801, 1805, 1808, 1810 — held at ADAH; not systematically digitized online.
- **Federal census:** 1810 (Mississippi Territory) and 1820 (State of Alabama) are the relevant federal enumerations.
- **Compiled index:** 'Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890' (id: 2016756) — 287,634 records, indexed, no images. Also: 'Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890' (id: 1927171) — 198,340 records, indexed, no images.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, territorial court proceedings.
- **Browse-only volumes:** FamilySearch vol. 004512889 — Alabama territorial court and land records, 1808–1819, 214 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable. Vol. 004512890 — Washington County deed and probate, 1803–1820, 96 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable.
- **Indexed collection:** 'Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985' (id: 1537764) — 438,210 records, indexed + images.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular survey. Alabama is a federal-land state.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** U.S. General Land Office; Huntsville Land Office opened 1811.
- **Where held:** BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) for patents; NARA for case files; ADAH for claims files. 'Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907' (id: 1919694) — 312,450 records, indexed + images — covers territorial-era Alabama land records before 1817.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War (1813–1814); War of 1812; territorial militia; Spanish colonial militia (Mobile).
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C. and Atlanta); Fold3 (fold3.com); ADAH for state militia records.

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) — sparse pre-1820 coverage.
- **Physical records:** Diocese of Mobile archives for Catholic cemeteries; interior Protestant burials largely unrecorded.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Mobile Centinel (founded 1811) is among the earliest; interior had very limited publishing before statehood.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com; ADAH microfilm; Library of Congress Chronicling America.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile; New Orleans.
- **Where held:** NARA (post-1820 passenger lists); Archivo General de Indias (Spanish colonial Mobile arrivals); Library of Congress.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial and county property and poll tax lists.
- **Where held:** ADAH; some microfilm at FamilySearch.
- **Substitute value:** Critical substitute for missing census years; places a person in a specific county annually.

### Other record types
- Spanish colonial records for Mobile District (1780–1813): Archivo General de Indias (Seville); copies at Library of Congress.
- French colonial records for Mobile (1702–1763): Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives.
- Territorial court minute books: document road assignments, poor relief, appointments — naming ordinary people in no other series.
- County and local histories: ADAH and university libraries.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 8 indexed collections (see above) + 3 browse-only volumes | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records | Subscription |
| NARA | National Archives holdings | Free (in-person) / some online |
| BLM GLO | Federal land patents | Free |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| ADAH, Montgomery, AL | Territorial censuses; tax lists; state/county records | In-person; archives.alabama.gov |
| NARA Southeast, Atlanta, GA | Federal territorial court and land records | In-person or NARA request |
| NARA, Washington, D.C. | Military service, pension, bounty land, GLO records | In-person, mail, or online |
| Mobile Municipal Archives | French colonial microfilm; early county records | In-person |
| Diocese of Mobile Archives | Catholic parish registers including pre-1813 records | In-person or written request |
| Library of Congress | Spanish colonial record copies; early maps/newspapers | In-person; loc.gov |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville | Original Spanish colonial records for Mobile District | In-person or written request |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence | French colonial records for Mobile | In-person or written request |
| County probate courts | Earliest deed books, probate files, court minutes | In-person or mail |

## Records NOT online
- Territorial censuses 1801, 1805, 1808 (ADAH)
- Spanish colonial census and church registers for Mobile District (Seville / LoC / Mobile Municipal Archives)
- French colonial records for Mobile (Aix-en-Provence / Mobile Municipal Archives)
- County court minute books for Washington County and earliest counties (browse-only at best)
- Early county tax lists (ADAH)
- Interior Protestant church registers (scattered or lost)

## Known record losses
No specific record destruction event for Alabama territorial-era records was confirmed by tool results in this survey. Sparse digitization results reflect coverage gaps, not confirmed destruction.

## Research tips
- Work Mississippi Territory and Alabama collections in parallel — records before 1817 are filed under the Territory.
- Mobile requires a separate colonial research track in French, Spanish, and English archives.
- Alabama is a federal-land state — search BLM GLO for patents, then request NARA case files for witness names.
- Use territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808) at ADAH as your earliest substitutes for the federal census.
- Tax lists fill annual gaps between censuses.
- Creek War pension and bounty land files at NARA name wives and children — use them as vital record substitutes.
- Church records are the only vital record source for this period.

---

# Locality Guide: Arkansas Region under Spanish Colonial Rule (pre-1800)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Arkansas Post established 1686 by the French as the first European settlement in the lower Mississippi Valley
- **Administrative center:** Arkansas Post (on the Arkansas River, present-day Arkansas County)
- **Colonial rulers:** France, 1686–1763; Spain, 1763–1800 (Treaty of Paris 1763 transferred Louisiana to Spain; Spain secretly retroceded to France in 1800; U.S. acquisition via Louisiana Purchase 1803)
- **Parent jurisdiction (Spanish era):** Province of Louisiana, under the Captaincy General of Cuba and ultimately the Viceroyalty of New Spain
- **Population during period:** Very sparse. The European and mixed-heritage (Creole, Métis) population at Arkansas Post numbered in the low hundreds at most; the surrounding region was dominated by the Quapaw nation
- **Economy:** Fur trade, subsistence agriculture, small military garrison
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole settlers, Spanish colonial soldiers and officials, mixed French-Native (Métis) families, Quapaw and other Native peoples, some enslaved Africans
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic exclusively

---

## Boundary changes

| Period | Status |
|---|---|
| 1686–1763 | Part of French Louisiana; authority ran through New Orleans |
| 1763–1800 | Part of Spanish Louisiana; district seat at Arkansas Post |
| 1800–1803 | Briefly retroceded to France under Napoleon, administered in practice by Spain |
| 1803 | Louisiana Purchase; becomes U.S. territory |
| 1819 | Arkansas Territory created from Missouri Territory |
| 1836 | Arkansas achieves statehood |

Records created before 1803 follow French and Spanish administrative and ecclesiastical systems entirely — no U.S. county structure, no civil registration, no American legal framework.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **None existed.** There was no civil vital registration before 1803. The only vital-event documentation is the Catholic sacramental register series.

### Church records *(most important source for this period)*
- **Denomination:** Roman Catholic exclusively (French Capuchin and later secular missionaries)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; some entries note ethnic identity (European, Native, African, or mixed)
- **Date range:** Early 1700s (French period) through 1800 and beyond
- **FamilySearch volume:** Image group **008814402** — 64 images of Arkansas Post sacramental registers, 1763–1800. **Not indexed, browse only, in Spanish.** Must be read image by image.
- **Where held:**
  - Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock (originals or surviving registers)
  - Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock (transcribed copies)
  - FamilySearch (image group 008814402 — browse only)

### Census records (Padrones)
- Spain periodically ordered household enumerations. Padrones list heads of household with family members, occupations, and sometimes ages — the closest analog to a census.
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission; Archivo General de Indias (Seville); microfilm at the Library of Congress
- **Digitization:** Not indexed; physical or microfilm access required

### Land records
- **System:** Spanish land concessions (concesiones). Settlers petitioned the commandant at Arkansas Post; grants were forwarded to the governor at New Orleans.
- **After 1803:** U.S. land commissioners required holders of Spanish/French grants to file confirmation claims. Those proceedings frequently transcribe the original Spanish documents and are a key access point.
- **Where held:**
  - Archivo General de Indias, Seville (original colonial grant files)
  - Arkansas History Commission (copies and transcriptions)
  - Library of Congress (microfilm of selected Spanish colonial records)
  - BLM General Land Office Records — U.S.-era confirmation patents: https://glorecords.blm.gov
  - NARA (confirmation claim files in U.S. District Court records)

### Probate and court records
- The commandant at Arkansas Post exercised civil and criminal jurisdiction. Records of local disputes, estate settlements, and contracts were kept at the post (military-administrative records, not civilian probate).
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias; Arkansas History Commission; Library of Congress microfilm

### Military records
- Arkansas Post maintained a small Spanish garrison throughout 1763–1800.
- **Record types:** Muster rolls (listas de revista), service records, commandant correspondence
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias (primary); Library of Congress microfilm

### Immigration records
- Settlers and soldiers arriving from France, Spain, Canada (Acadian exiles), and the Caribbean were sometimes documented in transport records filed at New Orleans or Havana.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias; Louisiana State Museum; Historic New Orleans Collection; Library of Congress microfilm

### Newspapers
- None existed in the Arkansas region before 1800. Not a resource for this period.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Image group 008814402: Arkansas Post Sacramental Registers, 1763–1800 (64 images, browse-only, in Spanish) | Free |
| BLM General Land Office Records (glorecords.blm.gov) | U.S. patents confirming Spanish-era land grants, searchable by name | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | U.S. District Court land confirmation files post-1803; some Louisiana colonial records | Free finding aids; some digitized |
| PARES portal (pares.culturaydeporte.gob.es) | Some Archivo General de Indias materials digitized | Free |

**Note:** The FamilySearch collections "Arkansas, County Marriages, 1837–1957" and "Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819–1870" begin after the colonial period and are **not** resources for pre-1800 research.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Arkansas History Commission**, Little Rock, AR | Spanish colonial records (copies/transcriptions), church register transcriptions, published finding aids — https://www.arkansasheritage.com/arkansas-history-commission |
| **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** | Original or custody-transferred sacramental registers from Arkansas Post (contact diocesan archivist) |
| **Archivo General de Indias**, Seville, Spain | Original Spanish colonial land grants, padrones, military muster rolls, commandant correspondence for Louisiana including Arkansas Post |
| **Library of Congress**, Washington DC | Microfilm of selected Spanish colonial Louisiana records, including Arkansas Post materials (some available through interlibrary loan) |
| **Historic New Orleans Collection / Louisiana State Archives** | New Orleans-based colonial administrative records touching Arkansas Post |

---

## Records NOT available online

The following record types exist for this period but are not in any name-indexed online database:
- Spanish colonial padrones (household censuses)
- Spanish land concession petition files
- Arkansas Post commandant correspondence and civil/criminal records
- Spanish military garrison muster rolls
- Capuchin mission records

The one FamilySearch volume (image group 008814402) is online but must be browsed in Spanish — it is not indexed.

The PARES portal (https://pares.culturaydeporte.gob.es) provides an online catalog and some digitized images. Those confirmation files at NARA and the BLM GLO frequently quote or summarize the original Spanish grant, naming family relationships and dates of settlement — often the most accessible entry point.

7. **Records document Native Americans.** The sacramental registers include baptisms and marriages of Quapaw individuals with French or Spanish names given at baptism alongside native names. Do not assume a Native ancestor is undocumentable.

8. **The French period (1686–1763) uses the same repositories.** Earlier records are in French rather than Spanish, but the Diocese of Little Rock, the Arkansas History Commission, and the Archivo General de Indias cover both colonial periods.

The most important surviving records are (1) Catholic sacramental registers held by the Diocese of Little Rock and Arkansas History Commission, (2) Spanish colonial administrative records (padrones, land grants, military rolls) at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville and on microfilm at the Library of Congress, and (3) U.S.-era land confirmation files carrying the colonial land trail forward.
