Here is the full guide.

---

# Locality Guide: Arkansas Region under Spanish Colonial Rule (pre-1800)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Arkansas Post established 1686 by the French as the first European settlement in the lower Mississippi Valley
- **Administrative center:** Arkansas Post (on the Arkansas River, present-day Arkansas County)
- **Colonial rulers:** France, 1686-1763; Spain, 1763-1800 (Treaty of Paris 1763 transferred Louisiana to Spain; Spain secretly retroceded to France in 1800; U.S. acquisition via Louisiana Purchase 1803)
- **Parent jurisdiction (Spanish era):** Province of Louisiana, under the Captaincy General of Cuba and ultimately the Viceroyalty of New Spain
- **Population during period:** Very sparse. The European and mixed-heritage (Creole, Metis) population at Arkansas Post numbered in the low hundreds at most; the surrounding region was dominated by the Quapaw nation
- **Economy:** Fur trade, subsistence agriculture, small military garrison
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole settlers, Spanish colonial soldiers and officials, mixed French-Native (Metis) families, Quapaw and other Native peoples, some enslaved Africans
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic exclusively (no Protestant congregations existed in the colony before 1800)
- **Key historical events:** French founding 1686; cession to Spain 1763; Spanish administration of Arkansas Post district 1763-1800; secret retrocession to France (Treaty of San Ildefonso 1800); Louisiana Purchase 1803

## Boundary changes

- **1686-1763:** Part of French Louisiana; all governing authority ran through New Orleans and ultimately France.
- **1763-1800:** Part of Spanish Louisiana. Arkansas Post served as the district seat. Governing authority ran through the governor of Louisiana at New Orleans, then through Havana (Cuba) to Madrid.
- **1800-1803:** Briefly retroceded to France under Napoleon but administered in practice by Spain until American arrival.
- **1803:** Became part of the United States under the Louisiana Purchase.
- **1819:** Missouri Territory organized; Arkansas Territory created.
- **1836:** Arkansas achieved statehood.

Records created before 1803 follow French and Spanish administrative and ecclesiastical systems entirely. There was no U.S. county structure, no civil registration, and no American legal framework. A researcher tracing the colonial period cannot use post-1803 Arkansas records to bridge backward without first connecting to the colonial record series at Arkansas Post.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** Civil registration did not exist during this period at any level. No statewide or territorial system of birth, marriage, or death registration applied here before 1803. Arkansas statewide vital registration began in the twentieth century, far beyond the scope of this guide.
- **What exists:** There are no civil vital records for this period. The only vital-event documentation is the Catholic sacramental register series (see Church Records below).
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Sacramental registers, padrones (household censuses), land grant applications naming family members.

### Church records

- **Denomination:** Roman Catholic exclusively. French Capuchin and later secular missionaries served Arkansas Post.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials. The registers also record confirmations and, in some entries, note the ethnic identity of the parties (European, Native, African, or mixed).
- **Date range:** Sacramental registers exist from the early 1700s (French period) through 1800 and beyond.
- **Digitization status:** FamilySearch holds 1 digitized volume (image group **008814402**, 64 images) covering Arkansas Post sacramental registers, 1763-1800. This volume is **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable** — it must be browsed image by image. The records are in **Spanish** and require the ability to read colonial Spanish script.
- **Where held:**
  - Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock (originals or transcripts of surviving registers)
  - Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock (transcribed copies)
  - FamilySearch microfilm/digital (image group 008814402 — browse only, in Spanish)
- **Note on coverage:** The FamilySearch wiki search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records states that French Catholic missionaries maintained sacramental registers at Arkansas Post from the early 1700s recording baptisms, marriages, and burials of both European settlers and Native Americans, with surviving registers held by the Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock and in transcribed form at the Arkansas History Commission.

### Census records

- **Padrones (Spanish colonial household censuses):** Spain periodically ordered household enumeration of its colonial settlements. Padrones for Arkansas Post list heads of household with family members, occupations, and sometimes ages. These are the closest analog to a census for this period.
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission; Archivo General de Indias (Seville); microfilm at the Library of Congress. Per the FamilySearch wiki search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records, Spanish colonial records including censuses (padrones) are held at all three repositories.
- **Digitization status:** Not indexed for this period. The one FamilySearch volume confirmed by `volume_search` covers sacramental registers; no separately catalogued padrón volume was returned. These records likely require physical or microfilm access.
- **Post-1800 note:** The FamilySearch collection "Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819-1870" (collection 2085124) begins only after the colonial period and does not extend back to pre-1803 Spanish records. It is not a resource for the period surveyed here.

### Land records

- **System:** Spanish land law. Grants were called concessions (concesiones). Settlers petitioned the commandant at Arkansas Post, who forwarded requests to the governor at New Orleans. Grants described land by metes and bounds, often referencing natural features.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The governor of Spanish Louisiana at New Orleans, acting under authority from the Captaincy General of Cuba.
- **Record types:** Petitions for land concessions, survey plats, grant documents. After the Louisiana Purchase, the U.S. Congress required holders of Spanish and French grants to file confirmation claims with the U.S. land commissioners. Those confirmation proceedings — at the U.S. District Court and through the General Land Office — constitute a continuation of the colonial land trail and frequently transcribe or reference the original Spanish documents.
- **Where held:**
  - Archivo General de Indias, Seville (original colonial grant files)
  - Arkansas History Commission (copies and transcriptions)
  - Library of Congress (microfilm of selected Spanish colonial records)
  - Bureau of Land Management, General Land Office Records (BLM GLO) — U.S.-era confirmation patents referencing original Spanish grants: https://glorecords.blm.gov
  - NARA (confirmation claim files in U.S. District Court records)
- **Digitization status:** BLM GLO patents are searchable online; the underlying colonial petition files are physical or microfilm only.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** The commandant at Arkansas Post exercised civil and criminal jurisdiction. Records of local disputes, estate settlements, and contracts were kept at the post. These are military-administrative records, not civilian probate in the American sense.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias; Arkansas History Commission; Library of Congress microfilm.
- **Digitization status:** Not indexed; physical or microfilm access required.

### Military records

- **Relevant context:** Arkansas Post maintained a small Spanish military garrison throughout the 1763-1800 period. Garrison commanders kept muster rolls, pay records, and correspondence.
- **Record types:** Muster rolls (listas de revista), service records, correspondence of the commandant.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias (Seville) — the primary repository for Spanish colonial military records. The Library of Congress holds microfilm copies of selected Louisiana colonial records, which include some Arkansas Post military correspondence.
- **Digitization status:** Not indexed. Physical visit to Seville or interlibrary loan of Library of Congress microfilm required.

### Cemetery records

- **What exists:** No formal cemeteries with surviving sexton records from this period are documented in the tool results. Burials were recorded in the Catholic sacramental registers (see Church Records above) and are the primary source for documentation of death.
- **Physical remains:** Some colonial-era burial sites near Arkansas Post have been identified archaeologically but have no genealogically useful records separate from the church registers.

### Newspaper records

- **What exists:** No local newspapers existed in the Arkansas region before 1800. The nearest colonial-era press was at New Orleans.
- **Value for this period:** Nil — newspapers are not a resource for Arkansas before 1800.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant records:** Settlers and soldiers arriving at Arkansas Post from France, Spain, Canada (Acadian exiles), and the Caribbean were sometimes documented in passenger or transport records filed at New Orleans or Havana.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias (Seville); Louisiana State Museum (New Orleans); Historic New Orleans Collection; Library of Congress microfilm.
- **Naturalization:** Not applicable under Spanish colonial law; settlers were subjects of the Crown, not citizens filing naturalization papers.

### Tax records

- **What exists:** Tax-equivalent records take the form of tribute lists and trade licensing records at the post level. No separate property tax rolls analogous to later American practice have been confirmed in tool results.
- **Substitute value:** Padrones and land concession files serve the role tax lists play in later American research — they establish residence, family composition, and economic activity.

### Other record types

- **Notarial records:** Contracts, sales, and personal agreements were sometimes recorded by the post commandant acting in a notarial capacity. These can document family relationships and property ownership.
- **Missionary and denominational records:** Capuchin mission records relating to evangelization of the Quapaw may survive in Capuchin provincial archives.
- **Correspondence and administrative reports:** Annual and special reports from the Arkansas Post commandant to the governor at New Orleans and to Havana survive in the Archivo General de Indias and constitute a rich (though not name-indexed) narrative source.
- **Published transcriptions and local histories:** Several Arkansas historians and genealogists have published transcriptions of colonial records. The Arkansas Historical Quarterly is the primary venue; the Arkansas History Commission maintains a bibliography.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Image group 008814402: Arkansas Post Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial), 1763-1800 — 64 images, browse-only, in Spanish | Free |
| BLM General Land Office Records (glorecords.blm.gov) | U.S. patents confirming Spanish-era land grants — searchable by name | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | U.S. District Court land confirmation files post-1803; some Louisiana colonial records | Free finding aids; some digitized |

The FamilySearch collection "Arkansas, County Marriages, 1837-1957" (collection 1920452) and the "Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819-1870" (collection 2085124) begin after the colonial period and are not resources for pre-1800 research.

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 1 digitized volume matching Arkansas before 1800. This is the complete result set (`totalResults: 1`; no `nextPageToken` was returned).

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock, AR | Spanish colonial records (copies/transcriptions), church register transcriptions, published finding aids | In-person; some materials through staff inquiry; https://www.arkansasheritage.com/arkansas-history-commission |
| Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock | Original or custody-transferred sacramental registers from Arkansas Post | Contact diocesan archivist |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Original Spanish colonial land grants, padrones, military muster rolls, commandant correspondence for Louisiana including Arkansas Post | In-person or PARES online portal (some documents digitized): https://pares.culturaydeporte.gob.es |
| Library of Congress, Washington DC | Microfilm of selected Spanish colonial Louisiana records, including Arkansas Post materials | In-person; some microfilm available through interlibrary loan |
| Historic New Orleans Collection / Louisiana State Archives | New Orleans-based colonial administrative records touching Arkansas Post | In-person or online catalog inquiry |

---

## Records NOT online

The following record types exist for this period but are not available in any name-indexed online database:

- Spanish colonial padrones (household censuses) for Arkansas Post
- Spanish land concession petition files
- Arkansas Post commandant correspondence and civil/criminal records
- Spanish military garrison muster rolls
- Capuchin mission records
- Notarial records from the post

The one FamilySearch volume (image group 008814402) is online but is not indexed and requires browsing in Spanish.

---

## Known record losses

Tool results do not document a specific destruction event for Arkansas Post's colonial records as a class. The volume of surviving material is small — 64 images on FamilySearch for 37 years of Spanish administration — which suggests substantial attrition over time (transfers between New Orleans, Havana, and Seville; subsequent American-era dislocations), but the tool results do not name a single catastrophic loss event. Report this as a coverage gap rather than confirmed destruction. Researchers should contact the Arkansas History Commission for a current assessment of what survives.

---

## Research tips

- **Begin at Arkansas Post, not at the state level.** For the period before 1800, essentially all European-documented activity in the Arkansas region centered on a single settlement. Any ancestor documented here will appear in Arkansas Post records, not in county-level or state-level records that did not exist yet. (Source: FamilySearch wiki search results at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)

- **The Archivo General de Indias is the master repository.** Spain centralized its colonial administrative records in Seville. The Arkansas Post district's land grants, padrones, and military records are among these holdings. The PARES portal (https://pares.culturaydeporte.gob.es) provides an online catalog and some digitized images. A researcher unable to visit Seville should identify specific legajo (bundle) numbers through PARES and request scans or hire a local researcher.

- **Work the Library of Congress microfilm as a bridge.** The Library of Congress holds microfilm copies of selected Louisiana colonial records. These are more accessible than a transatlantic trip and may cover the Arkansas Post materials needed. Contact the Manuscript Division to identify relevant reels.

- **Read the FamilySearch volume in Spanish.** Image group 008814402 requires competence in colonial Spanish script (letra procesal). If you cannot read it yourself, find a paleographer or a researcher experienced in Spanish colonial documents before concluding the volume contains nothing relevant.

- **Connect the colonial land trail to U.S.-era confirmation records.** Spanish land grants did not automatically survive the Louisiana Purchase — claimants had to file with U.S. land commissioners. Those confirmation files at NARA and the BLM GLO frequently quote or summarize the original Spanish grant, naming family relationships and dates of settlement. This is often the most accessible entry point for a colonial land claim.

- **Surnames shift across French, Spanish, and English records.** A French Creole surname may appear in Spanish records with Spanish phonetic spelling, then anglicized further in American records after 1803. Search under all plausible variants. The same person may be "Desruisseaux" in French, "Deruisso" in Spanish, and "Derosha" in American records.

- **Records document Native Americans.** The sacramental registers at Arkansas Post include baptisms and marriages of Quapaw individuals. Do not assume a Native ancestor is undocumentable — they appear in the same registers as European settlers, often with French or Spanish names given at baptism alongside a native name.

- **The French period (1686-1763) runs parallel and uses the same repositories.** If your research extends into the French colonial era, the same three repositories (Arkansas History Commission, Archivo General de Indias, Library of Congress microfilm) and the same Catholic church register series apply, with the difference that earlier records are in French rather than Spanish. The Diocese of Little Rock and the Arkansas History Commission are the best starting points for both periods.

output.text_response:
Here is the full locality guide the subagent produced:

---

# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1870)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Formed:** California admitted as the 31st U.S. state on September 9, 1850. Gold discovered at Sutter's Mill, January 24, 1848.
- **Administrative center:** Sacramento (capital from 1854); San Francisco was the principal port and commercial hub.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mexican territory until 1848 (Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo); U.S. military governance 1848–1850.
- **Population:** ~300,000 people migrated during 1848–1855. Population was heavily male and transient in the early years.
- **Ethnic composition:** Arrivals from across the U.S., Latin America (Chile, Mexico), China, Australia, and Europe. The **Foreign Miners' Tax** (1850, re-enacted 1852) targeted non-citizen miners.

---

## Boundary Changes

California entered the Union with its present general boundaries, but counties were created rapidly — 27 counties organized in 1850, many subdivided through the 1850s–60s. Always verify which county a mining district or town belonged to **at the date of the event**, not today's boundaries.

---

## Available Record Types

### Census Records (Most Important Starting Point)

- **1852 California State Census** (FamilySearch imageGroupNumber 006601001; 522 images; **88% name-indexed; full-text searchable**) — the most critical source for the peak Gold Rush years between the damaged 1850 and the 1860 federal censuses. Start here.
- **U.S. Federal Census:** 1850 (partially destroyed for California), 1860, 1870 — all indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Mortality schedules:** 1850 and 1860 censuses include lists of persons who died in the preceding year — valuable given the high Gold Rush-era death rate.

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)

- **County Births, 1850–1919** — FamilySearch collection ID 2017276 (789,456 indexed records; free)
- **County Marriages, 1850–1952** — FamilySearch collection ID 1452832 (567,890 indexed records; free)
- **Death registration for the 1850s is unconfirmed** — a significant gap. Alternatives: church records, mortality schedules, and newspaper notices.

### Church Records

- **Mission Records, 1769–1850** — FamilySearch collection ID 1804372 (98,765 indexed records; in Spanish/Latin)
- **Post-1850 Catholic registers** — held at the Archdiocese of San Francisco archives and Diocese of Sacramento archives (written request required; not digitized)
- Protestant and Jewish records scattered at local church offices and denominational archives.

### Land Records

- **Federal patents** — Bureau of Land Management GLO Records: [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) (free)
- **Mexican land grant files** — Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley and NARA
- **San Francisco Mining Claim Registers, 1849–1855** — FamilySearch imageGroupNumber 006601002 (340 images; 0% indexed; **browse only**)
- County deed books at county recorders' offices.

### Immigration & Passenger Records

- **Sacramento Port Arrival Registers, 1849–1858** — FamilySearch imageGroupNumber 006601003 (298 images; 0% indexed; **browse only**)
- **San Francisco passenger manifests** — NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno, CA (also partially indexed on Ancestry)
- Overland arrivals have no systematic registers — diaries and journals only.

### Great Registers (Voter Registration)

- **California Great Registers, 1866–1910** — FamilySearch collection ID 1923340 (1,345,678 indexed records; free). Each entry records **name, age, nativity, occupation, and physical description** — extremely useful for men who settled in California after the Rush.

### Military Records

- Mexican-American War and Civil War service/pension records at NARA, Washington, D.C.
- Fold3.com (subscription) has many digitized NARA military collections.

### Tax Records

- County property and personal property tax from 1850.
- **Foreign Miners' Tax records** — name non-citizen miners by county; held at county archives and the California State Archives.

### Newspapers

- **California Digital Newspaper Collection** ([cdnc.ucr.edu](https://cdnc.ucr.edu), free) — Gold Rush-era papers including the *Alta California* (San Francisco, 1849).
- Newspapers.com (subscription) and Bancroft Library for additional runs.
- Content: ship arrival lists, obituaries, estate notices, mining district news.

### Probate & Court Records

- From county formation (most Gold Rush counties organized in 1850).
- Mining disputes generated substantial county court records.
- **No digitized probate volumes** confirmed for the 1850s — physical/microfilm access required at county courthouses or California State Archives.
- Pre-1906 naturalization records filed at any court of record — search county, district, and federal courts separately.

### Cemetery Records

- Find A Grave (findagrave.com, free) and BillionGraves index many California cemeteries.
- Many small mining camp burial grounds have been relocated or lost — high mortality often went unrecorded.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories

| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | County Births/Marriages; Mission Records; Great Registers; 1852 State Census; SF Mining Claim Registers (browse); Sacramento Port Arrivals (browse) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census 1850/1860/1870; passenger lists | Subscription |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents | Free |
| California Digital Newspaper Collection (cdnc.ucr.edu) | Gold Rush-era California newspapers | Free |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records statewide | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical California newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military records (digitized NARA) | Subscription |

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| California State Archives, Sacramento | County court records, 1852 census originals, militia records, land commission records |
| Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley | Gold Rush manuscripts, diaries, letters, Mexican land grant files, county histories |
| California State Library, Sacramento | County/local histories, newspaper microfilm, biographical collections |
| NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno, CA | San Francisco passenger manifests, federal court records including naturalizations |
| County courthouses (El Dorado, Placer, Nevada, Tuolumne, Calaveras, Amador, Sacramento) | Deed books, probate files, mining claim registers, court minutes |
| Archdiocese of San Francisco / Diocese of Sacramento archives | Post-1850 Catholic baptism, marriage, and burial registers |

## Known Record Losses

- **1850 federal census for California was partially destroyed** — some county returns are missing. Use the 1852 state census to compensate.
- **Many Gold Rush-era mining camp burials were never formally recorded** — high mortality left many deaths with no documentary trace beyond occasional newspaper notices.
- **Death registration for the 1850s** is unconfirmed; verify directly with the California State Archives.

---

1. **Start with the 1852 California State Census** (FamilySearch imageGroupNumber 006601001; 88% name-indexed; full-text searchable). It is the single most important source for placing a miner in California between the damaged 1850 and 1860 federal censuses.
2. **Check ship passenger manifests at NARA San Bruno** for sea arrivals. Hundreds of thousands arrived by ship via San Francisco.
3. **Verify county boundaries at the date of the event** — California carved out new counties continuously through the 1850s.
4. **Use the Great Registers from 1866 onward** (FamilySearch collection 1923340) for men who remained in California after the Rush. Each entry records nativity, occupation, age, and physical description.
5. **Search the Foreign Miners' Tax records** if your ancestor was Chinese, Chilean, Mexican, or otherwise foreign-born — these records specifically name taxed miners by county and are held at county archives and the California State Archives.
6. **Do not overlook the Bancroft Library** for manuscript diaries, letters, and local histories naming individuals who appear in no surviving official record.
7. **Work both ends of the migration.** Gold Rush migrants were often transient; family and vital records may survive better in the state or country of origin. Research the origin alongside California.

### Church records
- Mission Records 1769-1850 (FamilySearch collection 1804372, 98,765 records) in Spanish and Latin. Post-1850 Catholic registers at diocesan archives (Archdiocese of San Francisco; Diocese of Sacramento). Protestant records at local churches and denominational archives.

### Probate and court records

### Land records

# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848-1870)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** California was admitted as the 31st U.S. state on September 9, 1850, bypassing territorial status entirely. Gold was discovered at Sutter's Mill in Coloma on January 24, 1848.
- **Administrative center:** Sacramento (state capital from 1854); San Francisco was the principal port and commercial hub.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mexican territory until 1848 (Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo); U.S. military governance 1848-1850 before statehood.
- **Population during period:** Approximately 300,000 people migrated to California from the rest of the United States and abroad during 1848-1855 (Wikipedia, California Gold Rush). The population was heavily male and transient in the early years.
- **Economy:** Gold and silver mining, maritime trade through San Francisco, Sacramento Valley agriculture, and commerce supplying mining camps.
- **Ethnic composition:** Arrivals from across the U.S., Latin America (especially Chile and Mexico), China, Australia, Europe (British Isles, France, Germany), and the Pacific. The Foreign Miners' Tax (1850, re-enacted 1852) specifically targeted non-citizen miners.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (dominant through the Mission era and among Hispanic and Irish immigrants); Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, Episcopal, and Jewish congregations established in San Francisco, Sacramento, and mining towns during 1849-1855.
- **Key historical events:** Gold discovery 1848; California statehood 1850; Foreign Miners' Tax 1850 and 1852; Chinese immigration surge mid-1850s; decline of placer mining by the late 1850s.

## Boundary changes

California entered the Union with its present general boundaries, but counties were created rapidly. The state organized 27 counties in 1850, and many were subdivided or reorganized through the 1850s-1860s. A record filed in one county in 1852 may belong to a county that no longer exists under that name or has had its territory transferred. Always verify which county a specific mining district or town belonged to at the date of the event — not today's boundaries.

Records predating statehood (1848-1850) fall under U.S. military governance or Mexican colonial administration. Mission records and Mexican land grant files are the primary pre-statehood documentation.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** FamilySearch has indexed collections beginning in 1850 for both county births and county marriages, suggesting county-level recording began at or near statehood. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for California Vital Records did not return California-specific content in this session; the researcher should consult those pages directly for the precise registration levels and dates.
- **What exists:** County-level birth records from 1850 — FamilySearch collection "California, County Births, 1850-1919" (collection ID 2017276; 789,456 indexed records; 394,728 images). County marriage records from 1850 — FamilySearch collection "California, County Marriages, 1850-1952" (collection ID 1452832; 567,890 indexed records; 283,945 images). Death registration volumes for the 1850s were not returned by the volume search — a significant gap for the high-mortality Gold Rush period.
- **Where held:** County recorder's offices; digitized and indexed collections linked above on FamilySearch (free).
- **Gaps:** Death registration for the 1850s is unconfirmed from this survey. The 1850 federal census was partially destroyed — some county returns are missing (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records). Many Gold Rush-era vital events went entirely unrecorded.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records, the 1852 California State Census, federal census mortality schedules (1850, 1860), and newspaper notices.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Catholic (continuous from the Mission era through statehood), Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, Episcopal, and Jewish congregations established in major towns during 1849-1855.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "California, Mission Records, 1769-1850" (collection ID 1804372; 98,765 indexed records; 49,382 images) covers the Spanish Mission era through statehood. Post-1850 Catholic records are held by the Archdiocese of San Francisco archives and the Diocese of Sacramento archives — written request required. Protestant records are scattered at local church offices and denominational archives.
- **Language:** Mission-era records are in Spanish and Latin. Post-statehood records are predominantly in English.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** 1850 (California's first; partially destroyed), 1860, 1870 — all indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry. The 1850 and 1860 censuses include mortality schedules listing persons who died in the year preceding the census — valuable given the high Gold Rush-era death rate.
- **State census:** California conducted a **state census in 1852**, which is a critical source for the peak Gold Rush years between the 1850 and 1860 federal censuses. FamilySearch volume (imageGroupNumber 006601001) covers the 1850-1852 California State Census: 522 images, **88% name-indexed, full-text searchable** — indexed + full-text, the most accessible digitized record set for this period.
- **Access:** The 1852 State Census volume is indexed + full-text searchable on FamilySearch. Federal censuses are fully indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories; naturalizations (filed in any court of record before 1906); name changes; civil suits; mining disputes (which generated substantial county court records).
- **Date range:** From county formation (most Gold Rush counties organized in 1850).
- **Where held:** County superior courts and county courthouses; the California State Archives holds some transferred records. Pre-1906 naturalization records are scattered across county, district, and federal courts — check all three levels separately.
- **Digitization:** The volume search returned no indexed or browse-only digitized probate volumes for this period. These records are likely physical-only or on microfilm. Contact individual county courts or the California State Archives.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** California is a federal-land (public-domain) state. Land was distributed through the U.S. General Land Office (GLO). Mexican-era land grants (ranchos) required confirmation by the U.S. Land Commission after 1851.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal patents issued by the GLO — records searchable free at the Bureau of Land Management GLO Records website (glorecords.blm.gov). Mexican land grant case files (Land Commission records) are held at the Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley, and NARA.
- **Types:** Federal patents, Mexican land grant confirmations, county deed books, and mining claim registers.
- **Mining claim registers:** FamilySearch volume imageGroupNumber 006601002 covers San Francisco Mining Claim Registers 1849-1855 (340 images; 0% name-indexed; not full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image).
- **Where held:** County recorders hold deed books. BLM GLO website for federal patents. Bancroft Library and NARA for Mexican grant files.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846-1848; California volunteers); Civil War (1861-1865, California troops serving in the West).
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (Mexican-American War veterans), draft registrations.
- **Where held:** NARA in Washington, D.C. for federal service and pension records; California State Archives for state militia records. Fold3.com (subscription) has digitized many NARA military collections.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Numerous Gold Rush-era cemeteries in the Sierra Nevada foothills (El Dorado, Placer, Tuolumne, Calaveras, Amador counties) and in San Francisco and Sacramento. Many small mining camp burial grounds have been relocated or lost.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com, free) and BillionGraves index many California cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records, where they survive, are held by county offices or local historical societies. Many 1850s mining camp burials were never formally recorded.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** Alta California (San Francisco, 1849), Sacramento Bee (1857), and numerous short-lived mining district papers published arrival lists, obituaries, legal notices, and mining news.
- **Where held:** California Digital Newspaper Collection (cdnc.ucr.edu, free) provides digitized access to many Gold Rush-era papers. Newspapers.com (subscription) and the Bancroft Library (physical and microfilm) hold extensive additional runs.
- **Content value:** Ship arrival lists, obituaries, Foreign Miners' Tax enforcement notices, estate notices, and mining district news all name individuals.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** San Francisco was the primary port of entry for sea arrivals. Overland arrivals came via the California Trail and other routes — these are typically documented only in diaries and journals, not systematic registers.
- **Record types:** Ship passenger manifests (arriving at San Francisco), port arrival registers. FamilySearch volume imageGroupNumber 006601003 covers Sacramento Port Arrival Registers 1849-1858 (298 images; 0% name-indexed; not full-text searchable — browse only).
- **Where held:** NARA Pacific Region (San Bruno, California) holds passenger manifests for San Francisco arrivals. Per the FamilySearch Wiki: "ship passenger manifests at San Francisco [are held] at the National Archives, San Bruno" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records). Ancestry.com indexes many passenger lists.
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 declarations of intention and naturalization petitions were filed in any court of record. Search county courts, district courts, and federal courts in California separately.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records

- **Types:** County property tax, personal property tax, and the **Foreign Miners' Tax** (1850 and re-enacted 1852), which specifically named non-citizen miners by county.
- **Date range:** County tax records from 1850.
- **Where held:** County assessors' offices and county archives; some transferred to the California State Archives.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists substitute for census gaps and are especially valuable for the years between the 1852 state census and the 1860 federal census.

### Other record types

- **Great Registers (voter registration):** FamilySearch collection "California, Great Registers, 1866-1910" (collection ID 1923340; 1,345,678 indexed records). Begin in 1866 — after the Gold Rush peak — but record name, age, nativity, occupation, and physical description, making them highly useful for tracing men who settled in California after the Rush.
- **Mining claim records:** County recorders maintained mining claim registers county by county. The San Francisco registers (imageGroupNumber 006601002) are the only digitized set returned by this survey; other county registers require direct contact.
- **Local and county histories:** Published county histories from the 1880s-1890s (for El Dorado, Placer, Nevada, Tuolumne, Calaveras, Amador, and Sacramento counties) contain biographical sketches of early settlers and miners, and sometimes transcribe records since lost. California State Library and Bancroft Library hold extensive sets.
- **Bancroft Library manuscript collections:** Gold Rush-era diaries, letters, and business records — physical access only, by appointment at UC Berkeley.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | County Births 1850-1919 (coll. 2017276); County Marriages 1850-1952 (coll. 1452832); Mission Records 1769-1850 (coll. 1804372); Great Registers 1866-1910 (coll. 1923340); 1852 State Census (imageGroupNumber 006601001); SF Mining Claim Registers 1849-1855 (imageGroupNumber 006601002, browse-only); Sacramento Port Arrival Registers 1849-1858 (imageGroupNumber 006601003, browse-only) | Free |

| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents for California | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch volume search returned 14 digitized volumes matching California for 1848-1870; the 3 volumes detailed above are the first page only. An additional 11 volumes were not examined. - **Ethnic composition:** Heavily male and transient; arrivals from across the U.S., Latin America, China, Australia, Europe.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic, Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, Episcopal, Jewish.

## Boundary changes
California organized 27 counties in 1850; many were subdivided through the 1850s-1860s. Always verify county at event date, not modern boundaries. Records predating statehood are under military governance or Mexican administration.

## Available record types

### Vital records
- County-level births from 1850 (FamilySearch collection 2017276, 789,456 indexed records). County marriages from 1850 (collection 1452832, 567,890 indexed records). No death registration volumes returned for the 1850s — a significant gap.
- Death registration coverage for the Gold Rush decade is unconfirmed; verify with California State Archives.

### Church records
- Mission Records 1769-1850 (FamilySearch collection 1804372, 98,765 records) in Spanish and Latin. Post-1850 Catholic registers at diocesan archives (Archdiocese of San Francisco; Diocese of Sacramento). Protestant records at local churches and denominational archives.

### Census records
- 1852 California State Census (imageGroupNumber 006601001; 522 images; 88% indexed; full-text searchable) — prime source for Gold Rush peak years.
- 1850 federal census (partially destroyed), 1860, 1870 — all indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry. Mortality schedules for 1850 and 1860.

### Probate and court records
- County-level from 1850. No indexed digitized volumes returned for this period — physical or microfilm access required. Mining disputes created substantial court records. Pre-1906 naturalizations in any court of record.

### Land records
- Federal patents via BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov). Mexican land grant files at Bancroft Library and NARA. Mining Claim Registers, San Francisco 1849-1855 (imageGroupNumber 006601002, 340 images, browse-only). County deed books at county recorders.

### Military records
- Mexican-American War veterans (bounty land warrants); Civil War California troops. Records at NARA Washington, D.C. and California State Archives. Fold3.com has digitized many collections.

### Cemetery records
- Find A Grave and BillionGraves index many California cemeteries. Many Gold Rush-era mining camp burials were never formally recorded.

### Newspaper records
- Alta California (SF, 1849), Sacramento Bee (1857), and many mining district papers. California Digital Newspaper Collection (cdnc.ucr.edu, free). Newspapers.com (subscription). Bancroft Library microfilm.

### Immigration/emigration records
- Ship passenger manifests at NARA San Bruno for San Francisco arrivals. Sacramento Port Arrival Registers 1849-1858 (imageGroupNumber 006601003, 298 images, browse-only). Overland arrivals via California Trail undocumented except in diaries/journals.

### Tax records
- County property/personal property tax from 1850. Foreign Miners' Tax (1850, re-enacted 1852) names foreign-born miners by county — at county archives and California State Archives.

### Other records
- Great Registers 1866-1910 (FamilySearch collection 1923340, 1,345,678 indexed records) — name, age, nativity, occupation, physical description.
- Bancroft Library manuscript collections (physical only): Gold Rush diaries, letters, business records.
- Published county histories (1880s-1890s): biographical sketches of early settlers.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | County Births 1850-1919; County Marriages 1850-1952; Mission Records 1769-1850; Great Registers 1866-1910; 1852 State Census; SF Mining Claim Registers; Sacramento Port Registers | Free |
| Ancestry.com | Federal Census 1850/1860/1870; passenger lists | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical California newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records | Subscription |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents | Free |
| CDNC (cdnc.ucr.edu) | Digitized California newspapers | Free |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| California State Archives, Sacramento | County courts, state census originals, militia, land commission | In-person |
| Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley | Gold Rush manuscripts, Mexican land grant files, county histories | In-person, by appointment |
| California State Library, Sacramento | Local histories, newspaper microfilm | In-person |
| NARA San Bruno | SF passenger manifests, federal court/naturalization records | In-person |
| County courthouses (El Dorado, Placer, Nevada, Tuolumne, Calaveras, Amador, Sacramento) | Deed books, probate, mining claims, court minutes | In-person or written request |
| Diocesan archives (SF, Sacramento) | Post-1850 Catholic registers | Written request |

## Records NOT online
- County probate records, 1850s
- Foreign Miners' Tax records
- Post-1850 Catholic parish registers
- Mining company employment and partnership records (Bancroft Library, physical only)
- Sacramento Port Arrival Registers 1849-1858 (digitized but browse-only)
- San Francisco Mining Claim Registers 1849-1855 (digitized but browse-only)
- County court minutes

## Known record losses
- 1850 federal census partially destroyed — some county returns missing.
- Many Gold Rush-era mining camp burials never formally recorded.

## Research tips
- Start with the 1852 California State Census (imageGroupNumber 006601001, FamilySearch) — 88% indexed, best source between 1850 and 1860 federal censuses.
- Check ship passenger manifests at NARA San Bruno for sea arrivals.
- Verify county at event date — boundaries changed frequently through the 1850s.
- Use Great Registers from 1866 for settlers who remained after the Rush.
- Search Bancroft Library and California State Library manuscript collections.
- Foreign Miners' Tax records name non-citizen miners by county — check county archives.
- Work both the California end and the origin-side records.

---

## New York City, 1700s — Genealogical Records & Repositories

**Overview**

New York City in the 1700s was a colonial port under Dutch and then English rule. Because no government required registration of births, marriages, or deaths during this entire period, **church records are the single most important starting point.**

---

### Key Record Types & Repositories

**1. Church Registers (Baptisms, Marriages, Burials)**
The Dutch Reformed, Anglican (Trinity Church), and Presbyterian congregations kept continuous registers that now survive in:
- **FamilySearch** — Collection 1469062, covering 1640–1940; one digitized Dutch Reformed volume specifically covers 1700–1776 (211 images, browse-only, in Dutch)
- **New-York Historical Society (NYHS)**
- **New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYG&B)**
- Individual church archives

**2. Probate Records**
The **Prerogative Court of New York** handled all colonial-era probate province-wide. The NYHS's published ***Abstracts of Wills*** series is the key index to it.

**3. Land Records**
Available as FamilySearch image collections, going back to 1630.

**4. Tax Lists & Militia Rolls**
Provincial tax lists and colonial militia rolls serve as census substitutes for the period before the first federal census (1790).

**5. The 1790 Federal Census**
The anchor record at the century's end; the oldest surviving federal census for NYC families.

---

### Important Caveats

- **Five separate counties:** The five modern boroughs were five separate colonial counties — records for each are held separately.
- **Dutch patronymic naming:** Dutch-descended families often changed surnames between generations, making tracing lineages more complex.

---

### Recommended Next Step

Build a research plan targeting a specific ancestor or surname in this place and time, using church registers as the first stop and working outward through probate, land, and tax records.

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775–1783)

## Jurisdiction Overview

Virginia was the most populous American state during the Revolution, operating under its 1776 constitution as a commonwealth. County courts served as the primary administrative unit. Key characteristics of the period:

- **Administrative structure:** County-based record-keeping dating to the 1630s
- **Population:** Most populous American state during this era
- **Ethnic mix:** English settlers, Scots-Irish and German communities in the Valley and Piedmont, enslaved African Americans, and Indigenous peoples on the western frontier
- **Denominations:** Anglican/Episcopal (established church until 1786 disestablishment), Baptist, Presbyterian, Methodist, Quaker, Mennonite, Lutheran

**Boundary changes:** Virginia subdivided counties rapidly during 1775–1783 (e.g., Kentucky County carved from Fincastle County in 1776). Always confirm which county existed on the event date before searching courthouse holdings.

---

## Key Record Types

### Military Records *(Primary focus)*

**Continental Line service records & muster rolls**
- Held at NARA (Record Group 93); Virginia contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony
- Online via **Fold3** (subscription: https://www.fold3.com/)
- FamilySearch wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War

**Virginia militia records**
- Held at the **Library of Virginia**, Richmond (county-based militia musters)

**Pension & bounty-land warrant applications** *(richest genealogical source)*
- NARA Record Group 15 — widows' files especially contain family histories, marriage evidence, and neighbor depositions
- Online via **Fold3** and **Ancestry** (https://www.ancestry.com/)

**Virginia State Navy records**
- Separate from Continental Navy; held at the Library of Virginia

**FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783" (ID 1945678)
👉 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678

---

### Tax Records *(Census substitute — critical)*

- **1782 personal property tax lists** are the earliest surviving statewide enumeration and the standard substitute for the **destroyed 1790 Virginia census**
- **FamilySearch volume 005301449** — Virginia state enumerations/tax lists, 1782–1799 (87 images; full-text searchable)
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850" (ID 1456723)
  👉 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723

---

### Church Records

- Anglican parish vestry books are the primary vital-record substitute (births/baptisms, marriages, burials) before 1786 disestablishment
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929" (ID 1598230)
  👉 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230
- Also held at: Library of Virginia; Virginia Historical Society; denominational archives

---

### County Court Records

Court order books recorded militia call-ups, Loyalist property seizures, road assignments, and poor-relief payments — naming individuals who appear nowhere else.

- **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920" (ID 2134567)
- **FamilySearch volume 005301448** — Augusta County order books, 1775–1795 (158 images; 61% name-indexed)

---

### Land Records

- Virginia was a state-land state; the Commonwealth issued grants through the Virginia Land Office
- Post-war bounty-land warrants for Continental veterans were granted in the **Virginia Military District of Ohio**
- **FamilySearch volume 005301447** — Virginia Revolutionary War land bounty warrants, 1779–1800 (341 images; **browse-only**, 0% indexed — budget significant time)
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900" (ID 1734285)
  👉 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285

---

### Probate & Vital Records

- **No statewide civil registration** until 1853; no civil birth/marriage/death records for this period
- Marriage bonds and licenses were recorded at county level (county courthouse)
- Wills, inventories, and estate records: FamilySearch collection ID 1734285 (above) covers these
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920" (ID 2134567)

---

### Newspapers

- **Virginia Gazette** (multiple editions through the 1780s): militia notices, casualty lists, Loyalist property announcements, estate advertisements
- Available via **Newspapers.com** and Library of Virginia digital holdings

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Military (ID 1945678), Church (ID 1598230), Land/Marriage/Will (ID 1734285), Tax (ID 1456723), Court (ID 2134567), 3 digitized volumes | Free |
| **Fold3** | Continental Line service records, pension files (NARA RG 93 & 15) | Subscription — fold3.com |
| **Ancestry** | Pension applications, some county records | Subscription — ancestry.com |
| **NARA** | RG 15 (pensions), RG 93 (service records) | Free finding aids; much digitized on Fold3 |
| **Library of Virginia, Richmond** | Militia records, land patents, tax lists, Virginia Gazette originals, county microfilm | In-person; lva.virginia.gov |
| **Virginia Historical Society** | Manuscript collections, family papers, unit rosters | In-person |
| **County courthouses** | Deed books, will books, order books for the period county | In-person or mail request |
| **FindAGrave** | Cemetery inscriptions, colonial-era churchyards | Free — findagrave.com |

---

## Known Record Losses & Gaps

- ⚠️ **1790 federal census destroyed** — British burned Washington in 1814; use 1782 tax lists as substitute
- ⚠️ **Some county courthouse losses** — particularly western counties; check the Library of Virginia's "Virginia Courthouse Disasters" finding aid before assuming completeness
- ⚠️ **No civil vital registration** for 1775–1783 — rely on church vestry books and county marriage bonds

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with pension files.** Revolutionary War pension applications (NARA RG 15 via Fold3/Ancestry) are the single richest source — widows' files frequently contain marriage proof, family histories, and neighbor depositions rarely found elsewhere.

2. **Use the 1782 tax list as your census substitute.** FamilySearch volume 005301449 (full-text searchable, 1782–1799) is the best household-location anchor for this period.

3. **Check bounty-land warrants for veterans.** FamilySearch volume 005301447 (browse-only, 341 images, 1779–1800) links Continental veterans to post-war land claims — but budget time, as it is 0% name-indexed.

4. **Mine county court order books.** Beyond litigation, these record militia call-ups, Loyalist property seizures, and administrative actions that name ordinary people. FamilySearch collection ID 2134567 is the starting point; Augusta County (volume 005301448) is 61% name-indexed for 1775–1795.

5. **Confirm the county in existence on the event date.** Virginia subdivided counties rapidly in the 1770s–1780s. A family in the Valley or Piedmont may appear under a different county name depending on the year.

6. **Loyalist confiscation records.** County courts administered Loyalist property confiscations; order books name both Patriots (as purchasers) and Loyalists — useful when allegiance affected property ownership.

7. **Search the Virginia Gazette.** Militia notices, casualty reports, and estate advertisements ran regularly; accessible via Newspapers.com and Library of Virginia.

---

**Recommended first steps:** Search pension application files on Fold3 or Ancestry (NARA RG 15) for any family member who served or was widowed, then cross-check against the 1782 personal property tax list on FamilySearch as a household-location anchor. For the county court records, start with FamilySearch collection ID 2134567.

The wiki place pages all returned the same generic fallback content rather than Virginia-specific pages, and the constructed-URL wiki_reads also resolved to a generic "Genealogy Records" page — I'll note those as gaps and rely on the wiki_search results and the collections/volume data actually returned. ---

# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775–1783)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Virginia was one of the original Thirteen Colonies; county-level record-keeping dates to the 1630s. The state did not formally ratify the U.S. Constitution until 1788, so for this period it operated as the Commonwealth of Virginia under its 1776 constitution.
- **Administrative structure:** County-based. Virginia maintained county courts as the primary unit of civil administration throughout the Revolutionary period.
- **Population during period:** Virginia was the most populous American state during the Revolution. The federal census was first taken in 1790 (shortly after the period); the 1790 Virginia schedules are destroyed (see Known record losses below).
- **Economy:** Tobacco plantation agriculture, iron foundries, milling, and trade.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English-descended settlers, plus Scots-Irish and German communities in the Valley and Piedmont, enslaved African Americans throughout, and remaining Indigenous peoples at the western frontier.
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican/Episcopal (the established church until 1786 disestablishment), Baptist, Presbyterian, Methodist, Quaker, Mennonite, Lutheran.
- **Key historical events:** Virginia raised Continental Line troops and militia continuously from 1775; the Yorktown campaign (1781) ended major combat on Virginia soil. Loyalist property confiscations were managed through county courts. Disestablishment of the Anglican church in 1786 fragmented church-record keeping.

## Boundary changes

Virginia's county boundaries shifted significantly during 1775–1783 as frontier counties were subdivided. Kentucky County was formed from Fincastle County in 1776; further counties were carved out through the period. Records follow the county that existed at the date of the event, not modern county lines. When researching a family in the Valley or western piedmont, confirm which county existed on the event date before searching courthouse holdings.

The Virginia Military District of Ohio (bounty-land grants awarded to veterans) created a separate record set in Ohio after the war — relevant to any family that relocated westward in the 1780s–1800s.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** Virginia did NOT have statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths during 1775–1783. Statewide registration did not begin until 1853. The FamilySearch wiki pages for Virginia-specific vital records returned generic content rather than confirmed dates; this 1853 figure is widely documented but the specific Virginia Vital Records page did not load with Virginia-specific content in this session.
- **What exists (1775–1783):** No state-mandated civil vital records for this period. Marriage bonds and licenses were recorded at the county level before 1853; these are the closest civil analog, held at county courthouses.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (Anglican/Episcopal, Baptist, Presbyterian, Quaker meeting minutes) are the primary source for births, baptisms, marriages, and burials. FamilySearch holds a collection titled "Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929" (Collection ID 1598230; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230).

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Anglican (Church of England / later Episcopal), Baptist, Presbyterian, Methodist, Quaker, Mennonite, Lutheran. The Anglican church was the established church until 1786; its parish registers are the most systematic for births/baptisms and burials before that date.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, vestry books (which also record poor relief and tithe lists). Quaker monthly meeting minutes record births, marriages, and deaths in distinctive format.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929" (Collection ID 1598230). The collection spans the target period.
- **Where else held:** Library of Virginia (Richmond); denominational archives (Virginia Historical Society; Presbyterian Historical Society; Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore).
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images for the FamilySearch collection; coverage varies by county and denomination.
- **Language:** English throughout for this period.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** The 1790 federal census is the first relevant census, taken seven years after the close of the war. Virginia's 1790 schedules were destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. This is a critical gap.
- **Substitute:** Virginia personal property tax lists beginning in 1782 (see Tax records below) serve as the primary census substitute. These lists enumerate free white male tithables and are the closest equivalent to a pre-1800 head-of-household census for Virginia.
- **State enumerations:** FamilySearch volume 005301449 covers Virginia state enumerations and tax lists, 1782–1799 (87 images; full-text searchable, not name-indexed — requires text search, not a name browse).
- **1800 census:** The earliest intact federal census for Virginia. Useful to work backward from.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianship records, county court order books (which record an enormous range of county business beyond litigation).
- **Where held:** County courthouse (county clerk's office) for the county that existed at the time of death. The Library of Virginia holds many original or microfilmed series.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900" (Collection ID 1734285; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285) covers this period.
- **FamilySearch volume:** Volume 005301448 covers Augusta County court order books, 1775–1795 (158 images; 61% name-indexed — partially searchable by name, partially browse-only).
- **Digitization level:** Partially indexed + images (Augusta County); varies by county for other localities.
- **County court order books:** These are especially important for the 1775–1783 period. They record not only litigation but militia muster calls, road maintenance assignments, overseers of the poor payments, and confiscation proceedings against Loyalists — naming ordinary people who appear nowhere else.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Virginia is a state-land state — the Commonwealth, not the federal government, granted land).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Commonwealth of Virginia through the Virginia Land Office. During and after the Revolution, Virginia granted bounty-land warrants to veterans for service in the Continental Line and state forces.
- **Types:** Land patents/grants (Virginia State Land Office), deeds (county courthouse deed books), bounty-land warrants (Virginia Military District series), and tax lists showing assessed property.
- **Post-war bounty-land grants:** Virginia awarded land bounties in the Virginia Military District of Ohio. Warrant and survey records at the Library of Virginia and the Virginia State Archives connect veterans to their land claims. The FamilySearch wiki search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands) confirms this series directly.
- **FamilySearch volume:** Volume 005301447 covers Virginia Revolutionary War land bounty warrants, 1779–1800 (341 images; 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — browse-only, image by image).
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900" (Collection ID 1734285) also encompasses deed and will series.
- **Digitization level:** Browse-only images for the bounty-warrant volume; partially indexed for the combined land/marriage/will collection.

### Military records

This is the primary record class for this research focus.

**Continental Line service records and muster rolls**
- Held at NARA (Record Group 93). These cover Virginia soldiers who served in the Continental Army proper.
- Online via Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) — subscription required.
- The FamilySearch wiki search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War) states Virginia contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony and that Continental Line records are in NARA RG 93.

**Virginia militia records**
- Held at the Library of Virginia, Richmond. Virginia maintained county-based militia musters throughout the war.
- The Library of Virginia has published indices to some militia records.

**Pension and bounty-land warrant applications**
- Held at NARA (Record Group 15). These files — filed by veterans or widows — are often the richest genealogical sources for Revolutionary War families, containing depositions, family histories, marriage evidence, and sworn statements by neighbors. Widows frequently filed decades after the war, providing detailed retrospective accounts.
- Online via Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) and Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/).
- The FamilySearch wiki search result confirms pension and bounty-land warrant application files are in NARA RG 15.

**Virginia State Navy records**
- Separately published. Virginia maintained its own state navy; records are distinct from Continental Navy service records.

**FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783" (Collection ID 1945678; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678) covers the exact target period.

**Digitization level for military:** Indexed + images on FamilySearch for the dedicated collection; Fold3 and Ancestry provide additional indexed access to federal pension/service files.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Personal property tax (tithables lists) and land tax, both beginning in 1782.
- **Critical importance:** The 1782 Virginia personal property tax list is the earliest surviving statewide enumeration of free white male heads of household after the revolution began — and the best available substitute for the destroyed 1790 census.
- **FamilySearch volume:** Volume 005301449 covers Virginia state enumerations/tax lists, 1782–1799 (87 images; full-text searchable, not name-indexed).
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850" (Collection ID 1456723; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723) begins within the target period.
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; county courthouses; FamilySearch microfilm.
- **Digitization level:** Full-text searchable (volume 005301449); partially indexed (collection 1456723).

### Probate and court records (county court order books)

- **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920" (Collection ID 2134567; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567) covers this period.
- County court order books recorded militia assignments, Loyalist confiscations, and road/bridge maintenance — all wartime administrative actions that name individuals.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (per the collection listing).

### Cemetery records

- **Coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) holds records for Virginia cemeteries, including colonial-era church graveyards. Coverage for pre-1800 burials is uneven.
- **Church graveyards:** Anglican/Episcopal churchyard records, where they survive, are the primary burial record for this period. Many rural churchyard inscriptions have been transcribed by the DAR and local historical societies.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records are rare for this period; most burial evidence comes from headstone inscriptions and vestry records.

### Newspaper records

- Virginia newspapers of the period (Virginia Gazette, multiple editions, 1736–1780s) published military notices, casualty lists, legal notices, estate advertisements, and runaway slave notices.
- **Where held:** Accessible via Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/), Colonial Williamsburg digital archives, and the Library of Virginia.
- **Value for this period:** Militia muster notices, Loyalist property announcements, and death notices appeared regularly in the Virginia Gazette.

### Land bounty warrants (post-war)

- As noted above, Virginia's bounty-land program for Continental veterans produced warrant and survey records now held at the Library of Virginia and connectable to the Virginia Military District of Ohio. These are distinct from federal bounty land warrants issued under later U.S. acts.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783 (ID 1945678); Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929 (ID 1598230); Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900 (ID 1734285); Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850 (ID 1456723); Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920 (ID 2134567); plus 3 digitized volumes (see below) | Free |
| Fold3 | Continental Line service records, pension files, muster rolls (NARA RG 93 and RG 15) | Subscription — https://www.fold3.com/ |
| Ancestry | Pension application files, passenger lists, some Virginia county records | Subscription — https://www.ancestry.com/ |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery inscriptions, including colonial-era Virginia churchyards | Free — https://www.findagrave.com/ |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Virginia newspapers including the Virginia Gazette | Subscription — https://www.newspapers.com/ |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Finding aids and some digital records for RG 15 and RG 93 | Free finding aids; some records free online — https://www.archives.gov/ |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 3 digitized volumes matching Virginia for this period (totalResults: 3; all 3 are detailed above — this is the complete result set for the query parameters used). The collections_search returned 5 indexed collections for Virginia, all detailed above.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia, Richmond | Virginia militia records, state land patents, Virginia Gazette originals, personal property tax lists, some county court records on microfilm | In-person; some finding aids online at lva.virginia.gov |
| National Archives (NARA), Washington DC / College Park | Continental service records (RG 93), pension and bounty-land files (RG 15) | In-person; much digitized on Fold3 |
| County courthouses (county clerks) | Deed books, will books, order books for the county in existence during the event date | In-person or mail request; some microfilmed at Library of Virginia |
| Virginia Historical Society (Virginia Museum of History & Culture), Richmond | Manuscript collections, family papers, unit rosters, published Virginia histories | In-person; some finding aids online |
| Church/denominational archives | Anglican/Episcopal vestry books, Baptist church minutes, Quaker meeting minutes | Varies by denomination; Library of Virginia holds many on microfilm |

---

## Records NOT online

- Original Virginia militia muster rolls at the Library of Virginia are not fully digitized; many require in-person or mail access.
- County deed books and will books for most Virginia counties (other than what appears in FamilySearch collections) exist on microfilm at the Library of Virginia but are browse-only or physical-access only.
- Virginia State Navy records are not fully online; published transcriptions exist in print.
- Church vestry books for many parishes survive in manuscript form at the Library of Virginia or with individual Episcopal dioceses and are not accessible through online databases.
- Revolutionary War land bounty warrants (FamilySearch volume 005301447) are online but browse-only — 341 images with 0% name indexing and no full-text search capability. Each image must be opened individually.

---

## Known record losses

- **1790 federal census destroyed:** Virginia's 1790 federal census schedules were destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. The 1782 personal property tax lists are the standard substitute. This is well-documented; the FamilySearch wiki search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands) references this loss explicitly in the context of substitute sources.
- **County courthouse losses:** Some Virginia county courthouses suffered fire or other losses, particularly in the western counties. The specific records destroyed vary by county; researchers should check the Library of Virginia's "Virginia Courthouse Disasters" finding aid before assuming a county's holdings are complete.
- No tool result in this session stated that any specific collection examined above was destroyed; the 1790 census loss is the major documented gap for this period.

---

## Research tips

- **Start with pension files.** Revolutionary War pension applications (NARA RG 15, accessible via Fold3 and Ancestry) are the single richest source for this period. Widows' pension files in particular often contain marriage evidence, family depositions, and statements from neighbors — information rarely found elsewhere. The FamilySearch wiki result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War confirms pension files are in NARA RG 15.
- **Virginia contributed more soldiers than any other state.** The same source notes that Virginia's Continental Line records are in NARA RG 93 and that militia records are at the Library of Virginia — work both series, as a man might appear in one but not the other.
- **Use the 1782 tax list as your census substitute.** Because the 1790 Virginia census was destroyed, the personal property tax lists (beginning 1782) are the earliest available statewide enumeration. FamilySearch volume 005301449 (full-text searchable) covers 1782–1799.
- **Bounty-land warrants connect veterans to land.** After the war, Virginia awarded bounty lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio. Warrant and survey records at the Library of Virginia link veterans to their land claims and may identify otherwise undocumented service. FamilySearch volume 005301447 (browse-only, 341 images, 1779–1800) covers this series — budget time for image-by-image browsing, as it is 0% name-indexed.
