The wiki-specific pages all resolved to a generic fallback. I now have enough from the collections search, volume search, and wiki search results to compile a thorough, tool-grounded guide. Here it is.

---

# Locality Guide: Indian Territory / Oklahoma (c. 1830–1907)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Status during period:** Indian Territory — land designated by the U.S. federal government under the Indian Removal Act of 1830 for relocated Native American nations. Oklahoma did not achieve statehood until 1907. There were no counties, no state government, and no civil vital registration during this period; the Five Nations governed themselves internally.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Federal government (U.S. Department of the Interior / Bureau of Indian Affairs)
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, ranching, salt production, and small-scale trade within tribal nations; later cattle drives crossing the territory.
- **Ethnic composition:** The Five Civilized Tribes — Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek (Muscogee), and Seminole — were the dominant nations. Each nation also included Freedmen (formerly enslaved people adopted into tribal citizenship after the Civil War). Smaller nations and bands occupied other parts of the territory (Osage, Quapaw, Pawnee, Comanche, Kiowa, and others).
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries were active from the 1820s onward, operating schools and churches inside the territory.
- **Key historical events:** Trail of Tears relocations (1830s–1840s); Five Nations Civil War alliances (1861–1865); post-war Reconstruction treaties (1866) that reorganized tribal citizenship and incorporated Freedmen; Dawes Act (1887) and Dawes Commission enrollment (1893–1914); Oklahoma Territory formed from unassigned lands (1889); statehood 1907.

## Boundary changes

- Before 1830: The territory was under various Spanish, French, and U.S. jurisdictions; tribal groups occupied the Southeast U.S.
- 1830–1889: The entire region was Indian Territory under federal administration. No counties. The Five Nations each governed their own geographic district within it.
- 1889: "Unassigned Lands" opened for settlement; Oklahoma Territory (with county government) created alongside Indian Territory.
- 1907: Both territories merged into the State of Oklahoma, at which point county government and state vital registration began.

Records generated before 1907 follow tribal-nation jurisdiction or federal agency jurisdiction — not county lines, because counties did not exist in Indian Territory. When searching for ancestors in the mid-1800s, do not look for county courthouses: look for tribal nation records and Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) agency records.

---

## Available record types

### Tribal enrollment rolls (the starting point)

This is the foundational record class for tracing families in Indian Territory. Multiple enrollment exercises were conducted at different dates by different authorities:

**The Dawes Rolls (1898–1914)** — The most comprehensive enrollment. Compiled by the Dawes Commission to allot land to individual tribal members. Lists name, age, sex, blood quantum, and tribal affiliation for members of the Five Civilized Tribes and their Freedmen. Persons who did not enroll were ineligible for allotments. FamilySearch has digitized and indexed these records.

**Earlier tribal rolls (pre-Dawes):**
- Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851)
- Drennen Roll (Cherokee, 1852)
- Various Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw, and Seminole rolls from the 1850s–1890s
- Annuity payment rolls (annual BIA records listing tribal members who received treaty annuity payments)

FamilySearch collections directly covering this period:

| Collection | Date Range | Records | FamilySearch Link |
|---|---|---|---|
| Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959 | 1851–1959 | 567,890 indexed | https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432 |
| Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907 | 1834–1907 | 234,567 indexed | https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872 |
| Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965 | 1820–1965 | 123,456 indexed | https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321 |

Volume search returned 1 digitized volume for the Indian Territory 1840–1870 period: image group 002298871, 940 images of Tribal Enrollment Cards, 99% name-indexed and full-text searchable. This is one result from a query that may not represent the complete set — check FamilySearch directly with a broader search for additional volumes.

**Digitization level:** Indexed + images for the Dawes Rolls and the major tribal censuses on FamilySearch. Some annuity rolls are browse-only.

**Critical warning:** Enrollment on the Dawes Rolls was required for land allotment eligibility, so some families refused to enroll or were excluded on contested blood-quantum decisions. Absence from the Dawes Rolls does not prove non-Native ancestry — check the rejected applications file (also held at NARA Fort Worth), which lists people who applied but were denied.

---

### Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) agency records

The BIA maintained agency records for each tribal nation's jurisdiction. These are held at the **National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), Fort Worth, Texas** (the primary repository for Indian Territory federal records) and at **NARA Washington, D.C.**

Record types in BIA agency files include:
- Annuity payment rolls (often annual, listing heads of household by name)
- Correspondence between tribal chiefs and federal agents (may name individuals in disputes, land claims, or welfare cases)
- School enrollment records (BIA-run and mission schools)
- Vital statistics collected at some agencies
- Permits and passes for non-citizens living in the territory

**Access:** NARA Fort Worth is the first place to contact for Indian Territory BIA records. Many are not digitized and require in-person visits or correspondence. NARA's online catalog (archives.gov) has finding aids.

---

### Vital records (civil registration)

**There was no statewide civil vital registration in Indian Territory before Oklahoma statehood in 1907.** The FamilySearch Wiki does not give an earlier registration date for Indian Territory at the territorial or federal level. After 1907, Oklahoma began county-level registration, though compliance was incomplete for the first several years.

For the mid-1800s, vital events (births, marriages, deaths) must be traced through:
- Tribal court marriage records (each nation maintained its own court system)
- Missionary and church registers (see below)
- Annuity rolls (birth of a child would appear the following year when the child is listed)
- Probate and estate files

---

### Church and missionary records

Christian missionaries were active in Indian Territory from the 1820s onward. Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries kept registers of converts, students, and community members. Some churches conducted services and kept records in the tribal languages (Cherokee syllabary, for example).

FamilySearch has indexed 123,456 records in the **Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965** collection (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321).

**Where held:** Denominational archives hold many original registers. The Oklahoma Historical Society (OHS) in Oklahoma City holds significant missionary records. Some are microfilmed at the Family History Library.

**Language note:** Some records are in Cherokee, Creek (Muscogee), or other Native languages, as well as English. Check whether a translator or language guide will be needed.

---

### Census records

**Federal census:** Indian Territory was not included in the standard federal decennial censuses in the same way as states. Tribal members were not enumerated in 1860 or 1870. In 1880, some BIA agents conducted enumerations. The 1900 census included Indian Territory as a separate enumeration district. Check both the regular census and the Indian Territory schedules.

**Tribal censuses:** Each of the Five Nations conducted its own censuses at irregular intervals. These are part of the BIA agency records and/or the tribal nation's own archives.

**Access:** The 1900 Indian Territory census is indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch. Earlier tribal censuses vary widely in access level — some are indexed, some browse-only, some physical only at NARA Fort Worth or tribal archives.

---

### Land records

The land system in Indian Territory was fundamentally different from the surrounding states. Tribal nations held land communally under treaty; there was no private land ownership (and therefore no county deed books) until the Dawes allotment process.

**Record types:**
- Treaty documents establishing tribal land boundaries (held at NARA and the National Archives' online catalog)
- Dawes allotment records: individual allotment files, tract books, and patents issued after enrollment — held at NARA Fort Worth and digitized in the FamilySearch collection **Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907** (234,567 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872)
- Intruder files: federal records of non-citizens who settled illegally in Indian Territory and were subject to removal proceedings — these can name intermarried white citizens and freedmen

**Survey system:** Not applicable in the standard sense before allotment. After allotment, the General Land Office (BLM GLO) issued patents.

---

### Military records

**Relevant conflicts:**
- Trail of Tears era (1830s–1840s): Some tribal members served in or resisted U.S. military operations.
- Civil War (1861–1865): Each of the Five Nations was divided; tribal members served in both Union and Confederate units. Confederate Indian Brigade and Union Indian Home Guard records exist.
- Indian Wars: Various campaigns involving tribes in western Indian Territory.

**Record types:** Service records and pension files are at NARA in Washington, D.C. Confederate pension files for Indian Territory veterans are at the Oklahoma Historical Society. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) holds military records online (subscription).

---

### Probate and court records

Each of the Five Nations maintained its own court system, which handled wills, estates, guardianships, and civil disputes. These tribal court records are a major underused source.

**Where held:** NARA Fort Worth holds a substantial portion of the Five Nations' court records. The Oklahoma Historical Society also holds tribal court records. Some records remain with the tribal nations themselves — contact the tribe's historic preservation office or tribal archives directly.

**Probate records** list heirs and their relationships, making them valuable when vital records are absent.

---

### Newspaper records

Each of the Five Nations published newspapers, some in both English and the tribal language:
- **Cherokee Phoenix / Cherokee Advocate** (Cherokee Nation)
- **Indian Journal** (Creek Nation)
- **Choctaw Telegraph** (Choctaw Nation)

These published legal notices, marriage announcements, deaths, and community news. The Oklahoma Historical Society holds significant newspaper collections. Some are digitized through the Library of Congress Chronicling America project (chroniclingamerica.loc.gov) and the OHS digital collections.

---

### Immigration and emigration records

For the Indian Territory context, the relevant "migration" records are:
- **Removal-era records (1830s–1840s):** Lists of tribal members enrolled for removal, emigration rolls, and subsistence records maintained by the U.S. Army — held at NARA.
- **Intruder permits:** Non-citizens (white settlers, freed persons from outside) who entered Indian Territory legally were issued permits; those who entered illegally were subject to removal. These records name individuals and families.
- **Freedmen records:** Post–Civil War, Freedmen (formerly enslaved persons) were adopted into tribal citizenship under the 1866 Reconstruction treaties. Their enrollment records — including prior names from enslavement — are in the Dawes Rolls Freedmen series and the BIA correspondence files.

---

### Tax records

Indian Territory had no county property tax system. The tribal nations levied their own taxes on non-citizen residents (traders, intruders). These records, where they survive, are in the tribal archives or BIA agency correspondence at NARA.

---

### School records

The BIA and the missionary societies operated schools throughout Indian Territory. BIA school records (enrollment, attendance) are at NARA. Mission school records are at denominational archives and the Oklahoma Historical Society. The Cherokee Nation operated its own school system with surviving records in the Cherokee Nation archives and the OHS.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959; Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907; Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965; Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995 | Free |
| Ancestry (ancestry.com) | U.S. Federal Census collections including Indian Territory schedules; Dawes Rolls index | Subscription |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military records — Civil War Indian Brigade units | Subscription |
| National Archives (archives.gov) | Finding aids for BIA agency records, tribal court records, removal-era rolls, allotment files | Free finding aids; records require request or visit |
| Newspapers.com (newspapers.com) | Historical newspapers including some Oklahoma/Indian Territory titles | Subscription |
| FindAGrave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records | Free |

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| NARA Fort Worth, TX | BIA agency records, Five Nations court records, Dawes allotment files, removal-era rolls, intruder files | In-person; some records requestable by mail/NATF form |
| NARA Washington, D.C. | Service records, pension files, treaty records | In-person; online ordering for some series |
| Oklahoma Historical Society, Oklahoma City | Tribal newspapers, missionary records, Confederate pension files, tribal court records, photographs | In-person; some digital collections online at okhistory.org |
| Cherokee Nation Archives, Tahlequah, OK | Cherokee Nation government records, Cherokee Phoenix/Advocate, school records | Contact tribe directly |
| Chickasaw Nation Archives, Ada, OK | Chickasaw Nation records | Contact tribe directly |
| Choctaw Nation Archives, Durant, OK | Choctaw Nation records | Contact tribe directly |
| Muscogee (Creek) Nation Archives, Okmulgee, OK | Creek Nation court and government records | Contact tribe directly |
| Seminole Nation Museum, Wewoka, OK | Seminole Nation records | Contact tribe/museum directly |
| University of Oklahoma Western History Collections, Norman | Extensive Indian Territory collections | In-person; some digitized |

---

## Records NOT online

- Most BIA agency correspondence files (NARA Fort Worth) — physical only
- Original tribal court records not yet digitized — physical at NARA Fort Worth, OHS, or tribal archives
- Many tribal nation annuity rolls — microfilm or physical
- Dawes rejected applications — not fully indexed online; NARA Fort Worth
- Intruder permit files — physical at NARA Fort Worth
- BIA school records — largely physical or microfilm

---

## Known record losses

No tool result in this survey specifically identified destruction of a particular Indian Territory record set. Coverage gaps exist because many BIA records and tribal records were never microfilmed or digitized, not necessarily because they were destroyed. The Oklahoma Historical Society and NARA Fort Worth are the authoritative sources on what survives for specific tribes and agencies — contact them directly if a series is not found online.

---

## Research tips

**1. Identify the specific tribal nation first.** "Native American in Oklahoma" is not searchable — you must know (or narrow to) which of the Five Nations or smaller tribes the family belonged to. The Dawes Rolls are organized by nation, and each nation's records are separate. If you do not know the nation, start with the 1900 Indian Territory census (which lists tribal affiliation) or family oral history.

**2. Search both the enrolled and the rejected Dawes applications.** Many families who clearly had Native ancestry were rejected on blood-quantum grounds or refused to enroll. The rejected applications file at NARA Fort Worth documents these cases and names family members — it is frequently overlooked.

**3. Freedmen ancestry requires a separate search path.** If your ancestor was an African-descended Freedmen adopted into one of the Five Nations after 1866, they appear in the Dawes Rolls Freedmen series (a separate roll from the "by blood" rolls). Pre-war, they may appear in enslavement records held by tribal members — which are in the tribal archives or BIA records, not in standard U.S. plantation records.

**4. Work backward from allotment to earlier rolls.** The Dawes Roll entry for a person will give age and blood quantum. Use that to calculate birth year and to search earlier annuity rolls or tribal censuses for the same person or their parents.

**5. The FamilySearch wiki search returned this directly about earlier rolls:** "Earlier rolls include the Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851) and the Drennen Roll (1852)" and noted they are "indexed online at FamilySearch and Ancestry" — search the FamilySearch collection Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959 for these. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls)

**6. Missionary and agency records name ordinary people.** The FamilySearch wiki search noted that "Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries kept registers of converts, students, and community members" and that "the Bureau of Indian Affairs maintained agency records (annuity payment rolls, correspondence, school records)." (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records)

**7. Tribal nation records run in a parallel hierarchy to U.S. civil records.** Just as church records run parallel to civil registration elsewhere, the Five Nations' own court, probate, and vital records run parallel to (and often predate or replace) any U.S. government records. Always search both tracks.

**8. Contact the tribal nation's historic preservation office.** Modern tribal governments maintain their own archives and can direct researchers to records that are not accessible through NARA or FamilySearch. Enrollment in a modern tribe also requires demonstrating descent from a Dawes Roll enrollee, so the tribes have strong institutional interest in helping researchers navigate these records.

**9. The 1866 Reconstruction treaties are key documents.** After the Civil War, each of the Five Nations signed a new treaty with the United States that reorganized tribal citizenship (including Freedmen) and set terms for allotment. Reading the specific treaty for the relevant nation explains the citizenship categories you will find in subsequent rolls.

---

---

This survey covers Indian Territory and Oklahoma from approximately 1830 to statehood in 1907 — the era when the region was governed as tribal land under federal oversight rather than as a U.S. state. The most important records for this period are tribal enrollment rolls (especially the Dawes Rolls, available free on FamilySearch), Bureau of Indian Affairs agency files held at the National Archives in Fort Worth, the Five Nations' own court and government records at the Oklahoma Historical Society and tribal archives, and missionary records. The biggest practical trap is searching for county courthouses or civil vital records — there were none in Indian Territory before 1907, and all the key records of this period flow through tribal governments and federal agencies instead.

The recommended next step is to identify which specific tribal nation the ancestor belonged to, then search the FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" as a starting point, working outward to NARA Fort Worth for undigitized BIA and tribal court records.

output.text_response:
The guide has been saved as `loc_001` in your project's research log. Here's what the locality-guide agent found:

---

**Pennsylvania Quaker Records, Late 1700s**

Pennsylvania had no statewide vital registration until 1906, so for Quaker families in the late eighteenth century, **meeting records kept by the Society of Friends are the primary — and often the only — documentation** for births, marriages, and deaths.

### Key Repositories

1. **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College** — Holds original minutes, membership registers, marriage certificates, and certificates of removal for Pennsylvania meetings.
2. **Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College** — Another major repository for the same record types.
3. **FamilySearch (microfilm/digital)** — Has microfilmed many Pennsylvania meeting records. One digitized browse-only volume (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800, 145 images) is available online; the bulk of monthly meeting registers for Chester, Bucks, Abington, and other key counties remain on microfilm.

### Best Starting Point

**William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*** — a name-indexed printed abstract of meeting records, available on Ancestry and in major genealogical libraries. It will direct you to the right meeting and the right microfilm roll before you need to browse any unindexed volume.

### Recommended Approach

Identify which specific **monthly meeting** served the township where your ancestors lived. Once that meeting is pinned down, search:
- The FamilySearch Catalog
- Swarthmore's finding aids
- Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia*

…together to pull every surviving record for the family.

quirks: Pennsylvania did not mandate statewide civil vital registration until 1906 — Quaker meeting records are the primary documentation for births, marriages, and deaths in the late 1700s, not a supplement to civil records.
Quaker records are organized by monthly meeting, not by township or county — identify the specific meeting that served the family's township before searching.
Certificates of removal are precise migration records: each transfer of membership between meetings generated a dated certificate naming family members; search both the sending and receiving meeting.

Disownment records (expulsion from the meeting) document the person's name, offense, and date — common in 1775-1800 for marrying outside the meeting, bearing arms, or taking loyalty oaths during the Revolution.
Quaker marriage certificates were signed by all attendees — the witness list identifies extended family, neighbors, and community connections.
The Philadelphia Yearly Meeting governed meetings in both Pennsylvania and New Jersey — families near the Delaware River may have belonged to New Jersey meetings; search both sides.

Volume search returned only 1 digitized volume for this period (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, image group 001188322, 145 images, browse-only); most monthly meeting registers are on microfilm at the Family History Library or in physical archives at Swarthmore or Haverford — search the FamilySearch Catalog by individual meeting name.
William Wade Hinshaw's Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy (6 volumes) abstracts Pennsylvania meeting records by name and is the fastest entry point before consulting original microfilm.
Pennsylvania county tax lists from 1769 and 1779 onward can locate a family in a specific township annually — use these to bridge the pre-1790 census gap.
Chester County (1682) gave rise to Delaware County in 1789 — events near the boundary after 1789 may be recorded under either county; check both.

Pennsylvania in the late 1700s had no statewide requirement to register births, marriages, or deaths — that did not come until 1906 — so for Quaker families in that era, the meeting records kept by the Society of Friends are the primary (and often the only) documentation for vital events. From here, the next step is to identify which specific monthly meeting served the township where your ancestors lived — once that is pinned down, the FamilySearch Catalog, the Swarthmore finding aids, and Hinshaw can be searched together to pull every surviving record for that family.

---

# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh (Allegheny County), Pennsylvania (1860–1910)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **County formed:** 1788 from Washington and Westmoreland Counties; Pittsburgh incorporated 1816.
- **Key annexation:** The City of Allegheny was absorbed into Pittsburgh in **1907** — workers there before that date had separate municipal records.
- **Mill towns are separate jurisdictions:** Homestead, Braddock, McKeesport, and Duquesne are their own municipalities within Allegheny County. Vital records for workers in those towns are filed at the borough or township level, not in Pittsburgh city records.
- **Workforce profile:** Irish, German, Welsh, English (arriving earlier), then massive waves of Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian immigrant labor from the 1880s onward — each clustering in specific mill towns and parishes.

---

## Records That Exist and Where to Find Them

### Civil Vital Records
| Record Type | Date Range | FamilySearch Collection | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Death Certificates | 1906–1968 | Collection 2255317 (4.2M records, indexed + images) | Statewide registration begins ~1906 |
| County Marriages | 1885–1950 | Collection 1921317 (524K records) | — |
| Civil Marriages | 1677–1950 | Collection 1571957 (312K records) | — |
| **Birth Certificates (1860–1905)** | **Gap** | **None indexed online** | Church baptism registers are the primary substitute |

### Church Records
Ethnic Catholic parishes (Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian) are explicitly identified by the FamilySearch Wiki as **"the best source for immigrant family data"** — often the only source for pre-1906 births and marriages.
- **FamilySearch collection:** Pennsylvania Church Records 1708–1985 (~1.2M indexed records + images)
- **Diocese of Pittsburgh archives:** Catholic parish registers — contact for inventory; appointment required
- **Languages:** German (Lutheran/Reformed registers through the 1880s); Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian; Latin headings in Catholic registers

### Federal Census (1860–1910)
- Lists occupation for every adult — directly identifies steel and iron workers
- 1880 census adds relationship to head + parents' birthplaces — critical for immigrant families
- **Mortality schedules (1860, 1870, 1880):** Name workers who died in the preceding year with occupation and cause of death — often the only death record for an industrial accident victim before 1906
- *Note: 1890 census largely destroyed (nationwide loss)*

### Probate Records
- **Collection 1999196** (3.2M images, 1683–1994) — **browse-only, no name index**; must be searched page by page at FamilySearch

### Naturalization Records
- **Critical cutoff: 1906.** Pre-1906 naturalizations can be filed in any court — check Allegheny County courthouse, Pennsylvania courts, and NARA Philadelphia branch.
- Post-1906 petitions are far more detailed: birthplace, arrival date and port, occupation, physical description, witnesses.
- **Digitized volume** (imageGroupNumber 008120443, 1790–1915): 15% name-indexed, rest browse-only; in English and German.

### Immigration / Passenger Records
- Most Eastern European immigrants arrived via New York (Castle Garden before 1892, Ellis Island after). Earlier Irish/Germans also came through Baltimore, Philadelphia, New Orleans.
- Indexed at **Ancestry** (subscription) and **FamilySearch** (free) for Ellis Island era. Examine the full manifest — all family members traveling together are listed.

### Military Records
- Civil War service and pension files (many Pittsburgh steel workers were veterans) — NARA; Fold3
- WWI draft registration cards (1917–1918) — Fold3
- Pension files list postwar address, family members, and occupation — useful for placing veterans in Pittsburgh after the war

### Cemetery Records
- Allegheny Cemetery (founded 1844), St. Mary's Cemetery, ethnic Catholic parish cemeteries, mill-town cemeteries
- **Find A Grave** (free) and **BillionGraves** have broad coverage for Allegheny County

### Newspapers
- Pittsburgh Gazette, Pittsburgh Post, Pittsburgh Dispatch; foreign-language ethnic press (Polish, Slovak, Croatian) from the 1880s–1900s
- **Content unique to this era:** mill accident and explosion reports, coroner's inquest notices naming workers, labor dispute and strike coverage, obituaries
- Available at **Newspapers.com** (subscription); Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds local history runs

---

## Occupational & Industrial Sources (Unique to Pittsburgh)

These records have no equivalent in most genealogical guides and are central to steel-era research:

| Source | What It Contains | Where Held |
|---|---|---|
| **Company employment records** (Carnegie Steel, U.S. Steel, predecessors) | Payroll, hire dates, mill assignments | **Senator John Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh); **Rivers of Steel archives** — contact directly; not digitized |
| **Union membership lists** (Amalgamated Association of Iron, Steel Workers) | Member names; useful before the Homestead Strike crushed the union in 1892 | Pennsylvania State Archives; Heinz History Center — inquire directly |
| **City directories** (annual, 1860s–1910s) | Head of household, occupation, address — fills gaps between census years | **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** holds runs from the 1810s; some years on Ancestry |
| **State factory inspector reports** | Names workers in accidents and fatalities; lists mill conditions | **Pennsylvania State Archives**, Harrisburg |
| **Coroner's inquest records** | Names deceased worker, witnesses, employer, cause of death for mill accidents | **Allegheny County courthouse** — not indexed online |

---

## Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | Best For | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Death certs (1906+), marriages, probate images, naturalization images, church records | Free |
| Ancestry (ancestry.com) | Federal censuses 1860–1910, Ellis Island manifests, some city directories | Subscription |
| **Senator John Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh) | Company employment records, immigration collections, labor history | In-person; contact archives |
| **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** | City directories 1810s+, local history, newspapers | In-person + some digital |
| **Diocese of Pittsburgh archives** | Catholic ethnic parish registers (baptism, marriage, burial) | Contact; appointment required |
| Allegheny County Courthouse | Probate, pre-1906 naturalization petitions, deed records, coroner inquests | In-person / mail |
| National Archives at Philadelphia | Federal court naturalizations (pre-1906), immigration records | In-person; NARA online ordering |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Factory inspector reports, state-level records | In-person; some via PA Digital Collections |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Civil War service/pensions, WWI draft cards | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records, Allegheny County burials | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Pittsburgh newspapers | Subscription |

---

## Known Gaps and Losses

- **No indexed birth collection for 1860–1905** — church baptism registers are the substitute; consult Diocese of Pittsburgh archives and FamilySearch microfilm
- **1890 federal census destroyed** (nationwide)
- **Company employment records have fragmentary survival** — not all Carnegie Steel or predecessor firm records survived; contact Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel directly to know what exists before making a research trip
- **Probate and naturalization records are largely browse-only** in FamilySearch — plan time for image-by-image searching

---

## Recommended Research Sequence

1. **Census runs (1860, 1870, 1880, 1900, 1910)** — establish the family's location, ages, occupations, and birthplaces year by year
2. **City directories (Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh)** — fill the intercensal years with address and occupation
3. **Ethnic Catholic parish registers (Diocese of Pittsburgh archives)** — birth/baptism, marriage, and burial records for immigrant families, especially pre-1906
4. **Post-1906 Pennsylvania death certificates (FamilySearch collection 2255317)** — fully indexed and searchable
5. **Naturalization records (Allegheny County courthouse + NARA Philadelphia)** — especially post-1906 petitions for detailed biographical data
6. **Company employment records and coroner inquests (Heinz History Center, Allegheny County courthouse)** — if you need to document a specific mill, hire date, or industrial accident death
7. **Newspapers.com** — obituaries, accident reports, strike-era coverage

The most important single step not covered by any online database is contacting the **Senator John Heinz History Center** in Pittsburgh — it holds the most concentrated collection of Carnegie Steel-era industrial and labor records, and its holdings are not searchable online.

---

# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh (Allegheny County), Pennsylvania (1860–1910)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Allegheny County was established in 1788 from parts of Washington and Westmoreland Counties. Pittsburgh was incorporated as a city in 1816.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pittsburgh
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** The population data tool returned no figures for this standardPlace, so no census-year counts can be stated from tool results. Wikipedia's Pittsburgh article confirms the city grew dramatically through this period as the center of America's steel industry.
- **Economy:** Iron and steel production (Carnegie Steel and predecessors), glass manufacturing, coal mining, river trade. Workers were employed at large mill complexes along the Monongahela, Allegheny, and Ohio river valleys.
- **Ethnic composition:** Massive waves of immigrant labor documented in the Wikipedia article: Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian workers, with Welsh and English ironworkers arriving earlier. Each ethnic group tended to cluster in specific mill towns and neighborhoods.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic parishes serving specific ethnic communities (Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian) are described as essential sources in the FamilySearch Wiki search results (source: [Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records)). German Lutheran and Reformed, Presbyterian, Episcopalian, and Methodist congregations also served the area.
- **Key historical events:** The Homestead Strike (1892) at Carnegie Steel's Homestead Works; the opening of the Bessemer converter era in the 1870s; the consolidation into Carnegie Steel (1892) and then U.S. Steel (1901). These events directly affect what company and union records may survive.

## Boundary changes

The City of Pittsburgh annexed the City of Allegheny (across the Allegheny River) in 1907, bringing its records under Pittsburgh's administration. Many mill communities — Homestead, Braddock, McKeesport, Duquesne — are separate municipalities within Allegheny County, not within Pittsburgh city limits, so vital records for mill workers may be filed at the municipality level rather than Pittsburgh's. If your ancestor lived in one of these towns, search for their specific borough or township records, not city records.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** The Pennsylvania Vital Records wiki page did not return a jurisdiction-specific page (the tool returned only generic content), so no specific statewide registration date can be stated from tool results. The general wiki overview confirms that many U.S. states did not require statewide registration until the early 1900s. Pennsylvania's statewide death certificates begin in the FamilySearch collection in 1906 (collection 2255317), which is consistent with a statewide requirement starting around that time. For births and marriages in the 1860–1905 period, local registration was uneven.
- **What exists:** Pennsylvania Death Certificates, 1906–1968 — FamilySearch collection 2255317, 4,218,763 indexed records with images (indexed + images level). Pennsylvania County Marriages, 1885–1950 — collection 1921317, 524,189 indexed records. Pennsylvania Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 — collection 1571957, 312,045 records. Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 — collection 1502909, 198,765 records, no images.
- **Where held:** Online at FamilySearch (free); Allegheny County courthouse for physical originals.
- **Gaps:** Birth certificates for the 1860–1905 period are a significant gap — no indexed birth collection for that window appeared in tool results. Pre-1906 death registration is similarly sparse.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism and burial registers are the primary substitute (see Church Records below).

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (with ethnic-specific parishes — Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian), German Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Episcopalian, Methodist. The FamilySearch Wiki search results explicitly identify Catholic ethnic parishes as "often the best source for family data" for immigrant steel workers ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records)).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. The Pennsylvania Church Records collection (collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) covers 1708–1985 and contains 1,245,830 indexed records with 607,220 images — note this collection ID appears to be a test fixture; verify it directly at FamilySearch before relying on record counts.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch microfilm holdings; diocesan archives (Diocese of Pittsburgh for Roman Catholic records); local parish offices for more recent registers. The FamilySearch Church Records wiki page also returned only generic content, so consult the Diocese of Pittsburgh archives directly for a comprehensive inventory.
- **Language:** German-language records for Lutheran and Reformed congregations through at least the 1880s. Slovak, Polish, Croatian, and Italian registers will be in those languages. Latin is used in Catholic sacramental headings.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** Available for 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900, and 1910 (1890 was largely destroyed). The 1870–1900 censuses list occupation for each adult, making them directly useful for identifying steel and iron workers. The 1880 census also records the relationship of every household member to the head, and the birthplace of each person's father and mother — critical for immigrant families.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct state censuses in this period; no intercensal enumerations fill the gaps.
- **Mortality schedules:** Federal mortality schedules covering deaths in the year preceding each census, 1860–1880, name the deceased with occupation and cause of death — directly useful for mill accident and industrial disease deaths.
- **Access:** Federal censuses are indexed + images at Ancestry (subscription) and FamilySearch (free for 1860–1880 and 1900–1910 via Ancestry partnership).

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions.
- **Date range:** Allegheny County probate records date from county formation (1788). Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994 — FamilySearch collection 1999196 — contains 3,200,560 images but 0 indexed records: this is a browse-only image collection. The corresponding digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 008120441, 1,180 images) is also 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — you must browse image by image with no search capability.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Register of Wills, Pittsburgh; FamilySearch images online (browse-only).

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Pennsylvania is a state-land (metes and bounds) state, not a federal rectangular-survey state. The Land and Property wiki page returned only generic content for this call.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax records. For steel-era workers renting company housing (as many did in mill towns), deed records are less directly useful than they would be for property-owning families.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds, Pittsburgh, for deeds. Tax records are at the county assessment office.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** The Civil War (1861–1865) falls just before or at the start of the target period; the Spanish-American War (1898) and World War I draft (1917–1918, just after the period) bracket it. Many Pittsburgh steel workers were Civil War veterans.
- **Record types:** Civil War service records and pension files at NARA; Civil War draft registration records (1863 conscription); WWI draft registration cards (1917–1918) at Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/). Pension files list the veteran's address, family members, and often occupation — useful for placing a worker in Pittsburgh after the war.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 online (subscription).

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Allegheny Cemetery (Pittsburgh, founded 1844), St. Mary's Cemetery, and numerous ethnic Catholic parish cemeteries. Mill towns had their own cemeteries.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers many Allegheny County burials. BillionGraves is an additional option.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records at individual cemeteries. Allegheny Cemetery has historical records at its office.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The Pittsburgh Gazette (founded 1786, continuing through the period under various names), the Pittsburgh Post, the Pittsburgh Dispatch, and foreign-language papers serving immigrant communities (Polish, Slovak, Croatian ethnic press emerged in the 1880s–1900s).
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) has historical Pittsburgh papers (subscription). The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds local history collections including city directories from the 1810s, noted in the FamilySearch Wiki search results ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records)).
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices, but also — uniquely important for this period — labor dispute coverage, strike lists, accident reports from mill explosions and fires, and coroner's inquest notices that name workers by name.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** Most Eastern European immigrants to Pittsburgh arrived through the Port of New York (Castle Garden through 1892, then Ellis Island from 1892 onward). Earlier Irish and German immigrants also came through Baltimore, Philadelphia, and New Orleans.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests (name-indexed at Ancestry and FamilySearch for Ellis Island era); naturalization records at the Allegheny County courthouse and the National Archives at Philadelphia — the FamilySearch Wiki search result explicitly names both repositories ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records)). The FamilySearch digitized volume for Pennsylvania Naturalization Records (imageGroupNumber 008120443, covering 1790–1915) is 15% name-indexed with images, in English and German — partially searchable but mostly browse-only.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (free, partially indexed); Ancestry (subscription, more extensively indexed for Ellis Island manifests); National Archives at Philadelphia for pre-1906 naturalization petitions.
- **Content note:** Post-1906 naturalization petitions (filed after the Bureau of Immigration took over) contain detailed biographical information — birthplace, date and port of arrival, occupation, physical description, and names of witnesses. These are significantly more informative than pre-1906 records. Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents — examine the full manifest for all family members when researching an immigrant family.

### Tax records

- **Types:** County property tax assessment records; personal property tax.
- **Date range:** Allegheny County tax records run from county formation.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County assessment office and the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Substitute value:** Tax records are especially useful for the 1860–1900 period to place a worker at a specific address between census years, and to track property acquisition as workers moved from renter to owner status.

### Occupational and industrial records (unique to this locality)

This category is central to Pittsburgh steel-era research and deserves special attention:

- **Company employment records:** Fragmentary survival. The FamilySearch Wiki search result ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records)) states that some Carnegie Steel and related company records survive at the **Heinz History Center** (Senator John Heinz History Center, Pittsburgh) and the **Rivers of Steel archives**. These are not indexed online — contact both institutions directly.
- **Union membership lists:** The Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers (the major union before the Homestead Strike crushed it in 1892) kept membership rolls. Surviving records may be at labor archives. The Pennsylvania State Archives and the Historical Society of Western Pennsylvania (now the Heinz History Center) are the first places to inquire.
- **City directories:** The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds Pittsburgh city directories from the 1810s onward. These list head of household, occupation, and address — published annually, they place a worker at a specific address in every year between censuses. This is one of the most important sources for steel-era Pittsburgh research.
- **State factory inspector reports:** Pennsylvania's factory inspection system, noted in the FamilySearch Wiki ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records)), generated annual reports that sometimes list accidents, fatalities, and the workers involved by name.
- **Coroner's inquest records:** Mill accidents were frequent. Allegheny County coroner's inquest records name the deceased worker, witnesses, employer, and cause of death. These are held at the Allegheny County courthouse and have not been systematically indexed online.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Pennsylvania Death Certificates 1906–1968 (4.2M indexed records, collection 2255317); Pennsylvania County Marriages 1885–1950 (524K records, collection 1921317); Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (3.2M images, browse-only, collection 1999196); Pennsylvania Naturalization Records (digitized volume 008120443, 15% indexed) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census collection (ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) including 1860–1910 censuses; Ellis Island passenger manifests | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records for Allegheny County | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Pittsburgh newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military records including Civil War service, pension, and WWI draft | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Pre-1906 naturalization petitions; federal census originals | Free to search; copies fee |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` tool returned a total of 3 digitized volumes matching Pennsylvania for this period — the full result set. These are broad Pennsylvania-level volumes, not Allegheny County-specific digitized volumes. This is a significant coverage gap: many county-level records may exist only on microfilm or in physical repositories rather than as named online collections.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Senator John Heinz History Center, Pittsburgh | Company employment records (Carnegie Steel and related firms); immigration records; labor history collections | In-person; contact archives department |
| Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area archives | Industrial and mill records | Contact directly |
| Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh | City directories from 1810s; local history collection | In-person and some digital |
| Allegheny County Courthouse | Probate records (Register of Wills); naturalization petitions (pre-1906); deed records; coroner's inquest records | In-person / mail request |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | State factory inspector reports; state-level records | In-person; some records via PA Digital Collections |
| National Archives at Philadelphia | Pre-1906 federal court naturalization records; some immigration records | In-person; NARA online ordering |
| Diocese of Pittsburgh archives | Catholic parish registers (baptism, marriage, burial) for ethnic parishes | Contact archives; appointment required |
| Historical Society of Western Pennsylvania (now part of Heinz History Center) | Union records; labor movement papers; manuscript collections | In-person |

---

## Records NOT online

The following record types exist for this place and period but are not systematically available in any online database:

- **Company employment records** (Carnegie Steel, U.S. Steel, and predecessor firms) — fragmentary survival; held at Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel archives, not digitized
- **Union membership lists** (Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers) — contact labor archives
- **City directories** (annual, 1860–1910) — available in print at Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh; some may be on Ancestry, but the run is not fully digitized online
- **Coroner's inquest records** (mill and industrial accident deaths) — at Allegheny County courthouse, not indexed online
- **State factory inspector reports** — at Pennsylvania State Archives, not indexed online
- **Pre-1906 birth registration** — no indexed birth collection for Allegheny County 1860–1905 appeared in tool results; church baptism registers are the primary alternative
- **Catholic ethnic parish registers** (pre-1880 especially) — some on FamilySearch microfilm; many remain at diocesan or parish archives

---

## Known record losses

No tool result in this survey specifically identified the destruction of Allegheny County's own registers. The destruction of the 1890 federal census is a nationwide loss, not a local one, and affects Pittsburgh as it does everywhere. The absence of indexed birth collections for 1860–1905 in the `collections_search` results is a coverage gap — it does not confirm that no local birth records were kept, only that none are indexed online. Consult the Pennsylvania State Archives for any surviving local birth registers filed before statewide registration.

---

## Research tips

- **City directories are the backbone of year-by-year tracking.** The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds city directories from the 1810s onward, noted at [Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records). For a worker who does not appear in a census, the directory gives occupation and address for every intervening year.
- **Ethnic Catholic parishes are the best source for immigrant family data.** The FamilySearch Wiki explicitly identifies Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian parish registers as the primary genealogical source for immigrant steel workers ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records)). Identify the ethnic parish that served the neighborhood where your ancestor lived, then contact the Diocese of Pittsburgh archives.
- **Naturalization records: the 1906 cutoff matters enormously.** Pre-1906 naturalizations can be filed in any court of record (federal, state, or local), so check the Allegheny County courthouse, the Pennsylvania courts, and the National Archives at Philadelphia. Post-1906 petitions are far more detailed biographically and were centralized under the Bureau of Immigration.
- **Don't overlook mill-town municipal records.** Homestead, Braddock, McKeesport, Duquesne, and other Carnegie Steel communities are separate municipalities in Allegheny County. Vital records and tax records for workers in those towns are filed at the borough or township level, not in Pittsburgh city records.
- **The 1892 Homestead Strike disrupted mill employment.** Workers who were union members before 1892 and non-union or blacklisted afterward may have different surname spellings in records (Americanization of immigrant names accelerated in this period). Search for variant spellings in all collections.
- **Mortality schedules name industrial deaths.** The federal mortality schedule for 1860, 1870, and 1880 (attached to the census) records every person who died in the preceding twelve months, with occupation and cause of death. For a mill worker who died of an industrial accident, this may be the only surviving death record from that period.
- **The four wiki place pages (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) all returned generic content** rather than Pennsylvania- or Allegheny-specific pages. This is a tool coverage gap for this invocation. Consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy for current, jurisdiction-specific guidance.

---

Pittsburgh in the late 1800s was one of the largest industrial centers in the United States, and the records left behind reflect both the standard genealogical toolkit and a distinctive layer of occupational and labor sources. The most important standard records are the federal census (1860–1910, with occupation listed), post-1906 Pennsylvania death certificates (FamilySearch collection 2255317, fully indexed), marriage records from 1885 onward (collection 1921317), and naturalization petitions at the Allegheny County courthouse and National Archives at Philadelphia. Statewide birth registration did not produce a complete indexed collection before 1906, so Catholic ethnic parish registers — Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian — are often the only source for births and marriages in that earlier window. The two repositories that hold the most uniquely Pittsburgh-industrial material are the Senator John Heinz History Center (company employment records, immigration collections) and the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh (city directories, local history). Records exist that no online database contains: company payroll and employment records, coroner's inquest files for mill accident deaths, and union membership lists all require in-person or mail contact with those repositories.

The natural next step is to identify which specific individual or family you are tracing, determine which mill town or Pittsburgh neighborhood they lived in, and build a research plan that sequences these sources — starting with the census runs to establish the family's location year by year, then the city directories to fill the gaps, and then the ethnic parish for vital events.

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (1793 — Yellow Fever Epidemic)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Philadelphia County** was founded in 1682; city and county were coextensive in 1793.
- **Population:** ~50,000 residents; the epidemic killed roughly 5,000 (one-tenth of the population) between August and November 1793.
- **Adjacent districts:** Northern Liberties and Southwark were legally distinct from the city — families there may have records filed under those district names, not "Philadelphia."

---

## Epidemic-Specific Documentary Sources *(most targeted for this research)*

These have no parallel in ordinary genealogical work:

1. **Mathew Carey's *"A Short Account of the Malignant Fever"* (1793)** — Multiple editions were published in 1793, each containing an appendix with names of the dead. This is the closest thing to a comprehensive mortality name list for the epidemic. Digitized and in the public domain on HathiTrust and Google Books. Also held at the **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)**.

2. **Committee of Health records** — The citizens' relief committee organized food, medicine, and money distribution during the epidemic. Its minutes, correspondence, and relief lists name individuals who died, received aid, or served as volunteers. Held at **HSP** and the **Philadelphia City Archives**.

3. **Bush Hill Hospital records** — The emergency epidemic hospital kept patient admission and death records. Held at HSP and the Philadelphia City Archives (completeness unconfirmed — verify directly with those repositories).

4. **Mayor Matthew Clarkson's accounts and city administration records** — Key documentary source named in the historical record. Held at the **Philadelphia City Archives**.

5. **Physician case notes** — Benjamin Rush and other doctors kept named patient records. Rush's papers are at the **Library Company of Philadelphia** and the **College of Physicians of Philadelphia**.

---

## Church Records *(primary substitute for civil registration)*

Pennsylvania had **no civil registration** of births, marriages, or deaths until 1906. Church burial registers are the essential record type for 1793 deaths.

| Congregation | Notes |
|---|---|
| Christ Church (Episcopal) | One of the largest in the city; burial register survives; microfilmed |
| Gloria Dei / Old Swedes' (Swedish Lutheran) | Oldest church in PA (1698); burial records survive from well before 1793 |
| St. Peter's Episcopal, St. Paul's Episcopal | Active in 1793 |
| Society of Friends (Quakers) | Vital registers at Haverford College and Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore; FamilySearch holds 1 browse-only Yearly Meeting Minutes volume (image group 001188322), which is administrative — not a vital-event source |
| German Lutheran (Zion, St. Michael's) & German Reformed | Registers in German/Latin; some transcribed by the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania |
| Roman Catholic (St. Mary's, Holy Trinity) | Archives of the Archdiocese of Philadelphia |
| Free African congregations (St. Thomas's African Episcopal, Bethel AME) | Critical for researching Black Philadelphian families who led epidemic relief; records at AME archives and HSP |

**Key warning:** Most 1793 church registers are in microfilm or physical form only — very little is name-searchable online. Identify the family's denomination first, then contact the relevant archive directly.

---

## Census Records

- **1790 federal census** (3 years before the epidemic) — Heads of household only, fully indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **1800 federal census** (7 years after) — A household present in 1790 but absent or reduced in 1800 may reflect epidemic deaths, flight, or remarriage.
- **Philadelphia ward tax lists (1793–1794)** — Intercensal substitute; comparing pre- and post-epidemic lists can reveal who disappeared from the rolls. Held at the Philadelphia City Archives and HSP.

---

## Probate Records

The epidemic produced a massive wave of estate administrations in late 1793 and into 1794 — far above normal volume. Types include wills, letters of administration, guardianship petitions (for orphaned children), and inventories.

- **FamilySearch:** Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994 (collection 1999196; 3.2 million images, **browse-only** — not name-indexed). Browse the Philadelphia County will books by date (fall 1793 through 1794) rather than by name.
- **Physical originals:** Register of Wills, Philadelphia City Hall; Philadelphia City Archives.
- **Tip:** An intestate administration filed suddenly in fall 1793 with no will is consistent with a rapid epidemic death. An orphaned child from 1793 may appear in guardianship petitions filed in 1794 or later.

---

## Newspaper Records

Philadelphia had the richest newspaper press in early America in 1793 — several papers published weekly mortality bills during the epidemic listing numbers and sometimes ward-by-ward names of the dead.

- **Key papers:** *Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser*, *Federal Gazette*, *General Advertiser*
- **Where held:** Library Company of Philadelphia, HSP, American Antiquarian Society
- **Online:** Chronicling America (https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/) — 1793 Philadelphia coverage is limited; Newspapers.com (subscription) — verify exact 1793 holdings; Readex/NewsBank (subscription, via libraries)

---

## Other Record Types

| Record type | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Almshouse records** | Philadelphia Almshouse (Blockley) admitted epidemic victims; admission and death registers at Philadelphia City Archives |
| **Land/deed records** | Properties changing hands rapidly in late 1793 via estate or sheriff's sale may document epidemic-disrupted families; Philadelphia deed books at the Philadelphia City Archives — not online |
| **Military/pension records** | A widow whose husband (a Revolutionary War veteran) died in 1793 may have filed a widow's pension, naming the death; records at NARA (via Fold3) |
| **Immigration records** | Many 1793 residents were recent immigrants; Saint-Domingue (Haitian) refugees arrived in 1793 and are linked to the epidemic's introduction; pre-1820 passenger lists are fragmentary — NARA Mid-Atlantic Region, partly published by GSP |
| **Naturalization records** | Philadelphia naturalizations at the Philadelphia City Archives, partially indexed by HSP |

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | What's there | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | PA Probate Records 1683–1994 (browse-only); Quaker Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (browse-only); PA Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 | Free |
| Ancestry | 1790 & 1800 federal censuses (indexed); some city directory collections | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War pension files (widow's pensions for 1793 deaths) | Subscription |
| Chronicling America | Some early Philadelphia newspapers (1793 coverage limited) | Free |
| HathiTrust/Google Books | Mathew Carey's epidemic accounts (digitized, public domain) | Free |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Key holdings |
|---|---|
| **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)** — https://hsp.org/ | Committee of Health records; Bush Hill records; Carey papers; church register transcripts; tax lists; Rush papers |
| **Philadelphia City Archives** — https://www.phila.gov/departments/department-of-records/philadelphia-city-archives/ | City admin records; almshouse registers; deed books; ward tax lists; naturalization records |
| **Library Company of Philadelphia** — https://librarycompany.org/ | Rush papers; colonial newspapers; Carey editions |
| **College of Physicians of Philadelphia** — https://www.collegeofphysicians.org/ | Physician case notes; medical society records |
| **Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg)** — https://www.phmc.pa.gov/Archives/ | Land records; some early county records |
| **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore** — https://www.swarthmore.edu/friends-historical-library | Quaker vital registers (births, marriages, deaths) |
| **Haverford College Quaker Collection** — https://www.haverford.edu/library/special-collections | Additional Quaker registers |
| **Archives of the Archdiocese of Philadelphia** — https://archphila.org/archives/ | Catholic church records |
| **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania (GSP)** — https://www.genpa.org/ | Published name indexes to many Philadelphia church records |

---

## Critical Research Tips

1. **Start with Mathew Carey's name list** — it is the closest thing to a comprehensive mortality roster and is freely available online.
2. **Identify the denomination first** — then go directly to that congregation's archive. A misspelled name in a German Lutheran register will not surface in a general name search.
3. **Use probate records as a proxy** — browse the Philadelphia County will books for late 1793 and early 1794 (the browse-only FamilySearch collection) for the spike in administrations.
4. **For Black Philadelphian families:** The Committee of Health records are essential — they name the Black relief workers (led by Absalom Jones and Richard Allen) and many African American individuals who do not appear in predominantly white church registers.
5. **Bracket with the censuses** — compare 1790 and 1800 entries by ward; households that vanished or shrank often reflect epidemic mortality.
6. **Absence of an online record means almost nothing for this period** — the vast majority of 1793 Philadelphia records are physical or microfilm only.
7. **Some deaths were never recorded at all** — clergy fled or were overwhelmed; the poor and those buried in common/potter's field graves are systematically underrepresented in surviving records.

I now have enough from the tools to compile a thorough guide. Note: the four `wiki_place_page` calls all returned a generic fallback page rather than Philadelphia- or Pennsylvania-specific content, and the `wiki_read` calls for the Church Records and Probate Records pages resolved to the same generic fallback.
