# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States (1620-1700)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Plymouth Colony founded 1620; Massachusetts Bay Colony founded 1628; merged into Province of Massachusetts Bay 1691
- **County seat / administrative center:** Boston (Massachusetts Bay); Plymouth (Plymouth Colony)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** English Crown (colonial charter)
- **Population during period:** Approximately 20,000 settlers arrived 1630-1640 (Great Migration, per Wikipedia); total colonial population grew through the century
- **Economy:** Agriculture, fishing, timber, trade; subsistence farming in early decades
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English Puritan settlers; small number of non-Puritan English; Indigenous peoples (Wampanoag, Massachusetts, Nipmuc, and others)
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (Puritan) as the established church of the colony; small number of other Protestant dissenters
- **Key historical events:** Great Migration 1630-1640; formation of first four counties 1643 (Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk); King Philip's War 1675-1676 (destroyed several towns and records); Plymouth Colony absorbed into Province of Massachusetts Bay 1691

## Boundary changes
- Plymouth Colony (1620-1691) and Massachusetts Bay Colony (1628-1691) coexisted as separate jurisdictions. A person or family could appear in either colony's records, or both.
- Four counties formed in 1643 (Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk): records created before 1643 route to the colonial General Court; records from 1643 onward route to the relevant county's probate court and registry of deeds.
- Plymouth Colony was absorbed into the Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691. Plymouth Colony records (1620-1691) are published and indexed separately and must be searched as a distinct trail.
- King Philip's War (1675-1676) resulted in the destruction of several town records and the physical destruction of some settlements; gaps in town vital records for the late 1670s in affected towns reflect this.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Town-level mandate began 1639 (Massachusetts Bay Colony), per the FamilySearch wiki_search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records). This is a **town-level** requirement, not a statewide or colony-wide civil registration system. The start date and completeness of surviving records varies town by town. Statewide civil registration did not begin until 1844.
- **What exists:** Births, marriages, and deaths recorded in town books from approximately 1639 onward for many towns. Plymouth Colony maintained similar town records from 1620.
- **Where held:** Original records held by individual town clerks; many are also at the Massachusetts Archives (Boston). The published 'Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850' series (Tanner-Corbin series) abstracts over 200 Massachusetts towns and is the recommended first step (FamilySearch wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).
- **FamilySearch collection:** Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890 (collection ID 2061550), approximately 3.4 million records with images — indexed and browsable at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550
- **Gaps:** Records before 1639 are sparse. King Philip's War (1675-1676) destroyed records in several affected towns. Towns established in the 1640s-1680s may have incomplete early runs.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Congregational church baptism, marriage, and burial registers.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregational (Puritan) was the established church and virtually the only denomination systematically maintaining registers for this period. Small numbers of Anglicans and Quakers generated separate records.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, church membership admission lists, and disciplinary proceedings (excommunications, admonishments). Confirmations were not a standard Congregational practice.
- **Where held:** Many early church records have been published in the Colonial Society of Massachusetts series and in local historical society publications. Original registers are typically at the specific church or at local historical societies. FamilySearch has digitized a significant body of these.
- **FamilySearch collection:** Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920 (collection ID 1921657), approximately 987,000 records — indexed at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657
- **Digitized volume:** Volume 007612045 covers Suffolk County Congregational church admissions and baptisms, 1630-1700 (121 images); this volume is **not name-indexed** but **is full-text searchable** — use keyword searches rather than name-index search.
- **Language:** English.
- **Note:** Congregational church records are described by the FamilySearch Wiki as central to early Massachusetts genealogy (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational). Church membership lists and disciplinary records name individuals who may not appear prominently elsewhere.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Does not begin until 1790 — no federal census exists for the 1620-1700 period.
- **Colonial enumerations:** No systematic census equivalent for this period. Tax lists, militia lists, and church membership lists serve as population substitutes.
- **Substitutes:** Colonial court records, town meeting minutes (see Town Meeting Records below), and probate inventories place people in specific localities. Church membership admission lists can document arrival in a community.

### Town meeting and proprietors' records
- **What exists:** Town meeting minutes record local governance, land proprietor grants, road maintenance assignments, poor relief, and the names of ordinary townspeople.
- **Digitized volume:** Volume 007612044 covers Massachusetts town meeting and proprietors' records, 1620-1698 (188 images). This volume is **browse-only** — it has 0% name indexing and is not full-text searchable. It must be examined image by image.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives, individual town clerks, and local historical societies.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions. For 1620-1643: the colonial General Court handled probate. From 1643: county probate courts (Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk).
- **Date range:** Probate records from the 1630s (Massachusetts Bay Colony) and from 1620 (Plymouth Colony, published separately).
- **Where held:** County probate courts; Massachusetts Archives holds many colonial-era originals. FamilySearch collection: Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991 (collection ID 1678901), approximately 567,000 records — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901
- **Note:** Probate inventories list household goods and debts and name neighbors, relatives, and associates. For the 1620-1700 period, they are among the richest sources of family-relationship evidence.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (the colony assigned town grants; individual lots within towns were distributed by town proprietors).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** English Crown granted charters to the colonial companies; individual land grants within towns were made by the town proprietors' meetings. County registries of deeds recorded land transfers from the 1630s onward, per the FamilySearch wiki_search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational).
- **Types:** Town proprietors' grants, deeds, mortgages. Colony-level land grants in early records.
- **Where held:** County registries of deeds (four original counties from 1643). Massachusetts Archives holds early colonial land records. Some deeds are in the town meeting and proprietors' records volume (007612044).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Pequot War (1636-1638); King Philip's War (1675-1676) — major conflict affecting most of the colony.
- **Record types:** Colonial militia muster rolls, service lists, and some pension-equivalent records. Published lists of King Philip's War participants exist.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives; published transcriptions available at NEHGS. No federal military records for this period (predates the United States).

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Burial grounds attached to Congregational meetinghouses in each town; some private family plots.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes many colonial-era burying grounds, though stone survival and legibility from this period varies widely.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records from the early colonial period are rare. Burial registers where they survive are typically in church records.
- **Note:** Many 17th-century stones are slate and have survived well; others have deteriorated or never existed (wooden markers). A burial ground visit or transcription project may be necessary.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The first American newspaper, Publick Occurrences, appeared briefly in 1690. The Boston News-Letter began in 1704 — outside this period. No regular Massachusetts newspapers exist for 1620-1700.
- **Alternative:** Legal notices and community information for this period appear in colonial court records and town meeting minutes, not newspapers.

### Immigration records (arrival)
- **Context:** For this period, 'immigration records' means ship passenger lists for arrivals from England and occasionally from other English colonies.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists and embarkation records. Many are English in origin (port records). Published compilations are the main access point — especially John Camden Hotten's 'Original Lists of Persons of Quality' and the Great Migration study series.
- **Great Migration Study:** The New England Historic Genealogical Society's Great Migration series documents every known settler arriving 1620-1643. This is the essential first source for any first-generation Puritan settler (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).
- **FamilySearch passenger lists collection:** Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891 (collection ID 1784312) covers 1820 onward — outside this period. For 1620-1700 arrivals, rely on published compilations and the Great Migration series, not this collection.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Colony and town tax lists; rate lists; the colony levied taxes on property and heads of household.
- **Date range:** Some lists from the 1630s onward.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives; published in local histories and the Colonial Society of Massachusetts series.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are a primary substitute for the absent census, placing individuals in specific towns in specific years.

### Other record types
- **Colonial court records:** The General Court (legislature/supreme court of the colony) records survive from the 1630s and are published. County courts from 1643 produced civil, criminal, and equity records naming ordinary people.
- **Town and county histories:** 19th- and early-20th-century published local histories frequently reprint early records, list founding families, and carry biographical sketches. Often the only surviving transcription of records since lost. NEHGS library holds a large collection.
- **Poor relief records:** Town records include poor relief grants and workhouse records — naming individuals who may not appear in church or vital records.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (collection 2061550) | Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890 (~3.4 million records, images) | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550 |
| FamilySearch (collection 1921657) | Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920 (~987,000 records, images) | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657 |
| FamilySearch (collection 1678901) | Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991 (~567,000 records, images) | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901 |
| FamilySearch (volume 007612045) | Suffolk County Congregational church admissions and baptisms, 1630-1700 (121 images, full-text searchable, not name-indexed) | Free — browse via FamilySearch |
| FamilySearch (volume 007612044) | Massachusetts town meeting and proprietors' records, 1620-1698 (188 images, browse-only) | Free — must browse image by image |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (not applicable for 1620-1700); may hold additional Massachusetts colonial transcriptions | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery records including colonial burying grounds | Free |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) | Federal records — not applicable for 1620-1700 colonial period | Free to query |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` returned 2 digitized volumes matching this place and period (totalResults: 2) — both are detailed above. The `collections_search` returned 5 collections; of the 5, only 3 (Town Vital Records, Church Records, Probate Records) have date ranges overlapping 1620-1700. The Passenger Lists collection begins in 1820 and the Naturalization Records collection begins in 1790 — both are outside this period.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts Archives (Boston) | Original colony records, governor's correspondence, court records from the 1620s onward, colonial land records, tax lists | In-person; some records available via state portal |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston | Largest genealogical library in New England; manuscript collections, published genealogies, Great Migration study series | In-person and membership-based online access (AmericanAncestors.org) |
| County Registries of Deeds (Essex, Suffolk, Middlesex, Norfolk) | Deed books from the 1630s onward in remarkably complete runs | In-person and some online via county portals |
| County Probate Courts | Probate files from county formation (1643) onward | In-person; some digitized via FamilySearch |
| Local historical societies (town-level) | Town records, church records, local histories, manuscript collections | Varies by society; contact individually |
| Colonial Society of Massachusetts | Published series of colonial church and civil records | Published volumes available at research libraries |

## Records NOT online
- Most colonial court records (General Court, county courts) exist in published print form but are not fully digitized or name-indexed online.
- Many town-level vital record registers from before 1639 (and some after) exist only in physical form at town clerks' offices or the Massachusetts Archives.
- Tax and rate lists from the 1630s-1690s are largely in manuscript at the Massachusetts Archives and in published local histories — not in any online searchable database.
- English embarkation records for the Great Migration are held by UK archives (The National Archives, Kew; port records) and are not systematically available online for this period.
- Plymouth Colony records (1620-1691) are published in print and some are online via NEHGS, but many supporting manuscript materials remain at Pilgrim Hall Museum (Plymouth) and Plymouth County courthouse.

## Known record losses
- King Philip's War (1675-1676) resulted in the burning of several Massachusetts towns, with attendant loss of local records. The FamilySearch wiki_search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records) names the Massachusetts Archives as the repository for surviving colony records — but does not enumerate specific town-by-town losses. Researchers working in towns destroyed during the war (e.g., Lancaster, Deerfield, Brookfield, Groton) should anticipate gaps and seek alternatives in church records, probate, and land records filed at the county seat rather than the town.
- Note: a zero result in volume_search or collections_search for a specific town is a coverage gap, not confirmed destruction. Consult the Massachusetts Archives and NEHGS directly for towns with sparse online holdings.

## Research tips
- **Start with the Great Migration series.** For any first-generation settler arriving 1620-1643, the NEHGS Great Migration study documents every known individual with compiled evidence. This is the single most important finding aid for this period. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records)
- **Use the Tanner-Corbin 'Vital Records to 1850' series.** Published abstracts for over 200 towns are the first step before consulting original town registers — they are indexed and widely available in research libraries and at NEHGS. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records)
- **Plymouth Colony is a separate trail.** Records are published and indexed separately. Do not assume a Bay Colony search covers Plymouth Colony families.
- **Counties formed in 1643.** For events before 1643, search the colonial General Court records, not county courts. For events after 1643, identify the correct county (Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, or Norfolk for the four original counties; later counties added as the colony expanded).
- **Church records and civil records overlap but are not identical.** A baptism in the church register and a birth in the town book are different entries — one may record information the other lacks. Search both.
- **Browse-only volumes require patience.** Volume 007612044 (town meeting records, 1620-1698) has no index and is not full-text searchable; it must be read image by image. Volume 007612045 (Suffolk church records, 1630-1700) is full-text searchable but not name-indexed — use the search box rather than browsing.
- **Tax lists substitute for the absent census.** No census exists before 1790. Colonial tax and rate lists (held at Massachusetts Archives) are the closest equivalent to census-style enumeration for this period.
- **Search the colony of origin.** Many Puritan settlers came from specific English counties (Essex, Suffolk, Lincolnshire, Kent). Once a family is identified in Massachusetts, searching English parish registers and English probate records for the county of origin often extends the line significantly. English records are held at The National Archives (Kew) and the relevant county record offices, with many available via Findmypast and Ancestry.

# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States (1620-1700)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Plymouth Colony founded 1620; Massachusetts Bay Colony founded 1628; merged into Province of Massachusetts Bay 1691
- **County seat / administrative center:** Boston (Massachusetts Bay); Plymouth (Plymouth Colony)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** English Crown (colonial charter)
- **Population during period:** Approximately 20,000 settlers arrived 1630-1640 (Great Migration, per Wikipedia); total colonial population grew through the century
- **Economy:** Agriculture, fishing, timber, trade; subsistence farming in early decades
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English Puritan settlers; small number of non-Puritan English; Indigenous peoples (Wampanoag, Massachusetts, Nipmuc, and others)
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (Puritan) as the established church of the colony; small number of other Protestant dissenters
- **Key historical events:** Great Migration 1630-1640; formation of first four counties 1643 (Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk); King Philip's War 1675-1676 (destroyed several towns and records); Plymouth Colony absorbed into Province of Massachusetts Bay 1691

## Boundary changes
- Plymouth Colony (1620-1691) and Massachusetts Bay Colony (1628-1691) coexisted as separate jurisdictions. A person or family could appear in either colony's records, or both.
- Four counties formed in 1643 (Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk): records created before 1643 route to the colonial General Court; records from 1643 onward route to the relevant county's probate court and registry of deeds.
- Plymouth Colony was absorbed into the Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691. Plymouth Colony records (1620-1691) are published and indexed separately and must be searched as a distinct trail.
- King Philip's War (1675-1676) resulted in the destruction of several town records and the physical destruction of some settlements; gaps in town vital records for the late 1670s in affected towns reflect this.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Town-level mandate began 1639 (Massachusetts Bay Colony), per the FamilySearch wiki_search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records). This is a **town-level** requirement, not a statewide or colony-wide civil registration system. The start date and completeness of surviving records varies town by town. Statewide civil registration did not begin until 1844.
- **What exists:** Births, marriages, and deaths recorded in town books from approximately 1639 onward for many towns. Plymouth Colony maintained similar town records from 1620.
- **Where held:** Original records held by individual town clerks; many are also at the Massachusetts Archives (Boston). The published 'Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850' series (Tanner-Corbin series) abstracts over 200 Massachusetts towns and is the recommended first step (FamilySearch wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).
- **FamilySearch collection:** Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890 (collection ID 2061550), approximately 3.4 million records with images — indexed and browsable at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550
- **Gaps:** Records before 1639 are sparse. King Philip's War (1675-1676) destroyed records in several affected towns. Towns established in the 1640s-1680s may have incomplete early runs.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Congregational church baptism, marriage, and burial registers.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregational (Puritan) was the established church and virtually the only denomination systematically maintaining registers for this period. Small numbers of Anglicans and Quakers generated separate records.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, church membership admission lists, and disciplinary proceedings (excommunications, admonishments). Confirmations were not a standard Congregational practice.
- **Where held:** Many early church records have been published in the Colonial Society of Massachusetts series and in local historical society publications. Original registers are typically at the specific church or at local historical societies. FamilySearch has digitized a significant body of these.
- **FamilySearch collection:** Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920 (collection ID 1921657), approximately 987,000 records — indexed at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657
- **Digitized volume:** Volume 007612045 covers Suffolk County Congregational church admissions and baptisms, 1630-1700 (121 images); this volume is **not name-indexed** but **is full-text searchable** — use keyword searches rather than name-index search.
- **Language:** English.
- **Note:** Congregational church records are described by the FamilySearch Wiki as central to early Massachusetts genealogy (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational). Church membership lists and disciplinary records name individuals who may not appear prominently elsewhere.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Does not begin until 1790 — no federal census exists for the 1620-1700 period.
- **Colonial enumerations:** No systematic census equivalent for this period. Tax lists, militia lists, and church membership lists serve as population substitutes.
- **Substitutes:** Colonial court records, town meeting minutes (see Town Meeting Records below), and probate inventories place people in specific localities. Church membership admission lists can document arrival in a community.

### Town meeting and proprietors' records
- **What exists:** Town meeting minutes record local governance, land proprietor grants, road maintenance assignments, poor relief, and the names of ordinary townspeople.
- **Digitized volume:** Volume 007612044 covers Massachusetts town meeting and proprietors' records, 1620-1698 (188 images). This volume is **browse-only** — it has 0% name indexing and is not full-text searchable. It must be examined image by image.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives, individual town clerks, and local historical societies.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions. For 1620-1643: the colonial General Court handled probate. From 1643: county probate courts (Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk).
- **Date range:** Probate records from the 1630s (Massachusetts Bay Colony) and from 1620 (Plymouth Colony, published separately).
- **Where held:** County probate courts; Massachusetts Archives holds many colonial-era originals. FamilySearch collection: Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991 (collection ID 1678901), approximately 567,000 records — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901
- **Note:** Probate inventories list household goods and debts and name neighbors, relatives, and associates. For the 1620-1700 period, they are among the richest sources of family-relationship evidence.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (the colony assigned town grants; individual lots within towns were distributed by town proprietors).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** English Crown granted charters to the colonial companies; individual land grants within towns were made by the town proprietors' meetings. County registries of deeds recorded land transfers from the 1630s onward, per the FamilySearch wiki_search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational).
- **Types:** Town proprietors' grants, deeds, mortgages. Colony-level land grants in early records.
- **Where held:** County registries of deeds (four original counties from 1643). Massachusetts Archives holds early colonial land records. Some deeds are in the town meeting and proprietors' records volume (007612044).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Pequot War (1636-1638); King Philip's War (1675-1676) — major conflict affecting most of the colony.
- **Record types:** Colonial militia muster rolls, service lists, and some pension-equivalent records. Published lists of King Philip's War participants exist.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives; published transcriptions available at NEHGS. No federal military records for this period (predates the United States).

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Burial grounds attached to Congregational meetinghouses in each town; some private family plots.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes many colonial-era burying grounds, though stone survival and legibility from this period varies widely.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records from the early colonial period are rare. Burial registers where they survive are typically in church records.
- **Note:** Many 17th-century stones are slate and have survived well; others have deteriorated or never existed (wooden markers). A burial ground visit or transcription project may be necessary.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The first American newspaper, Publick Occurrences, appeared briefly in 1690. The Boston News-Letter began in 1704 — outside this period. No regular Massachusetts newspapers exist for 1620-1700.
- **Alternative:** Legal notices and community information for this period appear in colonial court records and town meeting minutes, not newspapers.

### Immigration records (arrival)
- **Context:** For this period, 'immigration records' means ship passenger lists for arrivals from England and occasionally from other English colonies.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists and embarkation records. Many are English in origin (port records). Published compilations are the main access point — especially John Camden Hotten's 'Original Lists of Persons of Quality' and the Great Migration study series.
- **Great Migration Study:** The New England Historic Genealogical Society's Great Migration series documents every known settler arriving 1620-1643. This is the essential first source for any first-generation Puritan settler (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).
- **FamilySearch passenger lists collection:** Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891 (collection ID 1784312) covers 1820 onward — outside this period. For 1620-1700 arrivals, rely on published compilations and the Great Migration series, not this collection.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Colony and town tax lists; rate lists; the colony levied taxes on property and heads of household.
- **Date range:** Some lists from the 1630s onward.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives; published in local histories and the Colonial Society of Massachusetts series.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are a primary substitute for the absent census, placing individuals in specific towns in specific years.

### Other record types
- **Colonial court records:** The General Court (legislature/supreme court of the colony) records survive from the 1630s and are published. County courts from 1643 produced civil, criminal, and equity records naming ordinary people.
- **Town and county histories:** 19th- and early-20th-century published local histories frequently reprint early records, list founding families, and carry biographical sketches. Often the only surviving transcription of records since lost. NEHGS library holds a large collection.
- **Poor relief records:** Town records include poor relief grants and workhouse records — naming individuals who may not appear in church or vital records.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (collection 2061550) | Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890 (~3.4 million records, images) | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550 |
| FamilySearch (collection 1921657) | Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920 (~987,000 records, images) | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657 |
| FamilySearch (collection 1678901) | Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991 (~567,000 records, images) | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901 |
| FamilySearch (volume 007612045) | Suffolk County Congregational church admissions and baptisms, 1630-1700 (121 images, full-text searchable, not name-indexed) | Free — browse via FamilySearch |
| FamilySearch (volume 007612044) | Massachusetts town meeting and proprietors' records, 1620-1698 (188 images, browse-only) | Free — must browse image by image |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (not applicable for 1620-1700); may hold additional Massachusetts colonial transcriptions | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery records including colonial burying grounds | Free |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) | Federal records — not applicable for 1620-1700 colonial period | Free to query |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` returned 2 digitized volumes matching this place and period (totalResults: 2) — both are detailed above. The `collections_search` returned 5 collections; of the 5, only 3 (Town Vital Records, Church Records, Probate Records) have date ranges overlapping 1620-1700. The Passenger Lists collection begins in 1820 and the Naturalization Records collection begins in 1790 — both are outside this period.

| Colonial Society of Massachusetts | Published series of colonial church and civil records | Published volumes available at research libraries |

## Oklahoma Land Run of 1889 — Locality Research Guide

Here is a summary of the records and repositories that can help trace families in Oklahoma during the Land Run era:

---

### ⚠️ Research Context
Oklahoma in 1889 was essentially brand-new territory. Thousands of settlers arrived in a single day with almost no pre-existing government infrastructure. Critically:
- **No statewide birth or death records** exist before 1908
- **The 1890 federal census was destroyed** in a fire — a major gap for this exact era
- Records must be pieced together from land files, tax rolls, church records, and neighboring-state sources

---

### Key Record Types & Repositories

#### 1. Federal Land Records (Most Important)
- **Bureau of Land Management (BLM) General Land Office Records** — Free online at [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)
  - Search for original land patents issued to homesteaders
  - Patents name the claimant, the legal land description, and the date

- **Full Homestead Case Files — National Archives (NARA)**
  - These are the complete paperwork packets each claimant filed: affidavits, witness statements, and often details naming family members
  - Held at **NARA Washington D.C.** or the **NARA Fort Worth, TX** regional facility
  - Far more detailed than the patent alone

#### 2. Census Records
- **1880 census** — Search the state your ancestor lived in *before* the Run; this is your best pre-Oklahoma snapshot
- **1900 & 1910 federal censuses** — Available on FamilySearch and Ancestry; cover the territory fully
- The 1890 census loss means these land and church records must fill the gap

#### 3. Indian Enrollment Rolls
- **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914)** — If your ancestor had any connection to the Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, Seminole), the Dawes Commission enrollment records are essential
  - Available through the **National Archives** and on FamilySearch/Ancestry
- **Guion Miller Rolls** and earlier Cherokee rolls also useful for pre-statehood tribal connections

#### 4. County-Level Records (from 1890 onward)
- **Marriage registers** — Counties began recording marriages starting ~1890
- **Probate and court records** — Oklahoma Territory had federal district courts early on; case files are at NARA Fort Worth
- **Tax rolls** — County assessor records from the early 1890s can help establish presence and property

#### 5. Church Records
- Many early settlers organized churches immediately; registers may document births, deaths, and marriages before civil records began
- **Oklahoma Historical Society** holds many early church records

#### 6. Newspapers
- Territorial newspapers documented land claims, legal notices, and community news
- **Oklahoma Digital Newspapers** (through the Oklahoma Historical Society) and **Chronicling America** (Library of Congress) are the key online sources

---

### Primary Repositories

| Repository | What They Hold |
|---|---|
| **Oklahoma Historical Society (Oklahoma City)** | Territorial records, newspapers, county histories, early church records, tax rolls |
| **NARA Washington D.C.** | Land case files, Indian enrollment records |
| **NARA Fort Worth, TX** | Oklahoma territorial court records, some land files |
| **BLM GLO Records (online)** | Land patents, free and searchable |
| **FamilySearch** | 1900/1910 censuses, Dawes Rolls, some county records indexed |

---

### Recommended First Steps
1. **Search the 1880 census** in the state your ancestor was living before the Run — this gives you the family before Oklahoma
2. **Find the land patent** on glorecords.blm.gov to pin down the exact claim location and county
3. **Request the full homestead case file** from NARA — the affidavits often name family members and prior residence
4. **Check the Dawes Rolls** if there is any possibility of Native American heritage or tribal land connection
5. **Search 1900 and 1910 censuses** to find the family established in Oklahoma

# Locality Guide: Oklahoma (Land Run Era, 1880-1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Oklahoma Territory established May 2, 1890 (Organic Act) from the Unassigned Lands opened April 22, 1889. Oklahoma became the 46th state on November 16, 1907.
- **Administrative center:** Guthrie (territorial capital, 1890-1910).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Indian Territory and the federal General Land Office administered the area before 1890.
- **Population during period:** An estimated 50,000 settlers entered on April 22, 1889 alone. Subsequent runs in 1891, 1892, 1893, and 1895 continued rapid growth.
- **Economy:** Homestead farming (wheat, cotton), ranching, and nascent oil and gas. Coal mining in the Choctaw Nation / Indian Territory portion.
- **Ethnic composition:** Settlers from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, Arkansas, and Ohio. Significant African-American Boomer communities. Five Civilized Tribes occupied Indian Territory.
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist Episcopal, Baptist, Disciples of Christ, Presbyterian, and Catholic.

## Boundary changes
Oklahoma Territory (1890-1907) and Indian Territory existed as separate jurisdictions until statehood 1907. Records are under entirely different legal authorities. At statehood both merged; Indian Territory court records transferred to federal custody.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide birth/death registration before October 1908. County marriages begin at county formation (~1890).
- **What exists:** County marriages from 1890 (FamilySearch collection 2134789, 456,789 records).
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth or death registration before October 1908.

### Land records (the defining record class for this era)
- Homestead applications, final proof affidavits, and patents in Record Group 49 at NARA Washington D.C.
- Patents searchable free at glorecords.blm.gov.
- FamilySearch collection 1541872 (234,567 records) and digitized volume DGS 005221388 (74% name-indexed).

### Indian Territory / Dawes records
- FamilySearch collection 1987432 (567,890 records) — Indian Censuses and Rolls 1851-1959.
- Dawes Commission enrollment jackets: DGS 005221389 (browse-only, 0% indexed).

### Census records
- 1890 federal census largely destroyed. 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census at Oklahoma Historical Society.
- 1900 and 1910 federal censuses are indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Church records
- FamilySearch collection 1654321 (123,456 records); denominational and Oklahoma Historical Society archives.

### Probate and court records
- Territorial district courts (1890-1907) at NARA Fort Worth and Oklahoma State Archives.

### Military records
- Civil War pension files at NARA name settler families. Fold3 for online access.

### Tax records
- County tax rolls from 1890 at Oklahoma State Archives; substitute for missing 1890 census.

## Locality Guide: Alabama Region, Pre-Statehood (c. 1780–1819)

---

### Jurisdiction Overview

The present state of Alabama passed through several governing bodies before statehood on **14 December 1819**:

| Period | Governing Jurisdiction |
|---|---|
| 1702–1763 | French colonial |
| 1763–1780 | British colonial |
| 1780–1813 | Spanish colonial (Mobile area) |
| 1798–1817 | Mississippi Territory |
| 1817–1819 | Alabama Territory |

**Critical research note:** Almost everything you would search for from the 1790s–1810s must be looked up under **"Mississippi Territory"** — not "Alabama" — in online catalogs, NARA finding aids, and FamilySearch.

The early county structure is sparse: **Washington County** (formed 1800) was the first American county in present-day Alabama; **Baldwin County** followed in 1809; **Madison County** (north Alabama / Tennessee Valley) was formed 1808. Events before a county's formation date must be sought in the parent territorial government at St. Stephens.

---

### Key Record Types Available

#### Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)
- **No civil registration existed before 1819.** Statewide birth/death registration did not begin until 1908.
- **County marriage bonds and licenses** begin around **1809** in some counties.
  - FamilySearch: *Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950* (collection [1598408](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408)) — indexed + images.
- For earlier marriages, use church registers, estate inventories, and census substitutes.

#### Church Records
- **Catholic (Mobile):** Sacramental registers run continuously from 1702; these are among the oldest records in the region. Originals are in France (Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence) and Spain (Archivo General de Indias, Seville); the Diocese of Mobile Archives holds copies and American-era registers.
- **Baptist and Methodist:** Circuit congregations from c. 1808+; minute books record marriages and discipline cases that document family relationships.

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region, Pre-Statehood (c. 1780–1819)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Alabama achieved statehood 14 December 1819. Before that the same territory passed through: Mississippi Territory (1798–1817) and Alabama Territory (1817–1819). Earlier portions were under Spanish, British, and French colonial rule.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Territorial capital at Washington (later St. Stephens), then Huntsville for the Alabama Territory.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi Territory (1798–1817), created from Georgia cession and Spanish West Florida territory.
- **Population during period:** The population data tool returned no figures for this pre-state period. Wikipedia notes early European settlement concentrated around Mobile Bay (founded 1702); significant migration from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia followed the Creek War of 1813–1814.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, early cotton culture in the Tennessee Valley (north Alabama), fur trade, and commerce through Mobile port.
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee nations inhabited much of the interior. European settlers were largely of Scots-Irish and English descent migrating from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia. A French and Spanish Creole population was established around Mobile. Enslaved Africans and African Americans were present from the colonial era.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (dominant in Mobile under French and Spanish periods); Baptist and Methodist circuit riders began organizing congregations in the territorial period; small Presbyterian presence.
- **Key historical events:** Spanish transfer of Mobile to the US (1813); Creek War (1813–1814), which opened vast new lands to American settlement and drove a migration surge; formation of Alabama Territory (1817).

## Boundary changes
- The present Alabama territory was entirely within the Mississippi Territory from 1798. The Mississippi Territory originally covered only a narrow strip at the 31st–32nd parallels but was expanded in 1804 and again in 1812 to encompass all of present-day Mississippi and Alabama.
- In 1817 the western half of the Mississippi Territory became the state of Mississippi; the eastern half was reorganized as the Alabama Territory.
- Washington County (formed 1800) was one of the first American counties within present-day Alabama. Baldwin County was formed in 1809. Madison County (north Alabama, Tennessee Valley) was not formed until 1808. Researchers must identify which county, if any, existed for their location at the date of the event.
- Records created before a county's formation date will be found in the parent territorial or county jurisdiction — often Washington County or the territorial government at St. Stephens.
- The Mobile area's records before 1813 are colonial records, not American territorial records.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** There was no civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths in the territorial period (before 1819). At the county level, marriage bonds and licenses begin as early as 1809 in some Alabama counties (e.g., the FamilySearch collection "Alabama, County Marriages, 1809-1950" begins in 1809). Statewide registration of births and deaths did not begin until 1908.
- **What exists:** County-level marriage records from approximately 1809 onward (indexed + images, FamilySearch collection 1598408). No civil birth or death registration exists for the target period.
- **Where held:** County probate judge's office (originals); FamilySearch (digitized and indexed for marriages 1809+).
- **Gaps:** No birth or death registration at any level during the territorial period. Marriage records before 1809 are absent from civil records.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (Catholic in Mobile; Baptist and Methodist minute books); estate inventories listing surviving family members; census and census substitute records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mobile, from 1702); Baptist congregations from the early territorial period (c. 1808+); Methodist circuit churches; small Presbyterian congregations.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. Catholic registers for the Mobile Diocese are among the oldest continuous records in the region.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Church Records, 1803-1950" (collection 1986396) — indexed, with images — covers some of this period. Catholic diocesan archives (Diocese of Mobile) hold originals for the Mobile area. French colonial church records are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence; microfilm copies are at the Mobile Municipal Archives. Spanish colonial church records are at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress. (Source: [Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).)
- **Language:** Catholic records from the French period are in French; Spanish period records are in Spanish. American-period Baptist and Methodist records are in English.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The 1810 federal census is the first that covered present-day Alabama (as Mississippi Territory). It is available and indexed. No earlier federal census covered this territory.
- **Territorial censuses:** The Mississippi Territory conducted censuses in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 that enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama. Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)), these are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH) in Montgomery.
- **Other enumerations:** Spanish colonial census returns for the Mobile District exist at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress.
- **Access:** The FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810-1890" (collection 2016756) is name-indexed but has no images (index-only). The 1801, 1805, 1808 territorial censuses are physical-only at ADAH; they are not fully digitized online.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions; territorial court minute books.
- **Date range:** County probate courts begin with county formation — 1800 for Washington County, 1808 for Madison County, 1809 for Baldwin County, etc.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Probate Records, 1809-1985" (collection 1537764) — indexed + images — begins in 1809. Earlier territorial court records are held at ADAH. County courthouses hold originals.
- **Note:** Territorial court records (before county-level probate) are a key source for placing individuals in the territory before 1809 and are largely physical-only.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular survey (township and range), as Alabama is a federal land state. The US government — not the state — distributed public domain land.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The federal General Land Office (GLO) issued original patents. The Huntsville land office (from 1809) and St. Stephens land office (from 1807) were the two primary federal offices for present-day Alabama during this period.
- **Types:** Federal land patents/grants (GLO); Spanish and British colonial land grants for the Mobile area; territorial-era tax lists; deed books at county courthouses after county formation.
- **Date range:** Federal land sales in Alabama began around 1807–1809. Colonial grants in the Mobile area date from the early 1700s.
- **Where held:** Federal land patents are searchable and downloadable free at the BLM General Land Office website (glorecords.blm.gov). Colonial grants are at overseas archives (see Colonial Records under Church Records above) and the Library of Congress. County deed books are at the county courthouse and ADAH.
- **Digitization:** Federal patents are fully searchable and downloadable online at the BLM GLO. County deed books are largely physical-only for this period.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War (1813–1814); War of 1812; territorial militia service.
- **Record types:** Territorial militia rolls; War of 1812 service records and pension files; Creek War service records; bounty land warrants.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) holds federal service records, pension files, and bounty land warrant applications. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) provides online access to many NARA military records. ADAH holds some territorial militia records. The FamilySearch Wiki notes Fold3 as a key repository for military records.
- **Digitization:** Indexed + images on Fold3 (subscription) for War of 1812 and pension records. Physical-only at NARA for some series.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Earliest cemeteries are church-affiliated (Catholic in Mobile; Baptist and Methodist in north Alabama) and family burying grounds. Many early graves are unmarked or have deteriorated markers.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes many Alabama cemeteries, though coverage of pre-1820 graves is sparse and variable.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are inconsistent for this period. Early cemetery surveys by genealogical societies (held at ADAH and local historical societies) are valuable.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The first Alabama newspaper, the Mobile Centinel, began in 1811. The Huntsville Republican began c. 1816. Coverage of the target period (before 1815) is extremely limited.
- **Where held:** ADAH holds microfilm of early Alabama newspapers. Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) has some digitized Alabama papers, but pre-1820 coverage is minimal.
- **Content value:** Legal notices, land sale announcements, and occasional death and marriage notices appear even in early issues.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile was the principal port of entry for the Alabama region. New Orleans was also used for arrivals entering via the Gulf Coast.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists for Mobile and New Orleans; declarations of intention and naturalization records in territorial and early county courts; Spanish passport records for the colonial Mobile period.
- **Where held:** NARA holds passenger lists. The Archivo General de Indias (Seville) holds Spanish-era passport and emigration records for the Mobile District. FamilySearch and Ancestry index many naturalization records, though pre-1806 filings in territorial courts are largely physical-only.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. When researching a family's arrival, examine the full manifest.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial and county property tax lists; poll tax lists.
- **Date range:** Territorial-era tax lists exist from approximately 1809 onward at the county level (earlier for Washington County).
- **Where held:** ADAH and county courthouses. Some are transcribed in published genealogical compilations.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are especially valuable as census substitutes for years when no census exists (e.g., between 1801 and 1810 for some areas).

### Other record types
- **Compiled genealogies and local histories:** The Alabama Genealogy section of the FamilySearch Wiki notes that numerous 19th- and early-20th-century county histories name founding families. ADAH has extensive holdings of published county histories.
- **Indigenous records:** Creek and Cherokee tribal records are relevant for ancestors who lived in or near the Creek Nation before removal. Bureau of Indian Affairs records at NARA are the primary source.
- **Slave schedules:** Do not appear until the 1850 census. For enslaved individuals in the territorial period, plantation records, estate inventories, and bill-of-sale records in county deed books are the primary sources.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | County Marriages 1809-1950 (coll. 1598408); Probate Records 1809-1985 (coll. 1537764); Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index 1810-1890 (coll. 2016756); Church Records 1803-1950 (coll. 1986396) | Free |
| BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents for Alabama, searchable and downloadable | Free |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military service records, pension files, War of 1812 records | Subscription |
| Ancestry (ancestry.com) | U.S. Federal Census collection (includes 1810 Mississippi Territory) | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records (variable pre-1820 coverage) | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Guides to federal holdings; some digitized series | Free/varies |

**Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch volume_search returned 0 digitized browsable image volumes for Alabama in the 1780–1830 date range. This is a significant digitization gap: the pre-statehood period is not represented in FamilySearch's browse-image holdings. The four indexed collections above are the complete FamilySearch indexed holdings for Alabama at this scope. No nextPageToken was returned; the result set is complete.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery | Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808); territorial court records; county records on microfilm; published county histories; military records | In-person; some microfilm available via interlibrary loan |
| County courthouses (Washington, Baldwin, Madison, etc.) | Deed books, probate records, marriage records from county formation date | In-person or mail request |
| Diocese of Mobile Archives | Catholic sacramental registers from colonial period | Contact archives directly |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial records for Mobile area | In-person or written request; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial records for Mobile District: census returns, church registers, land grants | In-person or written request; copies at Library of Congress |
| Library of Congress, Washington DC | Copies of Spanish and French colonial records | In-person; some digitized online |
| NARA (Atlanta and Washington DC) | Passenger lists; military service and pension records; federal court records | In-person; some records digitized on Fold3/Ancestry |

## Records NOT online
- Territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, and 1808 (held physically at ADAH; not digitized)
- Territorial court minute books and early county court records before 1809
- County deed books and tax lists for most counties in this period
- French colonial church and civil records (microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives; originals in France)
- Spanish colonial records (originals in Seville; paper copies at Library of Congress)
- Most early Baptist and Methodist church minute books (held by individual congregations or ADAH)
- Many early family cemetery and sexton records

## Known record losses
No tool result returned in this survey stated that specific Alabama territorial records were destroyed. The absence of pre-1809 county-level records in FamilySearch collections reflects the general sparseness of record-keeping in the territorial period and the fact that many county governments did not yet exist — it is a coverage and digitization gap, not necessarily a destruction of records. Researchers should consult ADAH directly for guidance on what survives for any specific county and date.

## Research tips
- **Think in territorial jurisdictions, not modern counties.** Many Alabama events before 1809 occurred when only Washington County (formed 1800) or the territorial government at St. Stephens existed. Check which county, if any, had been formed at your date of interest before searching county records. (Source: [Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records))

- **Federal land patents are a prime source for placing families.** Because Alabama is a federal land state, the first land transaction for most families after American settlement is a federal patent, not a deed. Search glorecords.blm.gov free of charge.

The Diocese of Mobile Archives holds Catholic sacramental registers that span the colonial and American periods and is the best starting point for Mobile families.

- **Church records substitute for missing civil vital records throughout this period.** There was no civil birth or death registration at any level before 1819, and county marriage records begin only around 1809. Baptist minute books record not only marriages but discipline cases that name family relationships.
- **Adjoining jurisdictions to search:** Present-day Alabama borders Georgia (east), Tennessee (north), Mississippi (west), and Florida (south, then Spanish West Florida before 1821). Families crossing those borders generated records on both sides. Georgia state records, Tennessee territorial and county records, and Spanish West Florida records are all potentially relevant for border-area ancestors in this period.

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region, Pre-Statehood (c. 1780–1819)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Alabama achieved statehood 14 December 1819. Before that the same territory passed through: Mississippi Territory (1798–1817) and Alabama Territory (1817–1819). Earlier portions were under Spanish, British, and French colonial rule.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Territorial capital at Washington (later St. Stephens), then Huntsville for the Alabama Territory.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi Territory (1798–1817), created from Georgia cession and Spanish West Florida territory.
- **Population during period:** The population data tool returned no figures for this pre-state period. Wikipedia notes early European settlement concentrated around Mobile Bay (founded 1702); significant migration from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia followed the Creek War of 1813–1814.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, early cotton culture in the Tennessee Valley (north Alabama), fur trade, and commerce through Mobile port.
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee nations inhabited much of the interior. European settlers were largely of Scots-Irish and English descent migrating from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia. A French and Spanish Creole population was established around Mobile. Enslaved Africans and African Americans were present from the colonial era.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (dominant in Mobile under French and Spanish periods); Baptist and Methodist circuit riders began organizing congregations in the territorial period; small Presbyterian presence.
- **Key historical events:** Spanish transfer of Mobile to the US (1813); Creek War (1813–1814), which opened vast new lands to American settlement and drove a migration surge; formation of Alabama Territory (1817).

## Boundary changes
- The present Alabama territory was entirely within the Mississippi Territory from 1798. The Mississippi Territory originally covered only a narrow strip at the 31st–32nd parallels but was expanded in 1804 and again in 1812 to encompass all of present-day Mississippi and Alabama.
- In 1817 the western half of the Mississippi Territory became the state of Mississippi; the eastern half was reorganized as the Alabama Territory.
- Washington County (formed 1800) was one of the first American counties within present-day Alabama. Baldwin County was formed in 1809. Madison County (north Alabama, Tennessee Valley) was not formed until 1808. Researchers must identify which county, if any, existed for their location at the date of the event.
- Records created before a county's formation date will be found in the parent territorial or county jurisdiction — often Washington County or the territorial government at St. Stephens.
- The Mobile area's records before 1813 are colonial records, not American territorial records.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** There was no civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths in the territorial period (before 1819). At the county level, marriage bonds and licenses begin as early as 1809 in some Alabama counties (e.g., the FamilySearch collection "Alabama, County Marriages, 1809-1950" begins in 1809). Statewide registration of births and deaths did not begin until 1908.
- **What exists:** County-level marriage records from approximately 1809 onward (indexed + images, FamilySearch collection 1598408). No civil birth or death registration exists for the target period.
- **Where held:** County probate judge's office (originals); FamilySearch (digitized and indexed for marriages 1809+).
- **Gaps:** No birth or death registration at any level during the territorial period. Marriage records before 1809 are absent from civil records.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (Catholic in Mobile; Baptist and Methodist minute books); estate inventories listing surviving family members; census and census substitute records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mobile, from 1702); Baptist congregations from the early territorial period (c. 1808+); Methodist circuit churches; small Presbyterian congregations.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. Catholic registers for the Mobile Diocese are among the oldest continuous records in the region.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Church Records, 1803-1950" (collection 1986396) — indexed, with images — covers some of this period. Catholic diocesan archives (Diocese of Mobile) hold originals for the Mobile area. French colonial church records are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence; microfilm copies are at the Mobile Municipal Archives. Spanish colonial church records are at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress. (Source: [Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).)
- **Language:** Catholic records from the French period are in French; Spanish period records are in Spanish. American-period Baptist and Methodist records are in English.

- **Federal/national census:** The 1810 federal census is the first that covered present-day Alabama (as Mississippi Territory). It is available and indexed. No earlier federal census covered this territory.
