quirks: The Alabama region was the Mississippi Territory (1798-1817), then the Alabama Territory (1817-1819). Records created before 1819 are territorial, not state, records — search under Mississippi Territory as well as Alabama when looking for pre-statehood materials.

No digitized browsable image volumes were returned by FamilySearch volume_search for Alabama in the 1780-1830 date window — this is a significant digitization gap. The FamilySearch indexed collections (marriages, probate, census substitutes, church records) begin in 1803-1810 and capture only early post-territorial material.

Alabama is a federal land state. Land was distributed by the federal government, not the state. Original land patents are searchable and downloadable for free at the BLM General Land Office website (glorecords.blm.gov), not at state or county archives.

The Mobile area was under French (1702-1763), British (1763-1780), and Spanish (1780-1813) control before American jurisdiction. Colonial records for Mobile-area ancestors may be in Aix-en-Provence (French), Seville (Spanish), or London (British) archives, not Alabama depositories.

Territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama and are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH) in Montgomery — they are not fully digitized online.

There was no statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths in the territorial period (before 1819) or for most of the early state period. County-level marriage records begin as early as 1809 in some counties. Statewide vital registration did not begin until 1908 (births) and 1908 (deaths).

Washington County (formed 1800 from territorial jurisdiction) was one of the first American counties in present-day Alabama. Researchers with ancestors in north Alabama before 1809 will find few county-level records — Madison County was not formed until 1808.

Spanish colonial church records for the Mobile District include census returns, church registers, and land grants held at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress — not at Alabama repositories.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Alabama Region, Pre-Statehood (c. 1780–1819)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Alabama achieved statehood 14 December 1819. Before that the same territory passed through: Mississippi Territory (1798–1817) and Alabama Territory (1817–1819). Earlier portions were under Spanish, British, and French colonial rule.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Territorial capital at Washington (later St. Stephens), then Huntsville for the Alabama Territory.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi Territory (1798–1817), created from Georgia cession and Spanish West Florida territory.
- **Population during period:** The population data tool returned no figures for this pre-state period. Wikipedia notes early European settlement concentrated around Mobile Bay (founded 1702); significant migration from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia followed the Creek War of 1813–1814.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, early cotton culture in the Tennessee Valley (north Alabama), fur trade, and commerce through Mobile port.
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee nations inhabited much of the interior. European settlers were largely of Scots-Irish and English descent migrating from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia. A French and Spanish Creole population was established around Mobile. Enslaved Africans and African Americans were present from the colonial era.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (dominant in Mobile under French and Spanish periods); Baptist and Methodist circuit riders began organizing congregations in the territorial period; small Presbyterian presence.
- **Key historical events:** Spanish transfer of Mobile to the US (1813); Creek War (1813–1814), which opened vast new lands to American settlement and drove a migration surge; formation of Alabama Territory (1817).

## Boundary changes
- The present Alabama territory was entirely within the Mississippi Territory from 1798. The Mississippi Territory originally covered only a narrow strip at the 31st–32nd parallels but was expanded in 1804 and again in 1812 to encompass all of present-day Mississippi and Alabama.
- In 1817 the western half of the Mississippi Territory became the state of Mississippi; the eastern half was reorganized as the Alabama Territory.
- Washington County (formed 1800) was one of the first American counties within present-day Alabama. Baldwin County was formed in 1809. Madison County (north Alabama, Tennessee Valley) was not formed until 1808. Researchers must identify which county, if any, existed for their location at the date of the event.
- Records created before a county's formation date will be found in the parent territorial or county jurisdiction — often Washington County or the territorial government at St. Stephens.
- The Mobile area's records before 1813 are colonial records, not American territorial records.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** There was no civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths in the territorial period (before 1819). At the county level, marriage bonds and licenses begin as early as 1809 in some Alabama counties (e.g., the FamilySearch collection "Alabama, County Marriages, 1809-1950" begins in 1809). Statewide registration of births and deaths did not begin until 1908.
- **What exists:** County-level marriage records from approximately 1809 onward (indexed + images, FamilySearch collection 1598408). No civil birth or death registration exists for the target period.
- **Where held:** County probate judge's office (originals); FamilySearch (digitized and indexed for marriages 1809+).
- **Gaps:** No birth or death registration at any level during the territorial period. Marriage records before 1809 are absent from civil records.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (Catholic in Mobile; Baptist and Methodist minute books); estate inventories listing surviving family members; census and census substitute records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mobile, from 1702); Baptist congregations from the early territorial period (c. 1808+); Methodist circuit churches; small Presbyterian congregations.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. Catholic registers for the Mobile Diocese are among the oldest continuous records in the region.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Church Records, 1803-1950" (collection 1986396) — indexed, with images — covers some of this period. Catholic diocesan archives (Diocese of Mobile) hold originals for the Mobile area. French colonial church records are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence; microfilm copies are at the Mobile Municipal Archives. Spanish colonial church records are at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress. (Source: [Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).)
- **Language:** Catholic records from the French period are in French; Spanish period records are in Spanish. American-period Baptist and Methodist records are in English.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The 1810 federal census is the first that covered present-day Alabama (as Mississippi Territory). It is available and indexed. No earlier federal census covered this territory.
- **Territorial censuses:** The Mississippi Territory conducted censuses in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 that enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama. Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)), these are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH) in Montgomery.
- **Other enumerations:** Spanish colonial census returns for the Mobile District exist at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress.
- **Access:** The FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810-1890" (collection 2016756) is name-indexed but has no images (index-only). The 1801, 1805, 1808 territorial censuses are physical-only at ADAH; they are not fully digitized online.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions; territorial court minute books.
- **Date range:** County probate courts begin with county formation — 1800 for Washington County, 1808 for Madison County, 1809 for Baldwin County, etc.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Probate Records, 1809-1985" (collection 1537764) — indexed + images — begins in 1809. Earlier territorial court records are held at ADAH. County courthouses hold originals.
- **Note:** Territorial court records (before county-level probate) are a key source for placing individuals in the territory before 1809 and are largely physical-only.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular survey (township and range), as Alabama is a federal land state. The US government — not the state — distributed public domain land.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The federal General Land Office (GLO) issued original patents. The Huntsville land office (from 1809) and St. Stephens land office (from 1807) were the two primary federal offices for present-day Alabama during this period.
- **Types:** Federal land patents/grants (GLO); Spanish and British colonial land grants for the Mobile area; territorial-era tax lists; deed books at county courthouses after county formation.
- **Date range:** Federal land sales in Alabama began around 1807–1809. Colonial grants in the Mobile area date from the early 1700s.
- **Where held:** Federal land patents are searchable and downloadable free at the BLM General Land Office website (glorecords.blm.gov). Colonial grants are at overseas archives (see Colonial Records under Church Records above) and the Library of Congress. County deed books are at the county courthouse and ADAH.
- **Digitization:** Federal patents are fully searchable and downloadable online at the BLM GLO. County deed books are largely physical-only for this period.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War (1813–1814); War of 1812; territorial militia service.
- **Record types:** Territorial militia rolls; War of 1812 service records and pension files; Creek War service records; bounty land warrants.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) holds federal service records, pension files, and bounty land warrant applications. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) provides online access to many NARA military records. ADAH holds some territorial militia records. The FamilySearch Wiki notes Fold3 as a key repository for military records.
- **Digitization:** Indexed + images on Fold3 (subscription) for War of 1812 and pension records. Physical-only at NARA for some series.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Earliest cemeteries are church-affiliated (Catholic in Mobile; Baptist and Methodist in north Alabama) and family burying grounds. Many early graves are unmarked or have deteriorated markers.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes many Alabama cemeteries, though coverage of pre-1820 graves is sparse and variable.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are inconsistent for this period. Early cemetery surveys by genealogical societies (held at ADAH and local historical societies) are valuable.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The first Alabama newspaper, the Mobile Centinel, began in 1811. The Huntsville Republican began c. 1816. Coverage of the target period (before 1815) is extremely limited.
- **Where held:** ADAH holds microfilm of early Alabama newspapers. Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) has some digitized Alabama papers, but pre-1820 coverage is minimal.
- **Content value:** Legal notices, land sale announcements, and occasional death and marriage notices appear even in early issues.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile was the principal port of entry for the Alabama region. New Orleans was also used for arrivals entering via the Gulf Coast.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists for Mobile and New Orleans; declarations of intention and naturalization records in territorial and early county courts; Spanish passport records for the colonial Mobile period.
- **Where held:** NARA holds passenger lists. The Archivo General de Indias (Seville) holds Spanish-era passport and emigration records for the Mobile District. FamilySearch and Ancestry index many naturalization records, though pre-1806 filings in territorial courts are largely physical-only.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. When researching a family's arrival, examine the full manifest.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial and county property tax lists; poll tax lists.
- **Date range:** Territorial-era tax lists exist from approximately 1809 onward at the county level (earlier for Washington County).
- **Where held:** ADAH and county courthouses. Some are transcribed in published genealogical compilations.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are especially valuable as census substitutes for years when no census exists (e.g., between 1801 and 1810 for some areas).

### Other record types
- **Compiled genealogies and local histories:** The Alabama Genealogy section of the FamilySearch Wiki notes that numerous 19th- and early-20th-century county histories name founding families. ADAH has extensive holdings of published county histories.
- **Indigenous records:** Creek and Cherokee tribal records are relevant for ancestors who lived in or near the Creek Nation before removal. Bureau of Indian Affairs records at NARA are the primary source.
- **Slave schedules:** Do not appear until the 1850 census. For enslaved individuals in the territorial period, plantation records, estate inventories, and bill-of-sale records in county deed books are the primary sources.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | County Marriages 1809-1950 (coll. 1598408); Probate Records 1809-1985 (coll. 1537764); Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index 1810-1890 (coll. 2016756); Church Records 1803-1950 (coll. 1986396) | Free |
| BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents for Alabama, searchable and downloadable | Free |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military service records, pension files, War of 1812 records | Subscription |
| Ancestry (ancestry.com) | U.S. Federal Census collection (includes 1810 Mississippi Territory) | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records (variable pre-1820 coverage) | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Guides to federal holdings; some digitized series | Free/varies |

**Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch volume_search returned 0 digitized browsable image volumes for Alabama in the 1780–1830 date range. This is a significant digitization gap: the pre-statehood period is not represented in FamilySearch's browse-image holdings. The four indexed collections above are the complete FamilySearch indexed holdings for Alabama at this scope. No nextPageToken was returned; the result set is complete.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery | Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808); territorial court records; county records on microfilm; published county histories; military records | In-person; some microfilm available via interlibrary loan |
| County courthouses (Washington, Baldwin, Madison, etc.) | Deed books, probate records, marriage records from county formation date | In-person or mail request |
| Diocese of Mobile Archives | Catholic sacramental registers from colonial period | Contact archives directly |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial records for Mobile area | In-person or written request; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial records for Mobile District: census returns, church registers, land grants | In-person or written request; copies at Library of Congress |
| Library of Congress, Washington DC | Copies of Spanish and French colonial records | In-person; some digitized online |
| NARA (Atlanta and Washington DC) | Passenger lists; military service and pension records; federal court records | In-person; some records digitized on Fold3/Ancestry |

## Records NOT online
- Territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, and 1808 (held physically at ADAH; not digitized)
- Territorial court minute books and early county court records before 1809
- County deed books and tax lists for most counties in this period
- French colonial church and civil records (microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives; originals in France)
- Spanish colonial records (originals in Seville; paper copies at Library of Congress)
- Most early Baptist and Methodist church minute books (held by individual congregations or ADAH)
- Many early family cemetery and sexton records

## Known record losses
No tool result returned in this survey stated that specific Alabama territorial records were destroyed. The absence of pre-1809 county-level records in FamilySearch collections reflects the general sparseness of record-keeping in the territorial period and the fact that many county governments did not yet exist — it is a coverage and digitization gap, not necessarily a destruction of records. Researchers should consult ADAH directly for guidance on what survives for any specific county and date.

## Research tips
- **Think in territorial jurisdictions, not modern counties.** Many Alabama events before 1809 occurred when only Washington County (formed 1800) or the territorial government at St. Stephens existed. Check which county, if any, had been formed at your date of interest before searching county records. (Source: [Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records))
- **Search Mississippi Territory records, not just Alabama records.** The territory that became Alabama was the Mississippi Territory until 1817. Federal and territorial records filed before 1817 will be catalogued under Mississippi Territory, not Alabama.
- **Federal land patents are a prime source for placing families.** Because Alabama is a federal land state, the first land transaction for most families after American settlement is a federal patent, not a deed. Search glorecords.blm.gov free of charge.
- **The 1810 census is the first federal enumeration for this area.** No federal census covered present-day Alabama before 1810. Use the territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, and 1808 (at ADAH) and tax lists as substitutes for earlier years.
- **Colonial-era ancestors in the Mobile area require overseas archival research.** French and Spanish colonial records are not in Alabama; they are in France, Spain, and at the Library of Congress. The Diocese of Mobile Archives holds Catholic sacramental registers that span the colonial and American periods and is the best starting point for Mobile families.
- **Military service in the Creek War (1813-1814) and War of 1812 is a major research avenue.** Many men who settled Alabama afterward had prior or concurrent service. Pension files at NARA often contain detailed family information including birthplace, age, and names of wife and children.
- **Church records substitute for missing civil vital records throughout this period.** There was no civil birth or death registration at any level before 1819, and county marriage records begin only around 1809. Baptist minute books record not only marriages but discipline cases that name family relationships.
- **Adjoining jurisdictions to search:** Present-day Alabama borders Georgia (east), Tennessee (north), Mississippi (west), and Florida (south, then Spanish West Florida before 1821). Families crossing those borders generated records on both sides. Georgia state records, Tennessee territorial and county records, and Spanish West Florida records are all potentially relevant for border-area ancestors in this period.

Here is the full locality research guide returned by the specialist agent:

---

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region (1860–1890)
*Focused on Schuylkill County, with guidance applicable across the coalfield*

---

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **County seat:** Pottsville (Schuylkill County)
- **Formed:** 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties
- **Population (Schuylkill Co.):** 89,510 (1860) → 116,428 (1870) → 129,974 (1880)
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining; supporting trades (breaker operation, mule driving, ironworking, retail in mining patches)
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish immigrant population (Famine-era and post-Famine); Welsh, English, German miners; Eastern European immigration increasing by the late 1880s
- **Key events:** Rise of the Molly Maguires (1860s–1870s) and trials (1876–1877); Reading Railroad consolidation of coal lands; the Long Strike of 1875

---

## Boundary Changes

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties
- **County seat:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** 89,510 (1860); 116,428 (1870); 129,974 (1880)
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated entirely; supporting trades included breaker operation, mule driving, ironworking, and retail commerce serving mining patches
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish immigrant population (Famine-era and post-Famine arrivals); also Welsh, English, and German miners; Eastern European immigration increased toward the 1880s–1890s
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant among Irish), Welsh Calvinist Methodist, Welsh Congregationalist, Anglican/Episcopal, Lutheran, German Reformed
- **Key historical events:** Rise of the Molly Maguires (1860s–1870s) and associated trials (1876–1877); Reading Railroad consolidation of coal lands; labor strikes and the Long Strike of 1875

- **Major cemeteries:** Annunciation B.V.M. (Shenandoah), St. Clair Catholic Cemetery, Pottsville Catholic Cemetery, among others across the mining patches

| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (collection 1999196; 3.2M images, browse-only); Naturalization Records DGS 007936750 (1849–1915, 298 images, browse-only); Church Records DGS 007936751 (1842–1895, 187 images, browse-only, English/German); Deed Records DGS 007936752 (1815–1900, 543 images, 22% indexed); Marriage Records DGS 007936753 (1870–1910, 94 images, browse-only); Probate Records DGS 007936749 (1851–1930, 412 images, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | 1850 United States Federal Census - Schuylkill County (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/); Pennsylvania Tax and Exoneration Lists 1768–1801 (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7667/) | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch volume_search returned 5 total digitized volumes for Schuylkill County; all 5 are detailed above — this is the complete result set for the target period.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville | Deeds, court minutes, naturalization files, marriage licenses, probate originals | In-person or mail request |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Triennial tax assessments, state census substitutes, adjutant general records | In-person; some online finding aids |
| Diocese of Allentown Archives | Catholic parish registers for Schuylkill and Carbon counties (post-1961); pre-1868 registers may still be held by Diocese of Philadelphia | Contact the chancery |
| Diocese of Philadelphia Archives | Catholic parish registers predating the 1868 diocesan split; some original Schuylkill County registers | Contact the archives |
| Pottsville Free Public Library | Miners' Journal microfilm; local history collection | In-person |
| Schuylkill County Historical Society, Pottsville | County histories, family files, cemetery transcriptions, local newspapers | In-person; some mail requests |
| NARA Philadelphia | Federal court naturalizations, passenger lists for Philadelphia port | In-person; some online via Ancestry/FamilySearch |

## Records NOT online
- Catholic baptismal, marriage, and burial registers for most individual parishes (must contact diocesan archives)
- Pennsylvania triennial tax assessment ledgers for Schuylkill County
- Miners' Journal (Pottsville) in full digital form — microfilm only at Pottsville Free Public Library
- Colliery company employment and payroll records (access details on the FamilySearch Wiki coal-region page)
- Schuylkill County court of quarter sessions minutes (name ordinary residents, road assignments, poor relief)
- Sexton records and burial registers for individual cemeteries

## Known record losses
- The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed nationally by fire and water damage in 1921 — no Schuylkill County schedules survive for that year. Veterans' schedules from 1890 are partially intact and held at NARA.
- No tool result in this survey identified courthouse fires or other record-destruction events specific to Schuylkill County.

## Research tips
- **Coal-region specialized indexes:** The FamilySearch Wiki page [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records) describes the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index (41,000 workers, 1855–1898), colliery payroll sources, and triennial tax assessments unique to the five anthracite counties. Read this page before building a search strategy.
- **Payroll vs. inspection reports:** Company payroll indexes are the right tool for finding a named miner; mine-inspection and accident reports are organized by colliery, not person, and are a secondary source for establishing which colliery a man worked at after you have found him.
- **Diocesan jurisdiction matters:** Irish Catholic baptism and burial records are in parish registers held by diocesan archives, not the county courthouse. For Schuylkill County in 1860–1890, those registers predate the Diocese of Allentown (1961) and the Diocese of Philadelphia is the correct archive for pre-1868 material, the Diocese of Allentown for post-1868. Source: [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records).
- **Civil War pension files for Irish origins:** Pension application files at NARA often state the applicant's Irish county and sometimes townland of origin — for a male ancestor who served in the Civil War (1861–1865) this is one of the richest documents you can obtain.
- **Naturalization search sequence:** Search the Schuylkill County court of common pleas and court of quarter sessions first; then the U.S. District Court (Eastern District of Pennsylvania) via NARA Philadelphia. Pre-1906 declarations are often in county courts and were not forwarded to federal archives.
- **Miners' Journal obituaries and accident reports:** The Miners' Journal (Pottsville, from 1825) routinely named the decedent's townland or county of origin in Ireland in mining accident reports and obituaries — this is a direct bridge to Irish records.
- **Triennial tax assessments as census substitutes:** Because no reliable civil birth/death registration exists for 1860–1890, Pennsylvania's triennial assessments (from 1853) are the best tool for placing a family in a specific township between census years and for confirming nativity.
- **Browse-only volumes require patience:** Four of the five FamilySearch digitized volumes for Schuylkill County (naturalization, church, probate, marriage) are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — they must be browsed image by image with no search function.
- **Pre-1811 ancestors:** Any Schuylkill County records before 1811 will be found in Berks County or Northampton County archives, as the county was formed from those two parents that year.
- **Neighboring counties:** Families near Schuylkill County borders may have generated records in adjoining counties — the county's Neighboring Counties table on the FamilySearch Genealogy page did not resolve in this session; check Carbon, Dauphin, Lebanon, Berks, and Luzerne as the likely neighbors. Any ancestor in what is now Lackawanna County before 1878 is found under Luzerne County records.
- **Surveys still needed:** Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland counties each require their own locality survey before comprehensive anthracite-region research is possible.

Here is the locality-guide agent's full response:

---

**Vermont Pre-Statehood Locality Research Guide (persisted as `loc_001`)**

The guide is grounded in the FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy). Here is what was confirmed from the tools vs. what couldn't be:

---

### Confirmed from the FamilySearch Wiki

- **Statewide civil vital registration began in 1857** — far too late for your pre-statehood research. This means no centralized birth, marriage, or death records exist for your period.
- **The 1771 Grant Survey Schedule** is the earliest systematic resident list, naming approximately 1,800 grantees. This is a key finding aid for late-18th-century Vermont families.
- **Town clerk vital records** survive unevenly from the 1770s onward — researchers must contact individual town clerks directly, as Vermont's records are organized at the town level, not the county level.
- **19th-century town histories (1860–1900)** frequently reprint colonial-era proprietors' records, making them a critical source for this period.

---

### The Vermont Context: Pre-Statehood (c. 1750–1791)

Vermont was a contested territory during this window:
- **Before 1777**: Claimed by both New Hampshire (which issued "New Hampshire Grants") and New York, which disputed those grants.
- **1777–1791**: Vermont operated as an independent republic (the Vermont Republic).
- **March 4, 1791**: Vermont admitted as the 14th U.S. state.

Because jurisdiction was disputed, records from **New Hampshire archives** and **New York State archives** may be just as important as Vermont-held records for your ancestors' land transactions and legal matters.

---

### Key Record Types for This Period

| Record Type | Coverage | Repository |
|---|---|---|
| 1771 Grant Survey Schedule | ~1,800 grantees named | Vermont State Archives |
| Town vital records (VRs) | Uneven; some from 1770s | Individual town clerk offices |
| Land/proprietors' records | Pre-statehood grants | Vermont State Archives; NH & NY archives |
| Church registers | Baptisms & burials | Original churches; VHS microfilm |
| 1790 Federal Census | Heads of household only | FamilySearch, Ancestry |
| Town histories (pub. 1860–1900) | Reprint early records | Vermont Historical Society |
| Probate records | By county | County probate courts |

---

### Most Important Repositories

1. **Vermont State Archives and Records Administration (VSARA)** — land records, early legislative records, proprietors' records
2. **Vermont Historical Society (Barre)** — microfilmed town records, published town histories, surname files
3. **Individual town clerk offices** — the primary holders of vital and land records; Vermont is organized by *town*, not county
4. **New Hampshire State Archives** — New Hampshire Grants land records
5. **New York State Archives** — competing land-claim records
6. **FamilySearch.org** — digitized Vermont vital records (post-1760 some towns), 1790 census, some probate

---

### Honest Gaps

The FamilySearch Wiki's dedicated subpages for Vermont vital records, land, church, probate, and census returned generic redirects rather than Vermont-specific content — a genuine coverage gap in the wiki. Those details above come from what the primary Vermont Genealogy page confirmed, not from training-data assumptions.

The 1790 census is the only federal census covering the pre-statehood window, and it lists heads of household only — women, children, and non-head relatives are invisible in it.

---

### Suggested First Steps

1. Identify the specific **town** (not just county) where your ancestors lived — Vermont's town-based record system makes this essential.
2. Search the **1771 Grant Survey Schedule** if your family may have been early land grantees.
3. Check the **1790 federal census** for the head of household.
4. Contact the relevant **town clerk** for surviving vital and land records.
5. Search digitized records on **FamilySearch** and **Ancestry** for Vermont vital records, then supplement with the Vermont Historical Society for manuscript sources.

A targeted research plan can be built once you know the specific town. Would you like to proceed with that?

quirks: Deeds in Vermont are recorded at the town clerk office, not the county courthouse — every deed search must go to the specific town where the land was located.

The 1771 Grant Survey Schedule enumerates approximately 1,800 grantees of New Hampshire grants that New York refused to recognize; it predates any Vermont civil registration and is the earliest systematic resident list for the future state (per the FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki page).
Statewide civil registration did not begin until 1857. Town clerk vital records (some back to the 1770s) survive unevenly — contact each town clerk directly.

An ancestor's land title may appear across three separate repository systems: New Hampshire State Archives (grants pre-1764), New York State Archives (re-grants 1764-1777), and Vermont State Archives (Republic charters 1777-1791); search all three.

County boundaries were adjusted several times between 1778 and 1791 as new counties were created; an event may be filed under the original county or its successor — determine which county existed at the event date.

Vermont's northern border adjoins Quebec/Canada; a small number of Loyalist families crossed north during and after the Revolution. Vermont also borders New Hampshire (east), Massachusetts (south), and New York (west) — check adjoining jurisdictions for families near any border.

19th-century Vermont town histories (most published 1860-1900) often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access (per the FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki page) — consult these before making archive visits.
Town grand lists (annual property assessments at the town level) are the primary substitute for missing census coverage before 1790; they survive from the late 1770s for many towns.
The 1790 federal census was conducted June-August 1790, before Vermont's March 1791 statehood; it names only heads of household, with all other members counted but not named.
No state census was conducted by the Republic of Vermont; militia rolls and town grand lists serve as substitutes for intercensal population evidence.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Vermont, United States (Pre-Statehood, c. 1750–1791)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Vermont was admitted as the 14th state on March 4, 1791. Before that it existed as the independent Republic of Vermont (1777–1791), and before that the territory was contested between the Province of New Hampshire, the Province of New York, and independent settlers under the New Hampshire Grants (granted by Governor Benning Wentworth of New Hampshire beginning in 1749).
- **Administrative center during Republic period:** Windsor (first capital); Montpelier became the permanent capital after statehood.
- **Parent jurisdictions:** Province of New Hampshire (grants issued 1749–1764); Province of New York (claimed authority 1764–1777, never accepted by most settlers); Republic of Vermont (independent, 1777–1791).
- **Population during period:** The first federal census (1790) enumerated Vermont's population at approximately 85,341; that figure reflects the immediate pre-statehood era. No tool-returned population figure is available before 1791.
- **Economy:** Subsistence agriculture, timber, potash production, and small-scale trade. Settlement was frontier-era; many towns were just being incorporated in the 1770s–1780s.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly settlers of English descent migrating from Connecticut, Massachusetts, and New Hampshire. Small numbers of Scots-Irish and Dutch settlers.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist (dominant), Baptist, Methodist (arriving later in the period), Anglican/Episcopal (smaller presence). Quaker meetings existed in some communities.
- **Key historical events:** New Hampshire Grants dispute (1749–1777); Green Mountain Boys resistance to New York authority; American Revolution; Vermont Constitution of 1777 (first in North America to prohibit adult slavery and grant universal male suffrage); Republic of Vermont operates 1777–1791.

## Boundary changes
Three overlapping jurisdictional claims defined this period:
1. Before 1764: New Hampshire issued over 100 township grants. Records in New Hampshire colonial files.
2. 1764–1777: British Crown ruled territory fell under New York. New York re-granted many of the same lands; records in New York State Archives.
3. 1777–1791: Republic of Vermont operated independently, issuing its own land charters and court records — held in Vermont repositories.
Counties were established by the Republic's General Assembly beginning in 1778; pre-county records follow town-level and proprietary records. County boundaries were adjusted several times 1779–1791.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Statewide civil registration began in 1857 (FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy). No statewide registration existed during the pre-statehood period.
- **What exists for 1750–1791:** Some town clerk offices hold earlier town-level vital records dating back to the 1770s, but these survive unevenly; consult town clerk offices directly.
- **Where held:** Individual town clerk offices; Vermont State Archives holds some compiled early vital records.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records, family Bible records, published town histories, gravestone inscriptions, proprietors' records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregationalist (most numerous and best-documented), Baptist, Methodist, Anglican/Episcopal, Quaker.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, membership lists, disciplinary proceedings.
- **Where held:** Originating congregation; denominational archives (Congregationalist records at Congregational Library, Boston; Baptist records at American Baptist Historical Society); FamilySearch has microfilmed some Vermont church records.
- **Language:** English.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1790 federal census is the only federal census within the pre-statehood window. Names heads of household only; all other members are counted, not named. Indexed and available online at Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- **Republic of Vermont enumerations:** No systematic statewide enumeration identified. Tax lists and militia rolls serve as substitutes.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships, court minutes.
- **Jurisdiction level:** County-level from 1778 when counties were organized; before 1778, town-level records or no formal probate.
- **Where held:** Vermont Probate Court districts; Vermont State Archives. FamilySearch has microfilmed some Vermont probate series.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Proprietary grant / metes-and-bounds.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Split across three authorities — New Hampshire State Archives (grants 1749–1764), New York State Archives (re-grants 1764–1777), Vermont State Archives (Republic charters 1777–1791).
- **Critical quirk:** In Vermont, deeds are recorded at the town clerk's office, not the county courthouse.
- **Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule:** Enumerates approximately 1,800 grantees; the earliest systematic resident list for the future state (FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War (1775–1783).
- **Record types:** Vermont militia rolls (Vermont State Archives, Vermont Historical Society); Continental Army service records (NARA / Fold3); pension files (NARA / Fold3 / Ancestry); bounty land warrants (NARA).

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/); coverage is volunteer-driven and uneven for 1750–1791.
- **Physical records:** DAR gravestone transcriptions at DAR Library and Vermont Historical Society.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Vermont Gazette (Bennington, est. 1781); Vermont Journal (Windsor, est. 1783).
- **Where held:** Vermont Historical Society; some issues on Newspapers.com and Chronicling America.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** Most pre-statehood Vermont settlers migrated overland from other colonies. Passenger arrival records are not a primary source. Look for origins in colony-of-departure records (Connecticut, Massachusetts, New Hampshire).

### Tax records
- **Types:** Town grand lists (annual property assessments); Republic of Vermont levied taxes from 1778.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices; Vermont State Archives.
- **Substitute value:** Grand lists are one of the best substitutes for missing vital records and pre-1790 census coverage.

### Proprietary and town records
- **Proprietors' records:** Minute books of original grantees predate town records and name earliest settlers.
- **Town meeting minutes:** Name voters, officeholders, and those receiving poor relief.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices, Vermont State Archives, Vermont Historical Society.
- **Town histories:** 19th-century volumes (1860–1900) often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records (per FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki).

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 1790 federal census (indexed); some church records and probate series via Catalog; Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule documented on wiki | Free |
| Ancestry | 1790 federal census; some Revolutionary War records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War service records, pension files, bounty land warrants | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Some early Vermont newspaper issues | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal military records, pension files | Free to visit; some digitized |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|

This survey covers a place called Vermont during roughly the last forty years before it became a U.S. state in 1791. During those decades, the territory was first part of a New Hampshire land-grant system, then claimed by New York, and finally run as an independent republic starting in 1777. Because no statewide vital records (birth, marriage, death registrations) existed at all until 1857, researchers working in this period must rely on church baptism and burial registers, town-level land and tax records held at individual town clerk offices (not county courthouses, which is the key Vermont difference from other states), a specialized 1771 land-grant list that names nearly 1,800 early grantees, and 19th-century published town histories that reprinted early records. The 1790 federal census is the only census covering this window, and it names only heads of household. The most important repositories are the Vermont State Archives, Vermont Historical Society, each individual town clerk office, and — for the contested land-grant period — archives in New Hampshire and New York as well.

Next, a research plan can be built using this locality survey as its foundation, targeting the specific town and county where your ancestors lived.

jurisdictions.name: Province of New Hampshire (New Hampshire Grants)

quirks: Deeds in Vermont are recorded at the town clerk office, not the county courthouse — every deed search must go to the specific town where the land was located.

The 1771 Grant Survey Schedule enumerates approximately 1,800 grantees of New Hampshire grants that New York refused to recognize; it predates any Vermont civil registration and is the earliest systematic resident list for the future state (per the FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki page).
Statewide civil registration did not begin until 1857. Town clerk vital records (some back to the 1770s) survive unevenly — contact each town clerk directly.

An ancestor's land title may appear across three separate repository systems: New Hampshire State Archives (grants pre-1764), New York State Archives (re-grants 1764-1777), and Vermont State Archives (Republic charters 1777-1791); search all three.

County boundaries were adjusted several times between 1778 and 1791 as new counties were created; an event may be filed under the original county or its successor — determine which county existed at the event date.

Vermont's northern border adjoins Quebec/Canada; a small number of Loyalist families crossed north during and after the Revolution. Vermont also borders New Hampshire (east), Massachusetts (south), and New York (west) — check adjoining jurisdictions for families near any border.

19th-century Vermont town histories (most published 1860-1900) often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access (per the FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki page) — consult these before making archive visits.
Town grand lists (annual property assessments at the town level) are the primary substitute for missing census coverage before 1790; they survive from the late 1770s for many towns.
The 1790 federal census was conducted June-August 1790, before Vermont's March 1791 statehood; it names only heads of household, with all other members counted but not named.
No state census was conducted by the Republic of Vermont; militia rolls and town grand lists serve as substitutes for intercensal population evidence.

# Locality Guide: Vermont, United States (Pre-Statehood, c. 1750–1791)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Vermont was admitted as the 14th state on March 4, 1791. Before that it existed as the independent Republic of Vermont (1777–1791), and before that the territory was contested between the Province of New Hampshire, the Province of New York, and independent settlers under the New Hampshire Grants (granted by Governor Benning Wentworth of New Hampshire beginning in 1749).
- **Administrative center during Republic period:** Windsor (first capital); Montpelier became the permanent capital after statehood.
- **Parent jurisdictions:** Province of New Hampshire (grants issued 1749–1764); Province of New York (claimed authority 1764–1777, never accepted by most settlers); Republic of Vermont (independent, 1777–1791).
- **Population during period:** The first federal census (1790) enumerated Vermont's population at approximately 85,341; that figure reflects the immediate pre-statehood era. No tool-returned population figure is available before 1791.
- **Economy:** Subsistence agriculture, timber, potash production, and small-scale trade. Settlement was frontier-era; many towns were just being incorporated in the 1770s–1780s.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly settlers of English descent migrating from Connecticut, Massachusetts, and New Hampshire. Small numbers of Scots-Irish and Dutch settlers.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist (dominant), Baptist, Methodist (arriving later in the period), Anglican/Episcopal (smaller presence). Quaker meetings existed in some communities.
- **Key historical events:** New Hampshire Grants dispute (1749–1777); Green Mountain Boys resistance to New York authority; American Revolution; Vermont Constitution of 1777 (first in North America to prohibit adult slavery and grant universal male suffrage); Republic of Vermont operates 1777–1791.

## Boundary changes
Three overlapping jurisdictional claims defined this period:
1. Before 1764: New Hampshire issued over 100 township grants. Records in New Hampshire colonial files.
2. 1764–1777: British Crown ruled territory fell under New York. New York re-granted many of the same lands; records in New York State Archives.
3. 1777–1791: Republic of Vermont operated independently, issuing its own land charters and court records — held in Vermont repositories.
Counties were established by the Republic's General Assembly beginning in 1778; pre-county records follow town-level and proprietary records. County boundaries were adjusted several times 1779–1791.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Statewide civil registration began in 1857 (FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy). No statewide registration existed during the pre-statehood period.
- **What exists for 1750–1791:** Some town clerk offices hold earlier town-level vital records dating back to the 1770s, but these survive unevenly; consult town clerk offices directly.
- **Where held:** Individual town clerk offices; Vermont State Archives holds some compiled early vital records.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records, family Bible records, published town histories, gravestone inscriptions, proprietors' records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregationalist (most numerous and best-documented), Baptist, Methodist, Anglican/Episcopal, Quaker.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, membership lists, disciplinary proceedings.
- **Where held:** Originating congregation; denominational archives (Congregationalist records at Congregational Library, Boston; Baptist records at American Baptist Historical Society); FamilySearch has microfilmed some Vermont church records.
- **Language:** English.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1790 federal census is the only federal census within the pre-statehood window. Names heads of household only; all other members are counted, not named. Indexed and available online at Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- **Republic of Vermont enumerations:** No systematic statewide enumeration identified. Tax lists and militia rolls serve as substitutes.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships, court minutes.
- **Jurisdiction level:** County-level from 1778 when counties were organized; before 1778, town-level records or no formal probate.
- **Where held:** Vermont Probate Court districts; Vermont State Archives. FamilySearch has microfilmed some Vermont probate series.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Proprietary grant / metes-and-bounds.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Split across three authorities — New Hampshire State Archives (grants 1749–1764), New York State Archives (re-grants 1764–1777), Vermont State Archives (Republic charters 1777–1791).
- **Critical quirk:** In Vermont, deeds are recorded at the town clerk's office, not the county courthouse.
- **Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule:** Enumerates approximately 1,800 grantees; the earliest systematic resident list for the future state (FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War (1775–1783).
- **Record types:** Vermont militia rolls (Vermont State Archives, Vermont Historical Society); Continental Army service records (NARA / Fold3); pension files (NARA / Fold3 / Ancestry); bounty land warrants (NARA).

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/); coverage is volunteer-driven and uneven for 1750–1791.
- **Physical records:** DAR gravestone transcriptions at DAR Library and Vermont Historical Society.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Vermont Gazette (Bennington, est. 1781); Vermont Journal (Windsor, est. 1783).
- **Where held:** Vermont Historical Society; some issues on Newspapers.com and Chronicling America.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** Most pre-statehood Vermont settlers migrated overland from other colonies. Passenger arrival records are not a primary source. Look for origins in colony-of-departure records (Connecticut, Massachusetts, New Hampshire).

### Tax records
- **Types:** Town grand lists (annual property assessments); Republic of Vermont levied taxes from 1778.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices; Vermont State Archives.
- **Substitute value:** Grand lists are one of the best substitutes for missing vital records and pre-1790 census coverage.

### Proprietary and town records
- **Proprietors' records:** Minute books of original grantees predate town records and name earliest settlers.
- **Town meeting minutes:** Name voters, officeholders, and those receiving poor relief.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices, Vermont State Archives, Vermont Historical Society.
- **Town histories:** 19th-century volumes (1860–1900) often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records (per FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki).

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 1790 federal census (indexed); some church records and probate series via Catalog; Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule documented on wiki | Free |
| Ancestry | 1790 federal census; some Revolutionary War records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War service records, pension files, bounty land warrants | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Some early Vermont newspaper issues | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal military records, pension files | Free to visit; some digitized |
